News.title: Jewish Greens chair says she could leave party over 'Zionism is racism' motion
News.content:
The chair of Jewish Greens Vivien Lichtenstein has told the BBC it is "quite possible" she will leave the party after Green members adopted a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism.

The motion, which has divided senior party figures, also backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

It has been condemned by some Jewish groups and Israel's foreign ministry.

Asked by BBC Radio 4's Today programme about her future, Lichtenstein said: "I haven't decided yet...It is quite possible that I will leave the party...I'm giving it a little time and to talk with colleagues."

Lichtenstein, who is a former chair of her local party, said she had opposed the motion from the first time she heard about it.

"I don't think it's helpful and it doesn't make any difference whatsoever to Palestinians in Gaza who have suffered devastation, orphans left behind, it doesn't make any difference to Palestinians in the West Bank who are currently suffering, are currently being attacked and killed."

Members of the Green Party of England and Wales endorsed the policy motion, which was put forward by a group of activists at the party's conference in Brighton, by 1,022 votes to 813.

There are 230,000 members of the Green party overall and not everyone attended the conference.

The party's leader Zack Polanski, who is himself Jewish, had called for the motion to be amended to add in protections for Jewish members and remove language referring to a "single democratic Palestinian State". Both of these amendments were defeated.

Polanski did not stay at conference to vote on either this or the substantive motion. He left early to campaign in Holborn and St Pancras, where he is standing in a by-election to be the MP. A full list of candidates in the contest can be found here.

The motion, among other statements, "supports the establishment of a single democratic Palestinian State in all of historic Palestine with Jerusalem as its capital, equal rights for all, and the right of return for Palestinians and their descendants".

It defines Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state".

The Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership Council, which criticised the motion, said "Zionism is anti-racism, creating a refuge for Jews in their ancient homeland after millennia of persecution outside it".

Lichtenstein said she defines herself as "both Zionist and anti-Zionist" depending on the definition, and said a problem with the motion is that there are many definitions.

She said she was not concerned about "people accusing me of supporting Israel's right to exist and therefore I'm a racist, which of course is not the case", but said the "very bad motion...crosses a line".

One way in which it did that, she said, was that the proposers said they had consulted some Jews, but did not consult the Jewish Greens, who would have made some amendments to improve the motion.

She said there was a "vast range" of opinions among Jewish Greens, some who supported the motion entirely, others who supported aspects, and others who were against it. Some Jewish Greens also support one state, she added.

She said that party policy was that "it's up to Israelis and Palestinians to choose their future - one state or two".

Last month, the UK and 11 allies reiterated their support for a two-state solution, which would recognise a Palestinian state alongside an Israeli one. Israel rejects a two-state solution.

Her concern with the motion was that the Green Party may accuse UK, Israeli, or Jewish organisations, including those that partner with Palestinians, of racism. She said she supports many of these groups working "against the occupation and even go out on the ground to assist Palestinians".

She said she knows of some non-Jews who are planning on not staying in the party because "they think the motion crosses a line" and also because of their work, if they might not be able to be associated with a party that has "Zionism is racism" as a policy.

Asked whether she believed there were antisemites inside the party, including at senior levels, she said "there are certainly some antisemites in the party, I don't know about at senior level, that is not my experience".

News.title: Southport Inquiry: Violent material left online for weeks
News.content:
This phase of the inquiry is examining how the risks posed by violence-fixated individuals can be managed, and the role the internet and social media play in influencing and enabling them.

Nicholas Moss KC, counsel to the inquiry, said: "The report outlines the result of a single eight-hour search across a selection of online platforms including X, TikTok, Reddit, Instagram and Discord.

"It is right to recognise that there was a spectrum of material of concern.

"It ranges from material with violent overtones, but which might be argued to be newsworthy, to material which can fairly be categorised as very violent or strong gore material."

Moss said 98.9% of the material was publicly accessible and 92.3% was not subject to any age restrictions.

All of the material was reported to the platforms, but a week later 87.9% of it remained live, the inquiry heard.

Moss said 14 days after it had been reported, 83.8% of the content was still available.

He said the platform providers would be asked about the report and "what appears to be, in some cases, arguable delay and failures to remove the material even when it had been reported to them".

Representatives of platforms, including TikTok, Reddit, X and Alphabet, the parent company of Google, are expected to give evidence to the inquiry in November.

News.title: Pickford 'almost caused crash' with careless driving
News.content:
England goalkeeper Jordan Pickford nearly caused a crash with two other cars during a bout of careless driving in his Â£200,000 Lamborghini supercar, a court has heard.

The 32-year-old was pulled over by police after ignoring a give way sign, forcing two cars to slam on the brakes, and then speeding off into the distance.

The incident happened in the Cheshire town of Knutsford on 14 April, sparking a criminal prosecution for driving without due care or attention.

Pickford, who has 336 appearances for Everton and 92 England caps, has pleaded guilty to the charge and will next appear at Chester Magistrates' Court on 7 December.

According to court documents, PC Cecil Ricardo, from Cheshire Police, said he had just left the station when he saw Pickford's blue Lamborghini Urus complete with personalised number plates.

"I was stationary on Bexton Road, Knutsford, waiting for traffic signals to turn green," he wrote.

"I then witnessed a blue Lamborghini Urus driving along Princess Street.

"It reached the junction with Toft Road, completely ignored the give way lines and pulled onto Toft Road causing two vehicles to slam on their brakes to avoid a collision.

"The Lamborghini then sped down Toft Road, Knutsford."

News.title: Kemi Badenoch vows to build £10bn ‘Britannia Shield’ to fend off missile attacks
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Kemi Badenoch has pledged to build Britain its own £10bn ‘Iron Dome’ missile interception system aimed at protecting the UK from future military attacks.

“The world will not wait for Britain to get ready,” the Tory leader announced at the third day of the party’s annual conference in Birmingham, pointing to the transformational effect of cheap drones on the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East.

Ms Badenoch said: “If a missile or drone is launched at Britain, we do not get a second chance to wish we had prepared. That is why today we are announcing Britannia Shield — a new national missile-and-drone defence system to protect the whole United Kingdom, our sovereign territories and British bases overseas.”

The Conservatives would aim to have Britannia Shield fully operational by the end of their first term in government if elected at the next general election. Ms Badenoch has also vowed to bring defence spending up to three per cent of GDP by 2030 by reinstating the two-child benefit cap and reforming housing benefit.

open image in gallery Explosions from projectile interceptions by Israel's Iron Dome missile defence system are pictured over Tel Aviv on February 28 ( AFP/Getty )

James Cartlidge, the shadow defence secretary, is expected to unveil further details for ‘Britannia Shield’ at party conference on Tuesday. He will say that new investment is needed in advanced radar and interceptor missiles due to “the threats that we face” today, as reported by The Guardian.

Mr Cartlidge will give a timeline of five years for the system to come online at a ‘minimum deployable capability’, it is understood. Further improvements would follow over the five years thereafter.

The system is understood to be modelled on Israel’s Iron Dome defence system, which has played a key role in shooting down incoming threats from Iran, Hamas and Hezbollah. Its maker, Rafael, claimed in May the Iron Dome successfully intercepted 99 per cent of its targets since 2023.

Britannia Shield would bring together radar, command systems and interceptor missiles into an integrated network, giving the UK better reach to target foreign threats.

The UK defence committee warned late last year that Britain had “next to nothing” in terms of integrated air and missile defences, and pointed to the growing prevalence of aerial drone threats.

open image in gallery Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch unveiled her philosophy for government in a document titled The Right Way ( PA Wire )

Britain lacks missile interceptors like the US Patriots, which have proven vital in Ukraine’s defence against Russian missiles, and would currently rely on its six Type 45 destroyer ships for missile interceptions.

All six are due to be replaced with hybrid Common Combat Vessels by 2038 after plans for a guided missile destroyer were scrapped in June. Only three were operational in January 2026.

Labour has committed to spending at least 3.5 per cent of GDP on defence by 2035 - but at the end of August it was reported that new chancellor John Healey, who resigned as defence secretary in June over the lack of funding for the military, was expected to scrap his own target of spending 3 per cent by 2030 in the upcoming October budget.

open image in gallery HMS Duncan, a Type 45 or Daring-class air-defence destroyer ( Getty )

The government has set aside £298bn of investment over the next four years to improve defences in line with the Strategic Defence Review. But just £790m has been dedicated to protecting the UK and its bases overseas from air, drone and missile threats.

Dr Sidharth Kaushal, Senior Research Fellow, Sea Power, at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), assessed last year that based on current trends, improving UK national defences against subsonic cruise missiles should take precedence until 2030.

He urged a sequenced approach to developing interceptor capabilities, matching investment with the evolving threat and making use of existing multipurpose systems, as well as more bespoke options.

News.title: Jeffrey Archer: A gift for self-publicity but dogged by scandal – he was the nearly man of British politics
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Jeffrey Archer’s vivid and erratic political career, dogged by scandal and beset by obstacles, ended in July 2001, with the ultimate disgrace of him being imprisoned for four years for perjury and perverting the course of justice.

An Old Bailey jury found that he had lied in a libel action he had brought against the Daily Star newspaper 13 years earlier, in which he was awarded £500,000 damages.

And within hours of his arrival at Belmarsh top-security prison in south-east London, questions were being asked at the highest level about the whereabouts of the millions of pounds he allegedly raised for the Kurds and other causes, amid rising suspicion that little, if any, of it reached its proper destination.

Before his humiliating downfall, he was the nearly man of the British political scene.

His undisputed talents as a political cheerleader, his searing ambition and his dogged resolve to succeed often brought him close to where he wanted to go, but always short of the target he set himself – which was the top.

And whenever he was in sight of these targets, some grisly newspaper revelation would bring him plummeting, like a meteor, down to earth again, sometimes in disgrace.

open image in gallery Archer has died aged 86 ( PA )

But he also enjoyed the reputation of being the India rubber ball man of British politics. Whenever things went disastrously wrong – as they did from time to time – Archer was usually adept at bouncing back.

But the events which led to his Old Bailey trial and subsequent conviction were more than even a man of his Houdini skills could escape from.

He made millions out of his best-selling novels, became – at Margaret Thatcher’s insistence – deputy chairman of the Conservative Party, and he was the runaway Tory choice for the first mayor of London – an opportunity which collapsed in ruins when the perjury allegations landed on his doorstep.

Ambition was rooted in Jeffrey Archer – later to become Lord Archer of Weston-super-Mare – from an early age. He once said that when he was three he wanted to be four, and when he was four he wanted to be Prime Minister.

This brash young man had no hesitation in telling people whom he thought were destined to become Tory leaders: “I would very much like to be a member of your administration.”

Nor did he have any illusions about his chequered career. Indeed, he sometimes traded on it. Once he cheerfully told an audience that was electing a Tory candidate for the London mayoralty: “I’m no saint. If you want a saint don’t pick me.”

But they picked him nevertheless, only to see their choice yet again tumble from grace and fall by the wayside.

Jeffrey Howard Archer was born an only child on April 15 1940, in Weston-super-Mare, to William and Lola.

open image in gallery Archer with his mother, Lola ( PA )

After completing his education at Wellington School in Somerset, Archer arrived at Oxford in October 1963. He went for a one-year course, the Diploma in Education, but ended up staying for three years, just as though he were a typical undergraduate.

The Oxford Department of Education had a “semi-detached” status with the university in the 1960s which explained why some people were convinced that Archer was never really at Oxford University.

But as one of his biographers pointed out, education students were, and remain, full members of the universities, even if their tutors were not accepted as Oxford dons.

Archer was enrolled into Oxford University in October 1963 and his name appears in the university calendar for 1964 under Brasenose College. His Who’s Who entry implied that he graduated from Brasenose, which is not strictly correct.

Archer, an accomplished sprinter, won his first athletics blue in the varsity match of May 1964, running in both the 100 and 220 yards.

open image in gallery Jeffrey Archer attended Brasenose College, Oxford, and earned a blue in athletics ( PA )

That spring he was on the verge of international recognition and was picked for the Great Britain A side, a second team, against the Benelux countries. But his dreams of becoming an Olympic athlete were never realised.

Later, he was to launch a public relations and fundraising firm, Arrow Enterprises.

He entered politics in 1967, a year after leaving Oxford, when he secured a seat on the Greater London Council. Two years later he won a resounding by-election victory for the Tories.

He had made a fortune from his business and was about to forge a glittering political career. But then in 1974 came what he later referred to as “by far the worst thing that ever happened to me”.

Unwittingly caught up in the collapse of Aquablast, a fraudulent Canadian industrial cleaning company, he was suddenly brought to the brink of bankruptcy.

In an attempt to earn some money he set about writing a novel, drawing on the experience of his financial disaster.

The result, Not A Penny More, Not A Penny Less, was an instant best seller and launched him on a new path to riches as a writer.

open image in gallery Jeffrey Archer and his wife Mary leaving the High Court, in London, in 1987 after winning record damages at the time of £500,000 for the libel action against The Star Newspaper ( PA )

His books, which also included Kane and Abel, The Prodigal Daughter and First Among Equals, sold millions of copies around the world and made him a millionaire.

Archer had a gift for self-publicity, and for keeping himself in the public eye and on the front pages of the newspapers. He maintained his links with the Conservative Party, where he was adored by the women members. Archer was in regular demand as a speech-maker and fete-opener all over the country.

In short, he was the darling of important sections of the party. But there were those who regarded him as an unsafe pair of hands and too erratic to be entrusted with the kind of political post for which he yearned.

Even so, Margaret Thatcher had faith in him, and in 1985, despite his chequered history, she appointed him deputy chairman of the party, despite the serious reservations of the then chairman, Norman Tebbit. The prime minister admired Archer as a model Tory high achiever.

He more than once blotted his copybook, on one occasion saying publicly: “Would you buy a used car from this government?” – his own government. He later explained that he was merely trying to point out the government’s bad public image, and that he had been misunderstood.

But a year after his appointment his rise in the world of politics was abruptly halted for the second time – on this occasion by scandal.

He was forced to resign over what he described as a “lack of judgment” after sending £2,000 via an intermediary to the prostitute, Monica Coghlan, who was to die in a road accident a few years later.

He maintained he paid the money only to help Miss Coghlan escape hounding reporters by going abroad, and sued newspapers that suggested otherwise – bringing an action that netted £500,000 in damages. This was the case in which the judge, ill-advisedly many thought, spoke about Archer’s “fragrant” wife, Mary.

Once more, Archer had managed to turn adversity to his advantage, and soon he had regained political influence.

open image in gallery Then-prime minister Margaret Thatcher with Jeffrey Archer in 1986 when he was deputy chairman of the Conservative Party ( PA )

He remained an energetic, campaigning figure within the party. He was still as much in demand as a Tory speaker, nationwide, as even the prime ministers whom he served.

During the 1992 general election he became the Tory Party’s unofficial cheerleader. In the run-up to polling day he was never far from John Major’s side, warming up his audiences, giving advice and carrying his bags – in effect, doing his old job.

He was created a life peer in 1992, and was typically a brash and effective operator in the Upper Chamber. This was at least one of his many ambitions fulfilled.

But there was more scandal to come in 1994, involving the buying of shares in Anglia Television where his wife was a director. Days later the company announced a takeover bid and Archer sold the shares at a profit of £77,000. He denied insider trading and made claims which many seemed to think conflicting.

However, no action was recommended after an inquiry. And three years later he was told that the Department of Trade and Industry had decided there was no evidence to justify a new inquiry into the affair. Even so, it was another besmirching of his character.

In the following election in 1997, the year of Labour’s massive landslide victory, Archer was constantly warning about the effects Sir James Goldsmith’s Referendum Party would have on Tory fortunes. In the event, Labour’s triumph was so overwhelming that the impact of the Referendum Party on the outcome was virtually non-existent.

open image in gallery Archer was jailed in July 2001 ( PA )

However, many (not least himself) would have liked to have seen him as the Tory Party chairman during that disastrous campaign. Brian Mawhinney was ineffectual and unpopular and it was widely believed that Archer, with his massive enthusiasm and organisational skills would at least have reduced the calamitous scale of the Conservative Party’s rout.

But even the scale of that defeat did not – as it did many other Tory politicians – temper his frenetic political activities. He was made of sterner stuff.

Soon he was campaigning with characteristic vigour for the mayoralty of London – but some eyebrows were raised among Tory grandees about the suitability of Lord Archer as the Conservatives’ official candidate for this new, powerful and very high-profile role.

Undaunted by this and also by a smear campaign which was running against him, Lord Archer vowed that if elected he would clean up London and restore free milk to schoolchildren.

He had spent nearly two years travelling the globe, meeting other mayors – an odyssey which impressed the party leadership.

But there was still a nagging feeling that although he was easily the best cheerleader the Tories had, his unpredictable style was likely to land the party and himself in more embarrassment and trouble.

But he ran out an easy winner as the Tory candidate, gaining the backing of William Hague, the party leader and, even more importantly, that of Baroness Thatcher.

His supporters always said that his very charisma and enthusiasm would have more than compensated for the risks he might have posed.

The new job of being mayor of London was something Archer highly prized, especially as a man who had been rejected so often in the past because of what was becoming known as his colourful political career.

But this, too, ended in tears. A new scandal forced him to quit the candidacy for mayor and he was subsequently expelled from the party for five years.

Just as the London mayor campaign was getting under way, a newspaper claimed that shortly before the 1987 libel trial involving the Daily Star, he had asked an old friend, Ted Francis, to provide a false alibi for the night which Archer allegedly spent with Monica Coghlan – something which he always denied.

open image in gallery Archer with John Major, left, in 1996 ( PA )

The alibi was never used in the suit, which ended with Archer winning £500,000 damages plus £700,000 costs, which the paper, in 2000 was trying to recover, plus the interest. By then it would have been worth about £3 million.

But late in September 2000, Archer was charged with two counts of perjury, two counts of perverting the course of justice and one of falsifying documents. Archer was convicted, but Francis, his friend, whom Archer had allegedly asked to lie for him, was acquitted on one count of perverting the course of justice.

While serving his four-year sentence, Archer continued to write frenetically. He was also photographed umpiring prison cricket matches, and towards the end of his sentence was given an “outside” job helping behind the scenes at the Lincoln Theatre Royal.

But that job soon collapsed when he was found to have attended a drinks party at the home of Tory MP Gillian Shephard, in breach of the conditions of his weekend pass.

He was finally released on parole on July 21 2003, after serving two years and two days of his sentence. He decided, for the purposes of his probationary period, to make his home his penthouse flat in central London rather than his Cambridgeshire family home.

Within two months of his release, Archer delivered his first public speech since his freedom, addressing the Howard League of Penal Reform, with some recommendations on changes in the prison regime. But he insisted he was not a prison reformer.

open image in gallery Archer (right) with actors Ian McKellen (center) and Prunella Scales, and radio and TV personality Ned Sherrin ( PA )

By coincidence, the day on which Archer was charged he made his stage debut at Windsor in a courtroom drama he wrote himself called The Accused in which the audience were asked to determine whether he was guilty of murder or not.

But after a reasonably successful provincial run, the play flopped in the West End. It was playing to half-empty houses in the Haymarket Theatre before a decision was taken to cut the run short in January, 2001.

He had earlier made a successful debut as a playwright with Beyond Reasonable Doubt in 1987.

Not content with writing for the stage, he then decided to own one. He paid £1.2 million for a majority stake in London’s Playhouse Theatre in 1988, selling it four years later for £2.4 million.

In 2023, it was announced that Archer’s Kane and Abel book trilogy was to be adapted for television as a major new series by the producers of Sex Education.

Earlier this year, Archer was announced as a speaker for the Queen’s Reading Room festival at Chatsworth in Derbyshire.

Archer’s involvement with charity work extended from persuading the Beatles to help raise money for Oxfam while he was still at Oxford to his promotion of the Simple Truth concert, which was seen by more than 200 million people around the world and allegedly raised millions for Kurdish refugees following the Gulf War.

Archer remained in the House of Lords until his retirement in 2024.

Archer’s last book, Adam and Eve, is described by Harper Collins as “a breathtaking epic of courage, sacrifice and love forged in Britain’s darkest hour”.

When asked why he decided it would be his last book, he told the BBC in recent days on a visit to his former school: “I think everybody would like to run their last 100 metres at the Olympics and win the gold medal. I think the clever thing about life is to know when to get out.”

He married his wife, Mary, a professor of biochemistry at Imperial College, London, in 1966. She stood by him through all his trials and tribulations. The couple lived in Grantchester, Cambridgeshire, made famous by poet Rupert Brooke. They had two sons.

News.title: The gap between Americans identifying as Democrats over Republicans hasn’t been this wide since 2009
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

As both parties gear up for the midterm elections, the gap between Americans identifying as Democrats and Republicans has widened by more than 10 percentage points.

Fifty percent of Americans identified as Democrats or Democratic leaners, according to a new Gallup poll. This is 11 points higher than the 39 percent of Americans who identified as Republicans or Republican leaners in the third quarter of 2026.

The 11-point lead is the largest quarterly margin Democrats have recorded since the first quarter of 2009, poll aggregator Interactive Polls wrote on X Monday. At the time, former Democratic President Barack Obama had taken office after winning his first election, flipping nine states.

While the party in power typically loses congressional seats during the midterm elections, new polling shows just how much Democrats are gaining ground in Senate races in five red states just weeks before voters cast their ballots. This means Republicans will have to fight harder to keep seats that would normally be easy to win.

open image in gallery As both parties gear up for the midterm elections, the gap between Americans identifying as Democrats over Republicans has widened by more than 10 percentage points ( AFP via Getty Images )

Democrat James Talarico is leading Republican Ken Paxton 51 to 45 percent in Texas, according to New York Times/Siena University polls released Monday.

Democrat Mary Peltola is beating Republican Dan Sullivan 50 to 43 percent in Alaska and Democrat Sherrod Brown is beating Republican Jon Husted in Ohio 49 to 46 percent, according to the polls.

Iowa and Kansas are also seeing tight races. Republican Ashley Hinson is leading Josh Turek 48 to 47 percent and Democrat Adam Hamilton and Roger Marshall are tied at 45 percent in Kansas, the polls show.

The new polling favoring Democrats is a significant shift in public sentiment from when President Donald Trump won the 2024 election.

After he defeated then-Vice President Kamala Harris, Trump boasted about the “unprecedented and powerful” mandate the American people gave him as the Democratic Party was left to figure out what went wrong.

open image in gallery The new polling favoring Democrats is a significant shift in public sentiment from when President Donald Trump won the 2024 election ( Getty Images )

Trump had polled higher than Harris on major issues such as immigration and the economy.

But nearly two years into his second term as president, Trump faces a record-low approval rating amid a costly and unpopular war in Iran and scrutiny over how aggressive federal agents have been in carrying out his massive deportation of illegal immigrants.

The president has gone as far as to offer Americans a $5,000 “Trump Dividend” if voters help Republicans keep control of Congress, which he first announced during an usual two-day convention in Dallas that he headlined to drum up support for GOP candidates. Critics have accused Trump’s promise of $5,000 checks of amounting to bribery.

On Sunday, Trump wrote on Truth Social, “The Polls have ALWAYS underestimated MAGA.”

News.title: Trump says ‘threats’ led to US decision to remove bombers from RAF Fairford
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Donald Trump said on Monday that the United States pulled its strategic bomber warplanes out of RAF Fairford due to undisclosed “threats”.

“We actually know the people who made the threat,” the US president told reporters outside the White House, a day after the Pentagon confirmed it was removing aircraft from the base in the UK.

Asked whether there was a specific decision that led to the withdrawal, Mr Trump said: “Yeah I think we can say that. They didn’t fly out by accident. There were some threats.”

“Rather than tempting the enemy, we'll capture the enemy and beat the enemy. But why should we leave him there? So we moved him around a little bit. Not very far,” he went on.

The airbase was recently the target of a suspected terror attack. Five British men in their 20s were arrested after being seen running into fields from three vans parked near the base on September 27.

open image in gallery Donald Trump speaks to reporters on Monday ( AP )

Police said no explosive devices were found but a quantity of petrol was present.

The men have since been released on bail. A sixth man, a dual UK-Iranian national arrested on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts four days later, has also been released on bail.

Mr Trump said at the time of the first arrests that the plot had planned "big damage" and that it might have been connected to Iran. The US president later said he would not have released the suspects on bail.

Asked on Monday whether the UK was a safe place for US assets, Mr Trump said: “I think it is, and I have a very good relationship with your new prime minister, who's very good.

“He's liberal, very liberal, but I hear he's going to open up North Sea oil if he does that in Aberdeen. If he does that, you're going to have a rich country. If he doesn't, you're going to have a bankrupt country.”

Earlier on Monday, vice president JD Vance said that the decision to move B-1 bombers from a British airbase was done out of an abundance of caution after a suspected Iranian plot at the site last week.

open image in gallery A US Air Force Rockwell B-1 Lancer bomber at RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire last month ( PA Wire )

“We do feel with some confidence that the Iranians are, you know, they're trying to do what the Iranian state has done for 49 years, which is engaged in acts of terrorism against the United States (and others), so we are being extremely cautious, and that's all I'd say about that.”

But secretary of state Marco Rubio said there was no direct link between the sudden removal of the bombers and the suspected Iranian plot.

He said the Pentagon is “constantly reallocating resources where they need to be”, and that the US still has confidence in the security of all its bases.

A Nato military source told Reuters on Monday that it is still believed that Iran “poses an acute threat to US assets in the UK”.

While much about the incident remains unexplained, British prime minister Andy Burnham said any plot was likely backed by Iran.

For its part, Iran has said accusations that it was involved in any plot are baseless.

open image in gallery Marco Rubio said there was no direct link between the sudden removal of the bombers and the suspected Iranian plot ( AP )

Foreign minister Abbas Araqchi wrote on X last week: “I can confirm Iran's belief that releasing supposed terrorists working for foreign states really says it all. You're barking up the wrong tree.”

Fairford, located 90 miles (145 km) west of London, is one of the most important in Europe for the US, being one of only a few suitable for heavy bombers such as the B-1 aircraft.

It has played a key role in previous US campaigns in the Middle East, although its bombers are not stationed there permanently.

News.title: Myleene Klass reveals why she won’t join Hear’Say for 25th anniversary reunion tour
News.content:
Myleene Klass has revealed why she won’t be joining her fellow Hear'Say band members for their upcoming reunion tour.

The naughtiest band have announced they will be returning for a tour to mark 25 years since their number one record Pure & Simple.

Following the announcement last week, fans noticed Myleene was absent from the line-up, which includes band members Kym Marsh, Suzanne Shaw, Noel Sullivan and Danny Foster.

Myleene was quizzed about the tour when she appeared on Loose Women on Monday (5 September).

She explained: “They were really sweet and they did include me in the discussions but it’s not something I can commit to at the moment, I just really can’t.”

News.title: Phil Collins shares update on 24-year grudge with Paul McCartney
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Phil Collins has shared an update on the status of his relationship with Paul McCartney.

Collins, 75, and McCartney, 84, have been feuding since 2002 when the Beatle made a comment about the “In the Air” singer at the 2002 Queen’s Jubilee Concert.

Speaking on a recent episode of the Piers Morgan Uncensored podcast, Collins recalled of the initial exchange: “We had a rehearsal at Buckingham Palace and I had a first edition Hunter Davies book [on The Beatles], which was very quite rare. I took it to the rehearsal so Paul could sign it… Paul came up behind with Heather Mills, who he was married to at that point, and I said, ‘Paul, could you sign this?’

“He probably didn’t mean it like it sounded, but he said, ‘He’s a big Beatle fan, is our little Phil,’” Collins continued. “And I thought, ‘You asshole.’ I couldn’t help it. That’s just what I thought.”

Collins added of being stung by the remark: “I knew Paul. This wasn’t the first time I met him. I played on one of his albums. I played live with him with the Prince’s Trust. I’d given him an award at an award show in London, so I kind of knew him. So I was kind of surprised at that particular tone of reply.”

Phil Collins has shared an update on the status of his friendship with Paul McCartney ( Getty )

The “Sussudio” singer wrote about the incident in his 2016 memoir, Not Dead Yet, noting that McCartney had reached out via email but Collins did not reply.

He told Billboard in October of that year: “He's been in touch about it because he was upset. I certainly didn't get any flowers from him; I got more of a ‘Let's just get on with our lives.’ And I'm sorry he's upset that I kinda said something nasty about him - well, it wasn't really nasty. If people don't tell people that sometimes their attitude could be a bit better then you're not gonna get any better, y’know?”

Speaking to Morgan, Collins shared an update after McCartney recently got in touch after learning the Genesis band member was collecting memorabilia for a King’s Trust charity auction.

“He said, ‘While we’re on the phone.’ I thought, ‘Oh, here we go,’” Collins recalled to Morgan. “So he said, ‘What is all this about?’ I said, ‘I wish I’d never said it, Paul. I wish I’d never said it.’ He said, ‘I thought we were good, you know.’”

“I said I was sorry, because I really didn’t wish him…” Collins said before trailing off. “I mean, obviously, this had been bugging him because he likes to be liked, as we all do! Maybe him more than some other people. But we all like to be liked. I understand that.”

News.title: Jeffrey Archer, novelist and former Conservative MP, dies aged 86
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Bestselling author and former politician Jeffrey Archer has died at the age of 86, his publisher has said.

Harper Collins said he died "suddenly and peacefully at his home between writing sessions" on Monday.

He spent five years as a Conservative MP prior to serving as the party’s deputy chairman.

He had a successful career as a novelist alongside politics and was made a life peer in 1992 as Lord Archer of Weston-super-Mare, becoming the Conservatives’ choice to fight for the party in the first London mayoral election.

But his campaign ended when his political career crashed in 2001 with the disgrace of his being imprisoned for four years for perjury and perverting the course of justice.

An Old Bailey jury ruled he had lied during a libel suit against The Star newspaper 13 years prior, where he had been awarded £500,000 in damages.

Following an early release in 2003, he rejoined the House of Lords until retiring in 2024.

open image in gallery Alongside politics, he built a successful career as a novelist and became a life peer in 1992 ( PA )

Archer made millions out of his best-selling novels, most notably Kane And Abel, after his first publishing success with Not A Penny More, Not A Penny Less in 1976.

Harper Collins said the author had met and signed books for hundreds of fans at a sold-out event with broadcaster Gyles Brandreth at the Leicester Square Theatre in central London on Sunday.

Writing on X, Brandreth said: “Just yesterday I did a show with Jeffrey Archer to celebrate his new novel – he said it was to be his last.

“He was in the most wonderful, ebullient form and had such a great reception from a packed house. He was funny, engaging and self-deprecating – a great storyteller to the last.”

Archer was due to be at the Cheltenham Festival on Saturday to discuss his final novel, Adam and Eve.

He and his wife Dame Mary Archer celebrated their 60th wedding anniversary this year.

They had two sons and five grandchildren.

Former Tory minister Nadhim Zahawi paid tribute to Archer, writing on X: “Jeffrey Archer was a dear friend and an extraordinary human being. His gift for storytelling was matched by his wit, warmth and boundless energy. Life was never dull in Jeffrey’s company.

“Jeffrey, it was a privilege to call you my friend. You were one of a kind. May you rest in eternal peace.”

Kate Elton, HarperCollins UK chief executive and Archer’s editor, said: “It has been one of the great privileges of my publishing life to have been Jeffrey Archer’s editor.

“He was the master storyteller and an editor’s dream – phenomenally hard-working, utterly committed to completing draft after draft to get every word as perfect as possible, and a true champion of the ‘team’ nature of great publishing.

“When he set out to write Adam And Eve he told me from the very beginning that it would be his final novel – he was so excited about the scale of it and told me that if he could pull it off it would equal anything he’d previously written, on which basis he couldn’t imagine embarking on any future novels.

“He did indeed pull it off – and he was utterly thrilled by the early reader reactions.

“We’re all devastated to have lost a writer who has brought joy to generations of readers – and a true friend.”

News.title: Kemi Badenoch refuses to say if Brexit has benefitted London
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Kemi Badenoch has refused to say whether Brexit has been good for London despite lashing out at Andy Burnham for reigniting the debate to rejoin the European Union.

Ahead of the Conservative conference this week, the Tory leader was repeatedly quizzed on whether the capital had been better off after the UK left the EU following the 2016 referendum.

Ms Badenoch refused to answer and insisted that her party was moving forward and voters were “not interested in having a row, which we had 10 years ago”.

She told BBC London's political editor Karl Mercer: “The country voted, as did many people in London as well.”

Brexit could be a key issue in the 2028 London mayoral election after the prime minister reopened the debate during his Labour Party conference speech last week.

Asked whether Brexiteer and mayoral hopeful Sir James Cleverly was the right man for the “anti-Brexit” capital, Ms Badenoch said: “Well, the last Conservative mayor of London was also a Brexiteer, that was Boris Johnson, and he was somebody who people have very fond memories of.

“I don't think Labour has been good for London and the people of London will be voting whether it's Conservatives or Labour, not on Brexit.”

open image in gallery Kemi Badenoch insisted that voters are not interested ‘in having a row’ over Brexit ( AFP/Getty )

Sir James told The Independent that he was happy to make rejoining the EU an election issue and was ready to fight the plans, which he claimed would damage the capital’s interests.

Across all 33 boroughs in London, 59.9 per cent voted in favour of remaining in the bloc.

London mayor Sir Sadiq Khan renewed his demands for the UK to rejoin at the Labour conference and urged the prime minister to start doing the “heavy lifting”.

Mr Burnham has blamed Brexit for a decade of drift and division and insisted he could go “all the way” in proposing to rejoin the bloc.

He promised to set out the options to the country around the time of a UK-EU summit in November and later suggested that Labour’s next election manifesto could include an in-out referendum.

open image in gallery Andy Burnham signalled an in-out referendum in Labour’s next manifesto ( Reuters )

Ms Badenoch, who was a staunch Leave campaigner, described his proposal as “lazy” and accused him of “living in the past”.

She told The Telegraph: “Andy Burnham is living in the past. I wasn’t even an MP when we voted to leave the European Union. I voted Leave. The country voted Leave. And what they want politicians to do is make it work rather than still trying to go back into the EU.

“It is lazy. It is lazy thinking from somebody who has run out of ideas and wants to refight the battles of the past.”

A new poll by the Messina Group over the weekend found that 49 per cent of people support rejoining the EU, compared to the 28.5 per cent against.

The poll, which was first reported in The Guardian, also found that renegotiating Britain’s relationship with the EU could boost Labour’s vote share by as much as seven points.

News.title: Tories promise to scrap Labour’s mansion tax
News.content:
The Tories have pledged to scrap Labour’s “mansion tax” on homes worth more than £2m.

Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, pledged to abolish the “vindictive levy” in his keynote speech to the Conservative Party conference, warning it would hit people living in “ordinary homes”.

Under the tax, which was announced by Labour last year, properties valued at more than £2m face an extra levy on their council tax from 2028.

The shadow chancellor said: “They pretend it’s a mansion tax, but it will hit people here in Birmingham, in Manchester, and those living in ordinary homes making long commutes to our capital city. For many, it will be simply unaffordable.”

He pledged to follow in the footsteps of Nigel Lawson, Margaret Thatcher’s chancellor, and cut one tax at every Budget if the his party returns to power.

Elsewhere in his speech, Mr Griffith promised to scrap a net zero “grocery tax” which pushes up the cost of the weekly shop and cut the cost of a new build by £50,000.

The shadow chancellor also accused previous Tory leaders of failing to govern as free market conservatives, and said Andy Burnham and John Healey want to take Britain back to a “socialist fever dream of the 1970s”.

News.title: How worried should we be about the Russian plague lab leak?
News.content:
Russian media says 200 people are being quarantined. How likely is it that the disease could now spread?

Experts say the risk from this particular bacterium is low.

It can be treated with antibiotics and – although its possible others have been exposed – it seems unlikely it will spread far. The pneumonic form of the disease is spread by droplets and prolonged direct and close contact is required for the disease to spread.

Brendan Wren, professor of microbial pathogenesis at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, said the disease was less transmissible than Covid.

“Plague is still endemic in many parts the world, including western parts of the US, so there shouldn’t be too much concern as the transmission of Yersinia pestis between humans is generally poor.”

The incubation period of pneumonic plague is short – just a day in some cases – so if no one else falls in within the next week, the likelihood of sustained transmission is low.

What is plague exactly?

Plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis and is transmitted via rats and other small rodents.

The bubonic form of the disease – known as the Black Death when it spread throughout Europe in the Middle Ages – is characterised by swollen nymph nodes and has a 30 to 60 per cent mortality rate. This is the more common form of plague.

The pneumonic form of the disease is almost always fatal if left untreated. However, antibiotics are effective against it so early diagnosis and treatment is essential. But drug resistant forms of the disease are emerging.

Plague is endemic in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Madagascar, and is also present in some parts of the United States, including Arizona and New Mexico, where according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention there are an average of seven cases a year.

News.title: Extreme heat is increasing risks for pregnant women and babies, experts warn
News.content:
Soaring temperatures are increasing birth complications and defects in newborns, a new report has warned.

The report, which surveyed 1,000 doctors and midwives, found that at least 73 per cent of healthcare workers across Australia, Brazil, Britain, India and Zimbabwe had seen an uptick in heat-related complications in pregnancy and birth.

High temperatures can cause surface-level blood vessels to dilate, which in pregnant women can significantly decrease blood flow to the placenta and reduce oxygen and nutrients reaching the foetus.

This phenomenon can increase the risk of stillbirth, premature births, and low birth weight, the report, released by the Wellcome Trust, said.

Heat can also make it hard for newborn babies, whose bodies are already extremely fragile, to regulate their internal temperatures – which can significantly impact both their ability to breathe properly and feed from their mothers.

Extreme heat can also severely affect the health of a pregnant woman, placing heavy demands on the cardiovascular system and inadvertently increasing the risk of gestational diabetes, dangerously high blood pressure, and pre-eclampsia.

The effects are more severe on women who live in places where temperatures are newly or rapidly increasing, as opposed to women who have always lived in hot climates and whose bodies have acclimatised to the heat over time.

Insufferable heat can also impact women’s access to critical healthcare during pregnancy.

More than a quarter of healthcare workers surveyed by Wellcome said they had seen first-hand how fewer women travel to hospitals and clinics during heat waves, particularly in the developing world where millions access healthcare on foot.

The world experienced its hottest August on record in 2026, when the average global surface air temperature reached 16.96 degrees Celsius – roughly 1.65 degrees above pre-industrial levels.

Britain also saw its hottest summer since records began, with five heatwaves recorded over the course of just 40 days, and temperatures reaching 38 degrees in some parts of the country.

A Wellcome-funded project studying pregnant women in Wales, known as MAGENTA, has found that women in the UK have experienced negative birth outcomes as a result of the persistent heat.

Initial research has linked exposure to elevated temperatures exceeding 25 degrees with higher rates of premature births and stillbirths. A 1-degree increase in heat exposure can boost the chances of a preterm birth by around 5 per cent, the research found.

Climate change has been identified by the World Health Organization (WHO) as the greatest threat to global public health.

Between 2030 and 2050, experts project climate change will cause an additional 250,000 deaths every year.

The deaths will be due mostly to heat stress, malnutrition, and an increase in the prevalence of infectious diseases like malaria, which is spreading into new areas where mosquitoes can now more easily survive and spread disease, according to the WHO.

Dr Madeline Thomson, head of climate impacts and adaptation at Wellcome, said: “Extreme heat, fuelled by climate change, is impacting our way of life and our health - and yet many countries are not prepared. With El Niño pushing temperatures higher, the failure to act is costing lives.

“We already know many of the solutions to protect people - from early warning systems to cooler buildings.

“But the challenge is providing solutions to those who need them most, including pregnant women and newborns, who face serious risks but often receive inadequate information and support.”

News.title: ‘The dogs were eating their bodies’: Thousands of Yemenis flee war across the sea
News.content:
The Houthi militiamen had barely chased the government forces out of Alia Mohammad’s coastal village when the bombing began in a Saudi-backed attempt to recapture it.

Caught in the middle were Ms Mohammad, her family and their neighbours near the town of Dhubab, overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb strait, or ‘Gate of Tears’.

As the roar of planes split the sky over their heads and explosions shook their village, it took little time for them to decide what to do.

Born from generations of fishermen, they resolved to take to the sea and flee their homes in Yemen, to seek refuge across the strait in Djibouti.

More than 4,000 Yemeni refugees have arrived in the coastal Djibouti town of Obock in the past month, fleeing an offensive which has redrawn Yemen’s battle lines and strengthened Tehran’s hand in the Middle East energy crisis.

The offensive last month saw the Iranian-backed Houthi advance around 90 miles along the Red Sea coast in a 48-hour blitz that delivered what analysts have called the most consequential shift in Yemen’s front lines in years.

News.title: This is when to upgrade your tech (and when not to bother)
News.content:
The tech giants’ attempts to persuade people to upgrade to new gadgets every two years are proving less and less effective. According to YouGov polling, Brits are increasingly deciding to stick with the devices they have for longer, and it isn’t altogether surprising.

As well as the inherent wastefulness of the bi-annual upgrade cycle, year-on-year improvements are less dramatic than they used to be, and tech prices are sky-rocketing thanks to the growing needs of AI data centres.

Inevitably, however, there will come a time when you need to bite the bullet and buy a new model. These are the questions to ask yourself to decide whether that should be today, or whether you can kick the can a little further down the road.

How’s the performance?

A good place to start is to evaluate how your device functions day-to-day versus the day you bought it. Tech inevitably slows down over time, but the drop isn’t equal among devices: a five-year-old flagship smartphone may still outperform a budget model from last year.

If it’s still running smoothly enough, and isn’t broken in an unfixable way, then it probably pays to wait until it no longer passes this test. The longer you wait, the more appealing the upgrade choices will be.

The exception to this is if you’re bumping up against storage problems. If there’s no way to add more, and cloud storage isn’t cutting it, then you may need to upgrade early.

Are you missing key features?

News.title: Jibulu emerges as England World Cup bolter in Sale defeat of Saracens
News.content:
Could Nathan Jibulu, the Sale Sharks hooker, emerge as a bolter for England’s World Cup squad? With Steve Borthwick, the England head coach, watching from the stands, the 23-year-old produced the kind of “wrecking-ball” performance in this surprise victory for the North West side that suggested he is on course to do so.

After their tame defeat by Bristol Bears in the opening round, few had predicted that Alex Sanderson’s side had much hope against Saracens, who were looking to back up their impressive win at Welford Road last weekend. But Jibulu’s powerhouse display on either side of the ball typified their stout and physical resistance, backed up by a masterly display by George Ford.

Given the age and injury profile of England hookers Jamie George and Luke Cowan-Dickie, who both missed this contest, and the fact that Theo Dan has yet to make a forceful challenge for the position in the national side, Sanderson is in no doubt that Jibulu has the X factor required to break into Borthwick’s squad this season.

“This is the player that any time you watch him play, he impacts – he takes metres either side of the ball – and we knew that he had that in him,” Sanderson said.

“It shows he’s of international class. He nailed his line-outs, on the back of that he was a wrecking-ball runner causing havoc around the field.

“This is the person that we knew, this is the player that we knew we had in him. It could be the year where he explodes onto the international scene. I hope it is, but it’s early days.

“He’s that quality, he’s that kind of an athlete. You can get away with being fast and skilful in the Prem, but it’s another level again in terms of the power that’s required at international level. And he’s got that ability, he’s immensely strong.”

Borthwick will have left the StoneX Stadium on Sunday evening with a full notebook. Ben Bamber, Sale’s 6ft 9ins lock, has also been attracting his interest and it was Bamber who crossed for the decisive try, Sale’s third, hitting a great line off Ford to finish like an outside centre.

News.title: Brilliant Hamilton storms to podium despite another Ferrari blunder
News.content:
One of the big talking points heading into the weekend has been the cooling vests drivers wear under their overalls (as opposed to the jacket-like ones they wear when they’re out of their cars). Russell told us in our Brits media session on Thursday that Mercedes had decided to forego the vests here, since the technology was not yet refined. The system works by pumping a coolant through thin tubes stitched into the vest.

Drivers have complained that the connecting valve to the pump, which was originally placed on the side of the vest, proved uncomfortable when combined with the high G-forces experienced in an F1 car. On some vests the connector has been moved to find a more comfortable position, but the thick material and tubing have also proved cumbersome under the driver’s fireproof overalls. There are also concerns over the reliability of some systems and the possibility that a failure will mean the vest will have the opposite effect and work as a heat insulator.preferring to spend that money instead on car upgrades. The money to develop the vests comes out of the budget cap.

But Russell added that the FIA should make the tech mandatory and develop it themselves, describing this race as like being in a “sauna”.The Briton’s comments prompted a sarcastic response from Verstappen - who doesn’t wear the vests either, out of choice - who said Russell “shouldn’t make a fuss”.

“I don’t need it,” Verstappen said. “Maybe I suffer a bit less from the heat.. I find a Finnish sauna at 85 degrees a lot hotter... You shouldn’t make a fuss. Yes, it is hot, but that’s part of it. You have to train for that.”

The Dutchman added: “When I was 18, I had a bit more trouble with these conditions. But after that, I started training more in the heat, such as in the sauna and a steam room, so that I can handle the sweating better and the fact that your head gets very hot. Maybe I should take him (Russell) to the sauna a few times.”

These two have history, of course. They’ve sniped at each other for years. In 2024, in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, it reached a peak when Verstappen described Russell as being “two-faced” and said he had lost all respect for him. Russell responded by saying Verstappen was “a bully”. Earlier this year, the Mercedes driver said Verstappen could always retire from the sport and drive sports cars if he didn’t like the regs.

News.title: Rees-Zammit taunts Pollock as Bristol outplay Northampton
News.content:
Good afternoon and welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Bristol Bears vs Northampton Saints from the Gallagher Prem, with both teams looking to build on winning starts following the opening weekend of action.

Last season’s champions Northampton kicked off their title defence with an emphatic 59-26 victory over a new-look Newcastle Red Bulls outfit at Franklin’s Gardens.

While Henry Pollock’s new cornrow hairstyle was the centre of attention at kick-off, the limelight was soon stolen by Tommy Freeman and James Pater, who both notched hat-tricks for Phil Dowson’s side.

Of 19-year-old full-back Pater, who starts on the bench today, Dowson said afterwards: “He doesn’t let the occasion get to him. He has an incredible skill set, great speed and ability to manoeuvre away from defenders.”

Bristol, meanwhile, began their season with an impressive 34-24 victory away at Sale Sharks, with Pat Lam’s side ensuring Courtney Lawes’s return to the English game was a disappointing one.

Louis Rees-Zammit was operating in his favoured wing position and got Bristol off to a strong start with two tries in the opening 23 minutes, offering Lam hope of a fruitful campaign from the Welshman.

“When you look at our wingers in the past, they scored a lot of tries and Louis is a world-class finisher,” the Bristol director of rugby said. “You get the ball to him in space and you create the opportunity, there’s a good chance he’ll finish it.”

Northampton will be hoping for a repeat of the meeting between the sides at Franklin Gardens in May when they thumped Bristol 94-33, but they have not won at Ashton Gate since 2021.

Both teams have made a pair of changes following their opening-weekend victories, with England international Ellis Genge among the players to drop out after spraining his wrist against Sale.

Sports.title: Lionel Messi’s last ever opponents in horror preparation with staffer suffering blackout and no hot water in hotel
Sports.content:

LIONEL MESSI calls time on his international career with one last tango in the colours of Argentina.

Boss Lionel Scaloni says the 85,000-capacity Monumental Stadium in Buenos Aires could have sold out FIVE times over for the legend’s emotional farewell on Tuesday night.



Argentina team-mate Lautaro Martinez does not expect there to be a dry eye in the house when the superstar lines up against Benin.

Messi, 39, announced his retirement from the national team in August in the aftermath of Argentina’s defeat by Spain in the World Cup final and following the death of his father, Jorge.



He captained Argentina to World Cup glory four years earlier having previously suffered heartbreak against Germany in 2014’s final.

And it is the hottest ticket in town to see whether the country’s all-time leading scorer and most-capped player with 207 appearances can add to his tally of 125 GOALS.

Scaloni said: “If there were five Monumental Stadiums, they would be packed.

“It will be an unforgettable day. It will be his day, and his teammates’ day, who also gave him his greatest footballing joy.

“I’m grateful to be able to enjoy it.” Messi travelled from his home town of Rosario to Buenos Aires on Sunday and enjoyed a traditional barbecue with team-mates and staff before training with them for the final time yesterday.

Striker Martinez expects it to be a night to remember before his long-time skipper returns to concentrate on his club career with David Beckham’s MLS side Inter Miami.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

The Inter Milan ace said: “Tuesday’s game will surely be full of emotion.

“It will be very special and important. Hopefully we won’t cry too much.”

The prospect of trying to stop the world’s best player in front of his adoring public is a daunting one for Benin.

And the Cheetahs’ preparations for the friendly showdown have made that task even greater.



Reports in Africa claim that they travelled to South America on a 23-hour-long economy flight in which the team’s video analyst suffered a blackout.

And upon their arrival in Argentina, their hotel had no hot water.

Meanwhile, Italian club Roma were not willing to play ball for Messi’s farewell game.



The Serie A giants have blocked their duo Nahuel Molina and Paulo Dybala, both part of the triumphant 2022 side, from going to the eight-time Ballon d’Or winner’s send-off.

Roma claim the tough call was made with their return to domestic action against Como on Sunday in mind.

A statement said: “The club acknowledges the significance of the occasion for both players, who share a close bond with Lionel Messi and were part of Argentina’s 2022 World Cup-winning team alongside him.

“The decision was made for sporting and logistical reasons, taking into account the length of the intercontinental journey and the proximity of the club’s upcoming competitive fixtures.

“AS Roma has the utmost respect for Lionel Messi and his extraordinary career and wishes him and the Argentine FA a very special evening.”

PIERS MORGAN has lifted the lid on why Cristiano Ronaldo dramatically quit the Portugal camp after manager Jorge Jesus “pulled a Ten Hag”.

Jesus reportedly went back on his promises to Ronaldo regarding playing arrangements over the international break before the country’s record appearance- maker and goalscorer returned home.

The former Manchester United ace was left as an unused sub against Norway despite being asked to warm up.



Taking to social media, Ronaldo said he would speak publicly about the events of the rift in “due time”.

SunSport columnist and TalkTV host Morgan was the man Ronaldo turned to for a bombshell interview when he quit Manchester United.



That interview ended up being a massive attack against the club’s stagnation and manager Erik ten Hag, who had relegated Ronaldo to the bench.

LUKE LITTLER has named his all-time Manchester United Premier League IX – but there is no room for the current manager.

The Nuke, born and bred in Warrington, has been a loyal United fan all his life.



And in discussion with former United midfielder Paul Scholes on the The Good, The Bad & The Football podcast, the two-time world darts champion put together his Red Devils Dream Team.

The starting line-up was made up of players that the 19-year-old had watched play at Old Trafford in his lifetime.



In goal, he went for Spaniard David de Gea, a mainstay in Manchester for 12 years, but someone who overcame a lot of stick when he first moved to English football.

At full-back, he went for Ecuadorian Antonio Valencia on the right (“very good”) and Frenchman Patrice Evra on the left.

At centreback, Littler said “he’d put Rio (Ferdinand) and (Nemanja) Vidic in there”.

He has always been a huge fan of Marcus Rashford (“I’ve watched Rashford since his first game”) and he would go with the England star on the left-hand side of midfield.

Amad Diallo, the Ivory Coast winger, would be his choice on the right.

Michael Carrick, the boss of United since January, was an accomplished midfielder in his day.

During his time at the club he was the winner of five Premier Leagues, one FA Cup, three League Cups, the Champions League, Europa League and FIFA Club World Cup.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Though Scholes suggested Carrick as a viable option in central midfield, Littler, however, went for Portuguese leader Bruno Fernandes and Frenchman Paul Pogba.

Littler laughed: “There’s got to be someone better than Michael Carrick.”

Up front, he went for obvious choices – Cristiano Ronaldo and Wayne Rooney, two of the finest players to don the famous red shirt.



Scholes – winner of 11 Premier League titles – went for Peter Schmeichel in goal and a defence of Gary Neville (right-back), Denis Irwin (left-back) and Rio Ferdinand and Jaap Stam (centre-backs).

In an old school 4-4-2 formation, Scholes, 51, plumped for a midfield quartet of Ryan Giggs (left), Valencia (right), and then Roy Keane and Carrick in central positions.

In attack, Scholes chose Dutchman Ruud van Nistelrooy and Wayne Rooney.

Scholes argued: “I’m going to leave Cristiano out. Because how long did I play with Cristiano?

“Maybe three or four years. I played with Wayne a lot longer. I’ll bring Cristiano out with 20 minutes to go.



“Imagine somebody saying that now. F***ing hell. What is wrong with you?”

Littler, winner of the past two world darts titles, would happily swap another Sid Waddell Trophy if it meant he was able to watch United win the Treble for a second time.

Just like his dad Anthony did in 1999 when Sir Alex Ferguson’s side, with Scholes in the team, won the Premier League, FA Cup and then Champions League.

Littler, born in January 2027, said: “I think I’d say United won another treble. My dad witnessed the treble, I didn’t.”

THE romance of Match of the Day hosts Mark Chapman and Kelly Cates has stunned colleagues.

Sources say nobody at the BBC football show seems to have realised the pair were an item before it was revealed in The Sun yesterday.



An insider said: “The chatter in the BBC Sport department since their relationship was revealed has been off the charts.

“No one appears to have known they were dating.



“When the news came out, people were talking about it and were flabbergasted as no one knew it was going on.

“Chappers and Kelly have clearly been very professional and have been very discreet about their relationship.



“Their romance has been the best-kept secret in sport.”

Chappers, 52, was spotted shopping yesterday after his relationship with Kelly, 51, was revealed.



Mark, whose annual BBC earnings are about £340,000, got two ravioli ready meals and a microwavable spaghetti carbonara from an M&S in Cheshire.

He also talked on his phone while drinking a takeaway coffee.

Chappers and Kelly appeared together on Channel 4 show Celebrity Gogglebox this summer — and their body language was very different to when they were on the programme last year.

In 2025, his arms were folded and her hands were clasped down by her side as they awkwardly watched footage of an animal being castrated.



This year the pair were on the same sofa but were sat much closer, and there was no awkward arm-folding or hand-clasping.

They seemed far more relaxed.

Chappers grew close to Kelly after his three-year relationship with estate agent Clere Collier ended in April.

Kelly is understood to have been single since 2021 when she separated from TV producer Tom Cates after 14 years of marriage.



Those close to Chappers say he did not date Kelly and Clere at the same time.

Chappers, Kelly and Gabby Logan take it in turns to present Match of the Day.

The trio took over from Gary Lineker in 2025.

Sports.title: Phil Foden trapped in Man City maelstrom after guilty verdict amid miserable 34-game drought and England exile
Sports.content:
Next

PHIL FODEN looked like a player in a world of pain BEFORE the Manchester City verdict was handed down.

Now you have to wonder just how the midfielder feels, his inner turmoil surely intensified.



Being left out of the World Cup squad by Thomas Tuchel would have been a devastating blow for Foden, although City announced a new four-year contract on July 26.

Yet that came with City chiefs seemingly already knowing the direction of travel from the independent commission that was finally published last week.



In the light of what we now know, it looks like a defensive measure from a club that could face a lengthy transfer ban.

As for Foden, while City have won all seven competitive games this season, his scoring drought has continued.



His last goal in City colours came at Crystal Palace on December 14 – 34 MATCHES without finding the net.

When Tuchel came to watch him at the Manchester derby, Foden was dismissed after 23 minutes for an angry retaliation kick out which caught Bruno Fernandes amidships – even Enzo Maresca admitted the red card was correct.

It brought a three game ban, meaning Foden will be missing when City walk into a wall of vitriol at Anfield on Sunday.

But now City’s longest-serving player – as he noted in last month’s Instagram post, he is the only survivor from the squad picture ahead of the 2019-20 season – has been inadvertently caught up in the maelstrom unleashed by the commission.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

Foden made his City debut – against Feyenoord in the Champions League – in the 2017-18 season, the last campaign covered by the Prem’s currently-proven allegations against the club.

As a stalwart of the club’s domination under Pep Guardiola, nobody has won more in City colours.

Yet he would only be human if he wondered what it all added up to – especially as rival fans and clubs are understandably using the verdict as evidence for their argument that City’s successes are irredeemably tainted.

Foden is not responsible for any of that.



He is the stand-out example of City’s in-house production line. Club-raised, club-trained, club loyal.

Whatever did or did not happen elsewhere in the factory, Foden was unaware the loop even existed, let alone left out of it.

His love for the club, for what the shirt and badge represents to him and the fans, is total and absolute. His commitment, too.

Yet he is caught up in the crisis, the feeling that, for a decade, City paid lip service to the financial rules while blithely and deliberately ignoring them.

That prevailing view was that City believed they could do whatever they wanted, secure in the expectation that financial muscle meant nobody would be able to stop them.



Of course, it may be that City’s arguments find favour with the appeal panel. Or, if the case goes that far, the High Court.

Although when it comes to the sources of the income, that “comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence”, the arguments do appear to have been delivered in somewhat mixed and contradictory messages.

Apparent Government-level threats will hardly serve to lessen the feeling that City’s internal email chain has brought about their own potential downfall.



Nobody can argue that the UAE investment in the area around the Etihad and elsewhere in Manchester has not been transformative.

Indeed, the huge outlay has been a true boon for the city, just as it has been for City.

But it cannot, must not, be the case that the final sentence is commuted because of the potential economic impact.

If that happens, if the Commission and the Premier League – which, as the “prosecution”, will argue for the fitting sanction – does look to have been leant on, then what will be the point of having rules and regulations in the first place?

Anybody who tells you they KNOW what is going to happen is either lying or conceited by their own sense of self-importance.



If City are relegated, which seems almost certain if the verdict sticks, it is hard to see Foden, indelibly linked to the club, pushing for an exit.

You feel he would want to be the cornerstone of any rebuild and return. Yet this must be the most difficult, conflicted and testing of times.

EFL to reject City?

Amid all the theorising about City’s fate, one issue may not have been considered.

What if the EFL declines to accept them?

Rumours abound that a number of Championship clubs are already considering contesting a relegated City’s right to come into the competition if the Prem commission verdict is upheld.



Where there to be an expulsion from the Prem – as some top flight clubs and fans are demanding – the situation could become even more complicated.

Croatia’s catastrophe

It doesn’t matter that Croatia were, as Luka Modric admitted, a “catastrophe”.

England taking them apart in Rijeka was beyond fun.

The questions about Thomas Tuchel will not be answered until he has to make the big call in a game where it is all on the line

But making England enjoyable to watch will ensure most Three Lions fans will be prepared to give Tuchel the benefit of the doubt.



Managers off the hook

The two luckiest men in the Prem are Michael Carrick and Roberto de Zerbi.

What could have been a three week pressure-cooker, cranking up the scrutiny on both of them during the international break, suddenly disappeared as everything was about Manchester City.

Yet Saturday at Old Trafford is now looming and once the two managers have had their first say on City, it will be about their own clubs.



Ever since Spurs put three past Jose Mourinho’s United in the first weeks of the 2018-19 season, with the Portuguese firing back in his post-match press conference, matches between the two have seen added importance.

Mourinho was in the other dug-out by the time Tottenham won 6-1 at United in October 2020, while 12 months later a 3-0 home defeat in N17 was celebrated as a “win” as it spelled the end for Nuno Espirito Santo, heralding the arrival of Antonio Conte and a return to the Champions League.

Spurs have had the better of it since, with a run of eight unbeaten only ended when Cristian Romero was sent off as Carrick’s United won 2-0 in March.



That, of course, included the Europa League Final in 2024 – arguably the worst quality match ever witnessed with a major trophy at stake.

Yet with United 12th and winless Spurs rock-bottom, neither manager can afford a defeat this weekend.

Carrick’s honeymoon with the United fans appears over – last season is history, he is being judged on the here and now.

And having been handed the biggest warchest in Spurs history, with total control over where the money was spent, de Zerbi is fast running out of excuses.

By 7.30pm on Saturday night, one of them is likely to be even more exposed.



Infantino the Teflon Don

Another week passes without a challenger to take on Gianni Infantino.

For all the posturing from Uefa, finding somebody willing to put their head above the parapet and contest the scheduled Fifa Presidential election in March is proving more than difficult.

Senior Uefa figures are still insisting there “must” be a contender ready to bring Infantino down.

But the deadline to find the “white knight” is now barely six weeks away.

Hardly enough time for any potential leader of the global game to develop a serious manifesto.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Meanwhile, Infantino is going around the world, picking up endorsements again.

Despite everything since the summer, he looks increasingly likely to stay in post until 2031.

Sports.title: Man Utd included JJ Gabriel in first team squad photo before shock request to quit club ‘as family demands revealed’
Sports.content:
Next

MANCHESTER UNITED star JJ Gabriel is still set to depart Old Trafford despite being pictured in their team photo, according to reports.

The Red Devils are set to lose their 15-year-old prodigy after he sensationally demanded an exit from Old Trafford.



It is understood the wonderkid was unhappy about his lack of minutes in pre-season and hoped to break into Michael Carrick‘s squad this term.

Gabriel clearly had a big future at United after being snapped in the club’s team photo for the 2026-27 season.



The picture – which was taken on September 8, a week before his request to leave – shows him sitting centrally in the second row, just above Harry Maguire.

And Sky Sports has claimed Gabriel still sees his future away from the club, who hoped the photo would show he was valued.

However, the youngster family weren’t satisfied and felt his brief cameo for United in a pre-season friendly against Atletico Madrid wasn’t enough.

The report also claims his family pulled him out of Under-21s training because they felt it was “beneath him”.

They thought he should only be playing with the first team and made a series of demands over game time.

Sun Sport understands the family requested he played 20 minutes against Sabah in the Champions League.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

But Sky claim they also wanted him to feature for the same time period against Brighton in the Carabao Cup and Bournemouth in the Premier League.

Gabriel didn’t feature against Sabah because he was not listed on United’s A-list squad.

There were plans to include him against Brighton – but those were shelved after his shock request to leave.



It is said Gabriel’s camp hoped the player would chase historical records at the club.

But United were more focused on his long-term development and didn’t want to rush the player.

The club still believe United is the best place for Gabriel to push on, but it’s now “unlikely” he will ever play for them again, the report adds.

But United will consider legal action if he does leave amid interest from the likes of Real Madrid, Barcelona and Bayern Munich.

Should the player seal an exit, United would only be entitled to a meagre compensation fee.
