World.title: SA Explained | Shadrack Sibiya: Is The Madlanga Fallout Finally Catching Up With Him? | 05 October 2026
World.content:
When A Police Crisis Becomes A Systems Test

The pressure around Shadrack Sibiya is about more than one senior officer. It tests whether South Africa can turn explosive allegations and commission findings into durable institutional reform.

The Madlanga Commission has exposed a problem that is easy to describe but far harder to fix: what happens when allegations of criminal influence reach deep enough into policing that removing individual officials may not be enough to restore trust?

Suspended Deputy National Police Commissioner Shadrack Sibiya now sits at the centre of that question. The Commission has recommended disciplinary proceedings and further investigation against him, while he faces separate criminal charges that he denies. On 5 October, SAPS confirmed that his disciplinary hearing had begun but was postponed, while Sibiya also approached the Labour Court in an attempt to halt the process.

The temptation is to treat each development as a story about one man. That would miss the bigger institutional warning.

In SA Explained, Pule Letshwiti-Jones asks whether attempts to clean up the South African Police Service risk merely “replacing one faction with another”. Silindelo Sebata responds by pointing towards the less dramatic work of institutional reform: vetting, procurement and systems that can keep functioning when powerful individuals change.

That distinction matters because commissions are exceptionally good at making hidden relationships visible. They can compel testimony, connect people and events, identify failures and recommend action. But a commission cannot permanently supervise an institution after the hearings end. Its lasting value depends on whether the organisations it examines can convert exposure into rules, controls and consequences.

For SAPS, that means the test is larger than whether any particular allegation against Sibiya is eventually proved. Criminal proceedings must follow their own evidentiary standard, disciplinary processes their own rules, and accused people retain the right to challenge the case against them. Institutional reform operates on another track. It asks why vulnerabilities existed, whether safeguards worked, who was able to bypass them and whether the same weaknesses could survive under different names and different office-bearers.

That is where public trust becomes difficult to rebuild. Trust is not restored simply because a prominent official leaves office. It returns when the public can see that misconduct is harder to conceal, complaints cannot quietly disappear, procurement decisions leave a trace, conflicts of interest are identified, and disciplinary systems do not depend on political or factional convenience.

This is also why the idea of factionalism is so corrosive. If accountability is interpreted only as one camp defeating another, every investigation becomes vulnerable to the claim that it is political retaliation. The antidote is not rhetoric. It is process strong enough to survive changes in leadership and credible enough to be applied consistently.

South Africa therefore faces a harder question than whether the Madlanga Commission can expose wrongdoing. The real question is whether the institutions receiving its findings can make the next scandal more difficult to produce.

A commission can reveal where the system failed. Reform begins only when the system is redesigned so that the same failures are less likely to happen again.

References

SA Explained episode transcript, 5 October 2026.

The Presidency, “President Cyril Ramaphosa notes recommendations and referrals of the Second Interim Report of the Madlanga Commission”.

World.title: How KNEC plans to stop cheating in 2026 exams
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

The Kenya National Examinations Council (KNEC) Chief Executive Officer Dr David Njengere. [File]

The Kenya National Examinations Council (KNEC) will use smart padlocks to secure all examination storage containers as more than 3.6 million candidates sit the 2026 national examinations and assessments.

KNEC Chief Executive Officer Dr David Njengere said the council would monitor the containers from its headquarters to prevent anyone from accessing examination papers before the scheduled times.

“Last year KNEC piloted the use of smart padlocks in 250 containers. This year all containers will be secured using the smart padlocks which will be monitored from the KNEC headquarters,” said Dr Njengere.

Under the system, officials will open containers at designated times. Officials will access Kenya Primary School Education Assessment (KPSEA) and Kenya Junior School Education Assessment (KJSEA) papers at 6 a.m., while centre managers will collect Kenya Certificate of Secondary Education (KCSE) papers at 7 a.m. and 12:30 p.m.

However, Dr Njengere identified mobile phones as the biggest challenge in preventing examination malpractice.

“Mobile phones remain our biggest challenge in administration of KCSE examination,” observed Dr Njengere.

He warned that the council would not allow candidates or examination officials to have mobile phones at examination centres during examination sessions.

“Any contravention of this rule will constitute a malpractice as per the KNEC Act and the Rules and Regulations,” noted Dr Njengere.

The council will deploy 342,005 contracted professionals to administer and manage the examinations and assessments. They include centre managers, supervisors, invigilators, security officers and drivers.

For KCSE, KNEC will deploy 10,765 centre managers, 12,274 supervisors, 57,432 invigilators and 21,388 security officers. Each examination centre will have at least two police officers.

Centre managers will collect KCSE papers twice a day, and KNEC will place morning and afternoon papers in marked cartons to reduce mix-ups and unauthorised access.

KNEC has personalised question papers with candidates’ details, and examiners will receive anonymised scripts with those details removed.

The 2026 examination and assessment season will involve 3,634,846 candidates, a 6.13 per cent increase from the 3,424,836 registered in 2025.

KCSE rehearsals will take place on Friday, October 16. Examinations for papers with low candidature will run from Monday, October 19 to Friday, October 30, while papers with large candidature will run from Monday, November 2 to Friday, November 20.

KPSEA and KJSEA assessments will run from Monday, October 26 to Friday, October 30.

KNEC Chairperson Prof. Julius Nyabundi said the council was preparing for possible disruption from El Nino rains.

“As we start off the 2026 field administration season, one of the risks we contend with are the attempts to cheat in assessments and examination,” said Prof. Nyabundi.

He urged candidates, parents and examination officials to protect the integrity of the examinations, warning that malpractice could undermine public confidence in the education system.

“Cheating in examinations undermines public confidence in the credibility, fairness and quality of the entire education system,” noted Prof. Nyabundi.

KNEC will operate a 24-hour call centre with toll-free numbers for candidates, officials and members of the public to report incidents and seek assistance during the examination period.

The 2026 cycle will continue the implementation of Competency-Based Education assessments, including School-Based Assessments in primary, junior and senior school.

Grade 10 learners are undertaking their first School-Based Assessment, which will contribute 15 marks towards the Kenya Certificate of Basic Education.

World.title: Mbadi hits out at Sifuna, says opposition lacks economic agenda
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

National Treasury CS John Mbadi after opening new classrooms and administration blocks constructed by the M-Pesa Foundation at Ligongo Primary School in Suba South Constituency. [James Omoro, Standard]

The National Treasury CS John Mbadi has hit out at Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna, saying that criticising President William Ruto should not be an agenda for a presidential candidate.

Speaking when he opened new classrooms and administration blocks constructed by M-Pesa Foundation at Ligongo Primary School in Suba South Constituency, Mbadi said lack of economic agenda makes the opposition unsuitable to lead the country.

“I have heard of opposition leaders who want the presidency, but they do not have an agenda for the economic transformation of this country,” he said.

The CS claimed that none of the opposition leaders is suitable for the presidency.

“These opposition leaders cannot make any economic change in this country. They should not be elected,” he said.

He told Nyanza residents to shun the new wave of opposition led by Sifuna.

Mbadi claimed that opposition leaders lack political direction.

He said Sifuna had taken too long to unveil a political party that he will use to run for the presidency.

“Do not join the opposition bandwagon. We are just a few months away from the General Election, but Sifuna still doesn’t know a political party he will use to run for the presidency. They are still leaving in confusion,” Mbadi said.

He said Sifuna has not demonstrated how to improve this country’s economy.

“Former President Uhuru Kenyatta left the economy of this country in tatters. We have tried to improve it but we are not yet where we want it to be,” Mbadi said.

He urged Nyanza residents to support Ruto.

The CS said Ruto’s government had improved mega infrastructural projects across the country as part of economic transformation.

He cited the 74 km Mbita- Sindo- Sori road, Lake Victoria ring road and other infrastructure projects as some of the reasons residents should support Ruto.

“I urge you to support Ruto so that we can continue acquiring more development projects in this region,” Mbadi said.

Audio By Vocalize

Brenda Chemutai, 19, who allegedly committed suicide inside the Kericho Annex Prison where she was awaiting trial for an offence of being in possession of bhang that was seized in a vehicle allegedly belonging to a senior police officer. [Courtesy]

Questions are mounting over security and accountability at Kericho Annex Prison following the death of a 19-year-old remand prisoner in a suspected case of suicide.

Her family is demanding answers about how she obtained a bedsheet and why they were not notified until nearly 10 hours after the incident.

Brenda Chemutai was reportedly found hanging from a double-decker bed at around 9 am when her fellow cellmates were having breakfast on Friday.

The cell had eight inmates, who had gone for breakfast, according to a police report.

However, her relatives state they were not informed until about 7 pm, after her body had already been taken from the prison and transferred to the Kericho County Hospital Mortuary.

The delay has raised serious concerns for the family, which calls for authorities to clarify what happened between the time Chemutai was discovered and when her next of kin were contacted.

Kericho East Directorate of Criminal Investigation (DCI) officer, Kennedy Apindi, said police have launched investigations following reports from prison officials that the incident was a suicide.

He mentioned that preliminary information indicated Chemutai allegedly used a bedsheet.

The family, however, insists that investigators determine when she was found, who discovered her, when the incident was reported to police, who authorised her body’s removal, and why her relatives were not notified immediately.

“We had spoken with Brenda. She was expected to be released around December, and by January we would all have been together at home,” said her sister, Phyllis Cherotich.

Cherotich added that the family had seen no signs indicating Chemutai intended to take her own life.

"Her death has shocked us deeply. She never mentioned any plans of this nature. We want to understand how this was possible given the level of security at the facility," she said.

The circumstances surrounding the alleged use of a bedsheet have also raised questions for the family.

Her uncle, Michael Rono, questioned how such an item came into Chemutai's possession while she was in a remand facility.

"I am deeply surprised. When one enters the prison, one is carefully searched. Where did the bedsheet come from? We ask the government to ensure justice is done," Rono said.

Chemutai had been in remand since 2024, with her relatives saying she was arrested while still a minor and had spent nearly two years awaiting the conclusion of her case.

She was being tried for the offence of possession of bhang in a vehicle allegedly belonging to a senior police officer.

Her death has consequently brought renewed scrutiny to not only what happened inside the prison but also the circumstances that led to her prolonged detention.

Youth activists from the Voice of Youth Organisation, led by Kelvin Kipchichir, have joined the family in demanding investigations into both the death and the case that resulted in Chemutai's detention.

Kipchichir claimed Chemutai was arrested alongside other suspects in a vehicle allegedly linked to an Officer Commanding Station serving in Kakamega.

According to the activists, police recovered 32 rolls of bhang from the vehicle, while some of the suspects allegedly fled, leaving Chemutai behind.

The claims have not been independently established.

Kipchichir questioned why Chemutai remained in custody for such a prolonged period and called for scrutiny of the circumstances surrounding the vehicle and its alleged connection to the police officer.

“We are concerned that an OCS in the National Police Service could allow a vehicle to be used by an individual with a known criminal record,” he said.

He called on the Ministry of Interior to establish who owned or controlled the vehicle and under what circumstances it was allegedly being used.

The activists said the vehicle was still at Kericho Police Station.

For the family, the tragedy has been compounded by personal loss. Chemutai's father died while she was in remand, while she leaves behind a young child.

Relatives said detectives had informed them that the person alleged to own the bhang had since been arrested and was being held in Kisumu.

But the immediate question for Chemutai's family is what happened during her final hours.

They want a clear account of the period between the reported discovery of her body at about 9 am and the notification of the family nearly 10 hours later.

They also want investigators to establish how the bedsheet allegedly used in the incident came into her possession and whether prison officers followed all required procedures after she was found.

The activists are calling for the inquiry to extend beyond the death of Chemutai to her arrest, the length of her detention and the handling of the case against her.

The family has demanded a transparent and independent investigation, saying it wants answers on how a teenager who entered the justice system while still a minor ended up dead in remand custody.

The family says it wants those questions answered before proceeding with burial arrangements.

World.title: Pregnant woman found dead by roadside in Kirinyaga with head, hip injuries
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

The National Police Service (NPS) has launched investigations after the body of a pregnant woman was found by the roadside in the Itangi area of Mwea East Sub-County, Kirinyaga County.

The woman, identified as Catherine Njeru, was found early Friday morning along the Piai-Itangi Murram Road with visible injuries to her head and hip.

In a statement, NPS said the incident is being investigated as a suspected murder.

"The NPS condoles with the family, relatives, and friends of the deceased and commits to expeditious and conclusive investigations to ensure that any person or persons responsible for this barbaric crime are brought to justice," read the statement.

Police have urged residents of Itangi to remain calm and refrain from speculation as the investigation continues.

Anyone with information that could assist the investigation has been asked to report to the nearest police station or a law enforcement officer.

The matter is being investigated by Kirinyaga County Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI) officers, local Sub-County police and Central Regional Police Command, led by the Regional Criminal Investigations Officer.

According to NPS, the Inspector General of the National Police Service has also been briefed on the incident and directed the Director of Criminal Investigations to expedite the probe and establish the facts surrounding the woman's death.

World.title: Ruto downplays rivalry over oil refinery in East Africa
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Former Nigeria President Olesugun Obasanjo, Ali Dangote, President William Ruto and Uganda President Yoweri Museveni during launch of the Lamu Refinery on September 30, 2026. [PCS]

President William Ruto has played down suggestions of rivalry between Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania over competing refinery projects, saying East Africa’s growing demand for petroleum products can support several facilities across the region.

Speaking during a media interview at State House Mombasa, Ruto said Kenya had no objection to Uganda and Tanzania pursuing their own refinery projects, arguing that the different facilities could complement rather than compete with one another.

“There is no bad blood at all. There is no problem,” Ruto said.

His remarks came a day after he presided over the groundbreaking of the Lamu refinery project, which the government is positioning as a major component of a wider industrial complex on the Kenyan coast.

Ruto said he had discussed Uganda’s plans with President Yoweri Museveni and agreed that Kampala could proceed with a smaller refinery without threatening Kenya’s investment in Lamu.

He said Kenya would even be prepared to buy petroleum products from Uganda if they could reach the Kenyan market at competitive prices.

“If it is manufactured there in Uganda and the oil from that place is near Busia, and it can reach Busia at a lower price, we will buy oil from anywhere and bring it to Busia,” Ruto said.

The President argued that the size of the regional petroleum market meant there was room for more than one refinery.

“This one in Lamu cannot serve all of us; it will be necessary to expand,” he said, adding that East Africa had “enough opportunity” for multiple facilities.

Ruto also extended the same approach to Tanzania, saying Kenya could participate in a refinery project in Tanga if it is eventually developed.

“Even if the one in Tanga is built, we as Kenya will go and buy some shares there. There is no problem,” he said.

The comments point to a regional energy market in which petroleum products could move across borders depending on availability, transport costs and prices. Rather than treating refinery projects as competing national investments, Ruto said the facilities could strengthen economic cooperation within the East African Community.

The President said the Lamu refinery would also address some of the challenges Kenya faces from dependence on imported refined petroleum products.

“Lamu will give us an opportunity to have fuel without the fluctuations that we have now,” he said.

He linked the proposed refinery to the need to reduce Kenya’s exposure to international oil price shocks, disruptions caused by instability in oil-producing regions and costs associated with transporting petroleum products over long distances.

Ruto said local refining could reduce expenses related to insurance and transportation while providing Kenya with greater access to locally processed fuel.

However, he said the larger economic opportunity would extend beyond the refinery itself. The government plans to develop industries around the facility, including petrochemical, chemical and plastics manufacturing.

The refinery could also provide raw materials for industries producing fertiliser and bitumen, potentially reducing reliance on imports of some petroleum-based products.

The broader development is expected to create opportunities for employment, investment and trade while strengthening Lamu’s position as an industrial and logistics centre.

Ruto said Kenya’s policy would be guided by competitiveness, allowing businesses and consumers to obtain petroleum products from whichever regional facility can supply them efficiently and at favourable prices.

The President maintained that Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania therefore did not need to view their refinery plans through the lens of rivalry.

Instead, he said, multiple facilities could create a larger and more integrated petroleum market capable of serving the needs of East Africa.

World.title: Outrage as KDF officers detain human rights team along Malindi-Lamu highway
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Activists clashed with police at a Gamba roadblock after being stopped en route to Lamu. [Vocal Africa]

Six members of Muslims for Human Rights (MUHURI), including five staff and a board member, were detained by Kenya Defence Forces (KDF) officers along the Malindi-Lamu highway, prompting condemnation from human rights organisations.

The incident occurred on Monday as the team travelled from Lamu to Mombasa after a field mission. The officers reportedly intercepted them between Gamba and Minjila, detained them for about two hours, then released them.

The Kenya Human Rights Commission (KHRC) and MUHURI said the officers covered their faces and refused to identify themselves when the human rights team challenged them.

The five staff members were identified as Francis Auma, Abdulrahman Mwanga, Fredrick Okado, Lathan Yusuf and Mohamed Abdla, while the board member was identified as Khelef Khalifa.

In a joint statement, the two organisations said the officers' actions violated a High Court ruling by Justice Bahati Mwamuye requiring security personnel to wear clearly visible name tags or identifiable service numbers on their uniforms.

The ruling also prohibits security officers from wearing hoods, balaclavas or face masks to conceal their identities.

"We call on the KDF and other security agencies to comply with the court order. Officers who violate the directive should be held accountable and face legal consequences," the joint statement read in part.

The organisations also demanded immediate compliance with a recent court order lifting the dusk-to-dawn curfew that had been imposed for more than a decade along the Minjila-Lamu highway.

They argued that the curfew had created conditions for arbitrary stops, harassment and detention of travellers using the route, citing the detention of the MUHURI team as an example.

The organisations urged security agencies to respect court orders and protect the rights of travellers using the highway.

However, a senior Anti-Terror Police officer aware of the incident told The Standard that the officers from the Border Police Unit (BPU) manning such roadblocks and tactical borders conceal their faces to protect their identities.

"In high-risk areas prone to insurgent or terrorist retaliation, including Kanyoyo in Kitui heading to Garissa, Moyale and Lamu, anonymity is framed as a matter of personal and operational survival," she stated.

World.title: Kalonzo signals at working with Ruto if 2027 poll is free and fair
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Wiper Patriotic Front leader Kalonzo Musyoka at St Michael and All Angels ACK Cathedral in Bondo, Siaya County on September 27, 2026. [Clinton Ambujo, Standard]

Wiper Patriotic Front leader Kalonzo Musyoka has signalled that the Opposition could accept the outcome of the 2027 General Election and consider working with President William Ruto if he wins through a free and fair contest.

Speaking at St Michael and All Angels ACK Cathedral in Bondo, Siaya County, Kalonzo said the political class must commit itself to democratic competition and be prepared to accept the verdict of voters.

“If you beat us, we will have to consider if you have behaved yourself, and if we beat you, we have to look at all these things,” he said.

The Wiper leader also called for stronger democratic institutions, warning against political confrontation that could deepen divisions in the country.

“We have a nation here. We have to make this country truly democratic. I do not think we have a shortcut,” he said.

Kalonzo used the church service to make a broader appeal for a united and effective Opposition, saying political leaders had a responsibility to work together in the national interest.

“Kenya needs a functional official opposition; one that is united and does not thrive on disunity. As leaders, we have a responsibility to work together and play our part in fixing this nation,” he said.

He said he had remained in the Opposition even when some political allies moved into government.

“I have stood in the opposition all these years. Even when others joined government, my brother Eugene Wamalwa and I remained steadfast, and we will continue to stand firm,” he said.

Kalonzo also turned his attention to Parliament, claiming that the National Assembly had been “captured” and challenging lawmakers in both Houses to exercise their constitutional responsibilities.

“The National Assembly has been captured. Let this message reach every leader in the National Assembly and the Senate: you have the power to change things, not just to complain later,” he said.

He urged legislators to defend the interests of the people who elected them and to put the country ahead of political considerations.

The former Vice President also defended retired President Uhuru Kenyatta against claims that he is financing the Opposition ahead of the 2027 contest.

Kalonzo argued that presidential campaigns have historically relied on networks of political allies and supporters rather than family resources alone.

“But here we are saying, please let Uhuru rest; he is a retired President. Stop saying he is our financier,” he said.

Kalonzo cited previous presidential campaigns involving Uhuru, former President Mwai Kibaki and Raila Odinga, arguing that major political campaigns require support from friends and associates.

“Even when Uhuru was running for President, or Kibaki and even Raila, no family has enough resources to support a presidential campaign. It is friends who support you,” he said.

He warned that Kenya was at a delicate political moment and urged leaders to avoid actions that could deepen instability.

“We should not allow the country to get to a worse situation than where it is. We are on the edge of a cliff; the country is at a crossroads,” he said.

World.title: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor takes legal action against UK police over Epstein arrest
World.content:
King Charles’ younger brother Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has launched legal action against police in England over his arrest earlier this year on suspicion of misconduct in public office following revelations from the Epstein files in the United States.

Mountbatten-Windsor, 66, has asked for a judge to determine if Thames Valley Police’s actions against him earlier this year were lawful. The development was first reported by Britain’s The Telegraph newspaper on Sunday.

He has lodged a judicial review in relation to the search warrants that were executed at his home at the Sandringham Estate and his former home at Royal Lodge in Windsor.

A court hearing will be held on Thursday, British media reported Monday.

Thames Valley Police confirmed to CNN on Monday that it was “engaged in legal proceedings in relation to warrants previously obtained from the Central Criminal Court” and would not comment further with legal proceedings ongoing.

CNN has also reached out to the UK Judicial Office for comment.

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor leaves Aylsham Police Station on February 19 after he was questioned by UK police on suspicion of misconduct in public office. Phil Noble/Reuters

The former Duke of York became the first senior royal in centuries to be arrested in February, the latest extraordinary development in a yearslong scandal over his ties to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, which obliterated his reputation and has thrown the royal family into crisis.

He was detained by police on his 66th birthday at his new home on his brother’s Sandringham estate in Norfolk, eastern England, on February 19. He was taken to Aylsham police station where he was questioned for almost 12 hours before being released under investigation. No charges were filed; police have said its investigation is still ongoing.

Mountbatten-Windsor’s arrest came after the force previously said it was assessing whether the former prince had shared confidential information with Epstein during his decade as a UK trade envoy.

Mountbatten-Windsor has vehemently denied any and all wrongdoing in his dealings with Epstein, and has denied any personal gain from his role as a trade envoy, according to British media reports.

He stepped down from official royal duties in 2019 following a calamitous interview with the BBC over his friendship with Epstein. But headlines related to the late financier continued to plague the disgraced royal. In 2025, King Charles stripped his younger brother of his title as prince, following public outcry after the release of a posthumous memoir by Virginia Giuffre, a prominent accuser of Epstein who alleged that Mountbatten-Windsor had sexually assaulted her as a teenager.

Giuffre – who the prince claims never to have met – died by suicide in April 2025 at the age of 41. In addition to denying all allegations against him, Mountbatten-Windsor has also previously insisted he never witnessed or suspected any of the behavior of which Epstein is accused.

World.title: Researcher at Russian plague laboratory dies of ‘unknown’ infection
World.content:
Dozens of people were reported to be in isolation after a Russian laboratory worker at an institute dedicated to studying the plague and other infectious diseases died of an undisclosed illness.

The researcher, a 28-year-old female laboratory technician at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia, in the town of Shelekhov, died after being diagnosed with a pneumonia of “unknown” origin, according to Rospotrebnadzor, the Russian agency that handles infectious disease.

The agency played down the link between the researcher’s death and her work.

“No micro-organisms associated with the employee’s professional duties were detected in samples taken from the patient,” it asserted, adding that the “epidemiological situation” in the region was stable.

Nevertheless, the agency’s head, Anna Yuryevna Popova, traveled to Irkutsk on Friday, according to the local governor, Igor Kobzev, for what he described as an extraordinary meeting of the regional anti-epidemic commission.

The meeting was in connection with a “suspected case of a particularly dangerous infection affecting a resident of the region”, Kobzev said on Telegram.

Reached by phone on Monday, the institute where the researcher worked told CNN it was not commenting on the incident.

Laboratory workers at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East. The Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East/AP

Anti-epidemic measures

Regional authorities are implementing a “comprehensive set of anti-epidemic measures,” according to Maxim Modin, the mayor of the Shelekhovsky district in eastern Russia, near the Mongolian border.

The inpatient facility at the hospital where the worker was treated has been placed under quarantine, and several departments have stopped discharging or admitting patients, Modin said. Other hospitals in the region have also been closed, according to local media reports.

The woman’s death was confirmed by officials last week.

Ekaterina, a resident of Shekelov, told CNN on Monday that there were no visible changes in the city, but locals were anxious. “My acquaintances are slightly panicking,” she said.

Another resident, who wished to remain anonymous, said he was “shocked” by the news.

Unofficial reports, including by the independent regional news outlet Liudi Baikala, have said that nearly 200 people are under observation.

There have been no cases of infectious diseases reported among institute staff over the past 10 days, and all of the employee’s recent contacts are being tested and examined, Modin said.

In its only comment on the incident, the Kremlin said people should only trust updates coming from the official agency.

“One should rely on official statements from Rospotrebnadzor rather than listening to various rumors and speculation,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Monday.

Deadly but not easily transmitted

Angela Rassmussen, a virologist at the Vaccine and Infectious Disease Organization, told CNN that while pneumonic plague is deadly, it is not very transmissible and one would have to be exposed to a high viral load to become sick.

In that sense, it is unlike respiratory illnesses such as COVID, she said.

There is endemic plague among wildlife in parts of Siberia, Rassmussen added.

According to its website, the Anti-Plague Institute employs around 95 researchers and is a major public health facility responsible for monitoring and preventing outbreaks of high-risk bacterial and viral infections across Siberia and Russia’s Far East.

Irkutsk Antiplague Institute Irkutsk Antiplague Institute

The head of the neighboring republic of Buryatia, Alexei Tsydenov, said earlier that the employee died “possibly from the plague.” He also noted that “there are no plague outbreaks” in Buryatia.

Pneumonic plague is one of three types of plagues that are caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis.

The other two types typically spread from contact with infected fleas, animals or infected tissues.

An aluminum plant near the laboratory instructed staff to wear masks as a precautionary measure. The director of Irkutsk Aluminum Plant, Artem Fominikh, noted “conflicting reports” were circulating and called for calm.

The infection in the Irkutsk region is “most likely not the plague, but even if confirmed, there will be no spread of this disease,” a former head of Rospotrebnadzor, Gennady Onishchenko, said on Friday.

Onishchenko told state news agency TASS that the onset of cold weather would likely prevent transmission.

A US State Department spokesperson told CNN Sunday that it was aware of the possible death due to pneumonic plague in Russia.

“We are monitoring the situation closely with the CDC and our other interagency partners,” the spokesperson said. “Many details have not been confirmed. We encourage Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and openly.”

Patients with pneumonic plague develop fever, headache, weakness and and “a rapidly developing pneumonia with shortness of breath, chest pain, cough, and sometimes bloody or watery mucous,” according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

The World Health Organization notes that the plague has a high fatality rate, but is also easily treated with antibiotics.

World.title: Their jobs were among the first to be changed by AI. Now some are trying to avoid it
World.content:
In 2024, software engineer Laura Housh began using AI as a helper for coding and other tasks. Two years later, Housh says she has a love-hate relationship with AI.

“I’ve tried to use it for coding, and I just can’t get behind it,” she said.

AI can provide direction or serve as a second set of eyes, she said, but added that it lacks the context to be truly useful.

Housh isn’t the only one who thinks AI isn’t all that it’s cracked up to be.

Six in 10 tech workers who participated in a new survey say they try to avoid using AI, according to Stack Overflow, a popular question-and-answer site for programmers. The results of Stack Overflow’s 100-question survey, which includes responses from 30,000 software developers in 169 countries, were shared exclusively with CNN ahead of their Tuesday publication.

Software engineers have been at the forefront of the AI shift as one of the first industries to embrace the technology. Both tech giants and startups are increasingly using AI to write code, and “software developer” was ranked as the job most poised to be transformed by AI in an Indeed Hiring Lab report last year.

The survey’s results, like Housh’s experience, provide a glimpse at what that transition has been like for some developers, painting a mixed picture of both rising adoption and uncertainty about how the technology is reshaping their professions.

The Stack Overflow survey showed that 65 percent of responders use coding assistants or agents. Last year, Google’s research division published a survey of 5,000 tech professionals from around the world and found that 90 percent said they use AI in their job — a 14 percent increase from 2024.

But job unhappiness among respondents in Stack Overflow’s survey has also grown compared to last year. Nearly one in three said they are not happy in their current roles, compared to 28.4 percent last year. About 45 percent described themselves as “complacent” with their jobs and only 22.3 percent are “happy.”

The biggest factors among those who are complacent or unhappy are burnout, tech fatigue, economic uncertainty and a lack of clarity about upward mobility in their role.

Many of those anxieties would exist regardless of AI. But the fast pace of AI advancement has “augmented” some of those concerns, according to Stack Overflow CEO Prashanth Chandrasekar.

“People have to completely retool their jobs, and so it is quite unnerving for folks to know exactly how much of what they’re doing will be automated,” Chandrasekar told CNN.

Software developers are grappling with concerns that are more nuanced than whether their jobs will be replaced, according to Chandrasekar. Senior programmers may feel the skills they’ve honed are no longer as relevant, he said. Entry-level workers are expected to operate as if they have three years of experience since “the bar has been raised” because of AI. Tech workers often use their spare time to learn the latest coding tools, he said.

Wires are seen in a Trainium2 UltraServer at an Amazon Web Services QA lab in Austin, Texas, on February 3, 2026. Mark Felix/AFP/Getty Images

AI has its limitations

Housh says she’s familiar with the pressures of learning and keeping up with AI. She said she watches AI-focused videos and reads platform documentation in her personal time — and she still struggles to keep up.

“It’s taxing because you have a lot of noise saying, ‘Do this, do this, do this, or you’ll get left behind,’” she said.

For programmers like Housh and Audrey Eschright, a software engineer with 20 years of experience, it’s not about a lack of desire to embrace the new technology. Rather, the problem is that AI agents have neither the broad general knowledge of an experienced developer nor the job-specific context of a longtime employee.

That can cause friction and more fatigue for developers, said Housh. What’s more, using AI instead of writing code manually can leave developers out of the loop of the solution, Eschright said.

“Writing code is how you solve problems,” said Eschright. “As a software engineer, the process of figuring out what a system does is to change it.”

This sentiment is also captured in Stack Overflow’s survey results. A little more than 74 percent of respondents said AI is useful for implementing code, and about 72 percent said it’s helpful for debugging — but only 34.4 percent say AI is useful for other job functions like communication and design.

The survey showed that just 6.6 percent trust AI with important decisions.

And about 78 percent said that source attribution is important when checking AI-generated code.

Developers are particularly careful about trusting AI today because the stakes are higher as more companies move AI projects from the pilot phase to mainstream use, according to Chandrasekar. A January report from Deloitte found 54 percent of the 3,200-plus business and IT leaders it surveyed expected to move 40 percent or more of their AI experiments into production in the next three to six months.

“I don’t like losing control; I like critical thinking and curiosity,” said Housh. “It’s just so important to be more curious than ever.”

World.title: ‘I’m here to save lives’: Inside the unlikely Biden-Trump partnership to secure a Gaza ceasefire
World.content:
Secure rooms in the US Capitol are cavernous compared to the White House Situation Room. They are designed for full committees or larger gatherings, not intimate discussions. On Nov. 20, 2024, Jake Sullivan and I had gone to one of those rooms to brief our successors two weeks after Donald Trump resoundingly defeated Kamala Harris.

Sullivan was Biden’s national security advisor. His named successor was Mike Waltz, a congressman from Florida. I was Biden’s lead on the Middle East and a chief negotiator on talks to free hostages held by Hamas in Gaza in exchange for a ceasefire with Israel. My named successor was Steve Witkoff — a real-estate tycoon and Trump’s best friend.

Shortly after the election, I had called Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and former Middle East hand. My message was that we had a chance to secure a Gaza deal so long as we could be seen as working together without any daylight between the incoming and outgoing teams. That was a tall order given the polarization in Washington, but it was the only chance we had — and for the first time in months, circumstances trended in our favor.

The hostage talks had collapsed in August, when shortly after Biden, together with the leaders of Egypt and Qatar, presented a new proposal endorsed by Israel, Hamas terrorists murdered six hostages in a tunnel under Rafah, a city in southern Gaza. One of those hostages was Hersh Goldberg-Polin, an American who had been grievously wounded and lost an arm in Hamas’s attacks at the Nova music festival on Oct. 7, 2023, before being taken captive.

People mourn as Hersh Goldberg-Polin is buried during his funeral in Jerusalem on Sept. 2, 2024. Avishag Shaar-Yashuv/The New York Times/Redux

Following the collapse of the negotiations, Israel had won a string of military victories. It started on Sept. 17, 2024, with an operation that exploded thousands of beepers carried by Hezbollah militants in Lebanon. I first heard about what became known as Operation Grim Beeper from a contact in Mossad, Israel’s external intelligence service, who told me, “We just blew the dicks off Hezbollah.”

In many cases, that was not metaphorical.

Hezbollah, like Hamas, a terrorist group backed by Iran, had made the fateful decision to join in the Hamas attack on Israel. On Oct. 8, 2023, it began firing daily rocket barrages into northern Israel, eventually displacing nearly 80,000 people. Israel had been prepared to forgo an operation against Hezbollah if there was a hostage deal. But with no deal in sight, Israel soon followed the beeper operation with a ground assault into the Hezbollah strongholds of southern Lebanon.

By the end of September, Hezbollah’s leader, Hassan Nasrallah, was dead, together with most of his senior lieutenants, buried in an underground Beirut compound.

On Oct. 1, following Nasrallah’s death, Iran made its own foolish — and fateful — decision to launch another massive ballistic missile attack against Israel, following on a failed attack it had launched months earlier. This time, Iran launched nearly two hundred missiles at once, exceeding its earlier salvo.

In the Situation Room that afternoon, as interceptors destroyed incoming missiles at the edge of outer space, we received reports of a direct hit on a college dormitory in Tel Aviv. I was seated just across from Harris, less than five weeks from Election Day. She mouthed, “Oh, shit.” We knew that if Iran inflicted significant Israeli casualties, the Israelis were prepared to launch a massive counterattack into Iran.

White House Coordinator for the Middle East and North Africa Brett McGurk and White House Press Secretary Karine Jean-Pierre listen as National Security Advisor Jake Sullivan speaks on the Iranian missile attacks on Israel at the White House on Oct. 1, 2024. Kent Nishimura/Getty Images

Fortunately, that report, like many first reports, was wrong. Only remnants of a destroyed missile struck the building, causing little damage. The attack was mostly defeated, dismaying the Iranians, who had believed their larger salvo of missiles would be successful.

About two weeks later, on Oct. 16, Israeli forces killed Hamas’s leader, Yahya Sinwar. He was found in Rafah, not far from where Hersh and five other hostages had been shot to death in a tunnel. Sinwar’s death removed a major obstacle to a deal — him — and allowed the Israelis to be more flexible on some terms now that the mastermind of the Oct. 7 attacks could no longer reclaim power. For Israel, it was akin to the United States military killing Osama bin Laden after 9/11.

Finally, on Oct. 26, Israel conducted stealth air attacks against Iran, targeting and destroying many of its strategic air defense systems. We worked closely with the Israelis on this counterattack, walking the Israelis back from a more aggressive response.

Biden told Netanyahu that we would deploy more air defenses to Israel and received assurance from Netanyahu in return that Israel’s response would focus on Iran’s own air defense batteries. The aim was to change the balance of power without triggering a wider war. We messaged Iran’s leaders afterward that their country was now wide open to air attacks should Israel (or the United States) choose to launch them. With Russia bogged down in Ukraine, Iran could not soon replace the destroyed air defense batteries, most of which were Russian and had proved ineffective against Israel’s capabilities. Iran never responded to Israel’s counterattack.

With the tables turned on Iran, Sinwar dead, and Hezbollah’s leadership decimated, we predicted that Hezbollah would soon accept a ceasefire deal with Israel. That would be the moment to return to the Gaza deal — picking up where we had left off in August.

The first major insider account of the high-stakes negotiations to free the hostages taken by Hamas on October 7—written in gripping detail by the American mediator who was in the room through it all. Penguin Random House

My case to Kushner was straightforward. If Israel and Hamas knew that Trump would implement the deal on the table, we had a chance to close it before he took office. But if not, we would lose the best chance we had had since the war began. It was time to seize the moment, and the only way to do that was by working together.

Kushner fully agreed.

He told me that he would not be joining the new administration but said my successor on the Middle East was someone close to Trump, a pragmatic problem-solver who would want to work with me to the extent appropriate. He did not mention Witkoff, whose name emerged days later as Trump’s likely Middle East envoy.

Biden invited Trump to the Oval on Nov. 13, 2024, mostly for a one-on-one. When the cameras came in briefly, Biden promised a smooth transition. “Politics is tough,” Trump said. “And it’s in many cases not a very nice world, but it is a nice world today, and I appreciate very much a transition that is so smooth, it’ll be as smooth as it can get.”

President Joe Biden meets with US President-elect Donald Trump in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, DC, on Nov. 13, 2024. Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty Images

I saw Biden afterward. Unlike many Democrats at the time who saw the election as an existential disaster, Biden — at least with me — was focused on working with the incoming team wherever we could. That was especially so on the hostage crisis.

According to Biden, the two presidents agreed to coordinate, setting the stage for my meeting with Sullivan, Waltz, and Witkoff seven days later.

In the secure room at the Capitol, Sullivan snapped open a document pouch and arrayed briefing materials in front of him, including maps of the region and background on Iran’s nuclear program. We sat alone at a large table, waiting for Trump’s team to arrive.

Waltz entered, followed by Witkoff. The former was a retired military officer with perfect hair and rod-straight posture. The latter was a brash real estate developer known for carrying a pistol in a sock through the alleys and streets of New York, where he built a multibillion-dollar empire. Both exhibited a lighthearted manner, something that I had lost handling the Gaza crisis, where tens of thousands had died, over one hundred hostages remained in tunnels underground and the region stood on the brink of an all-out war.

The meeting began awkwardly, the four of us standing at the corner of the large table in the oversize room, introducing ourselves by titles. Waltz took his seat, and we followed.

“Trump told us to solve everything, that’s our mission,” Witkoff said, laughing.

“Solve it!” Waltz added.

Senator JD Vance, the incoming vice president, popped in unexpectedly. We stood. He asked what we were talking about, and when we said the Middle East, he told us that was his cue to leave. (Run as fast as you can, I thought.) Vance, Waltz, and Witkoff discussed recent calls they’d each had with Trump, comparing notes on what they had heard — apparently different things. The calls had come at all hours, and Waltz asked both men whether Trump ever slept. Witkoff answered, “I’ve known him for forty years, the answer is — no, not very much.”

“Force of nature,” Waltz remarked.

In this February 2025 photo, US Special Envoy to the Middle East Steve Witkoff and then-US National Security Advisor Mike Waltz speak to reporters outside of the West Wing of the White House in Washington, DC. Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP/Getty Images

Witkoff explained that he had been Trump’s real-estate attorney before branching out on his own. “I’ve had success, but there’s only one Trump,” he told us. Vance came around the table to shake my hand, and Sullivan’s. He said he wanted to work with us during the transition period, which seemed sincere, and then left the room.

With a map on the table, Sullivan walked through what had changed in the Middle East since the hostage talks collapsed in August. It was head-spinning even for those of us who had been living and breathing the issues every day since then. For Witkoff, I recounted my difficult experience on the hostage talks, and explained why we might now, finally, have a shot.

Of course, for that to happen we had to be seen — by both Hamas and Israel — as working together, as both parties would demand to know Trump’s views.

“The only reason I’m here is to save lives,” Witkoff said. “It’s the most noble thing anyone can do with their life, to save another life. So, I’m all in, count on it.”

He asked what we needed from him, and from Trump. I took out the text. Every detail of a carefully negotiated agreement — from the extent of Israel’s redeployment during a ceasefire, to the timing and sequence of hostages and prisoner exchanges, to the minute-by-minute details on delivery of humanitarian assistance with the guns silent — was reflected in a package of texts that had been hammered over months shuttling between Doha, Jerusalem, and Cairo.

A tent is surrounded by rubble in Jabaliya, northern Gaza, on February 10, 2025. Saher Alghorra/The New York Times/Redux

The outstanding issue was agreement from Hamas on the hostages to come out during the first stage of the ceasefire, a category that included women, the elderly, and the sick or wounded, something the group still had never seriously engaged on. There would not be a hostage deal, I explained, without an agreed list of the hostages to be released.

Witkoff claimed that he knew most of the leaders in the Middle East from his real-estate business, and he asked whether we’d be comfortable with his traveling to the region to reengage and to preview his new role. Sullivan said that would be fine, so long as he was not negotiating, and kept in close contact with me before and afterward. Witkoff wrote down his number, and we agreed to speak regularly from that moment forward.

For the remainder of the briefing, we discussed Iran. With Trump entering office and Iran now vulnerable to direct attack, the Israelis believed Tehran might race to enrich uranium to weapons grade — the precursor for a nuclear bomb. Throughout the crisis, since Oct. 7, Iran had been enriching uranium to 60% grade, a step away from the 90% required for a bomb. It was the only country in the world without a weapons program to do so.

The previous week, Sullivan had convened the Principals Committee to war-game the scenario of Iran enriching to weapons grade. Participants were unanimous that if we saw such indications, we’d recommend a US military strike against Iran’s nuclear facilities, including its deeply buried facility at Fordow. The operation had been rehearsed over the past year should the president — or a future president — need it. We dispatched a message to Iran’s leaders warning them not to think about escalating their nuclear program.

Witkoff raised his hands. “Trump says I’ve got Iran, but maybe I don’t want it. Are you f**king kidding with all of this?”

Finally, Saudi Arabia. We reviewed a package of agreements that we had completed on a deal for normalization between Israel and Saudi Arabia, before the Oct. 7 crisis. I explained that the deal might be possible over Trump’s term, so long as Gaza could be settled. Netanyahu’s hard-right coalition government made everything more difficult, but it might not outlast Israel’s next election in 2026. (These elections are now scheduled for later this month.)

Witkoff came around to my side of the table. He extended his hand: “I’m here to save lives. I don’t give one shit about politics. If we save one life, we save the world.”

The table was now set for that, I assured him.

World.title: Coptic Orthodox Church congratulates al-Sisi, Armed forces on October victory anniversary
World.content:
The Coptic Orthodox Church, headed by Pope Tawadros II, congratulated on Sunday, October 4, 2026, President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces, the Armed Forces and the Egyptian people on the 53rd anniversary of the October Victories.

In a statement Sunday, the church said the anniversary would remain firmly embedded in the memory of Egyptians, adding that the “spirit of October” would continue to inspire Egyptians from all walks of life to advance their country and confront domestic and external challenges.

The Church reaffirmed its support for all efforts serving the nation and stressed its commitment to contributing to preserving national unity and strengthening social cohesion.

It also expressed confidence in the wisdom of the state leadership, the patriotic commitment of its institutions and their ability to overcome various challenges.

The church prayed for Egypt’s leadership and people, wishing the country continued progress and prosperity.

World.title: Agriculture Minister: Agriculture Museum, Egypt Flower Exhibition open free for 3 days for October Victory celebrations
World.content:
Minister of Agriculture and Land Reclamation Alaa Farouk has decided to open the Agricultural Museum and Egypt Flower Exhibition in Dokki, Giza, free of charge to visitors on October 8, 9 and 10, as part of celebrations marking the October 6 Victory.

The minister directed that all halls of the Agricultural Museum be opened free of charge, allowing visitors to explore Egypt’s agricultural history and development through the ages.

The museum features heritage collections, scientific exhibits, the Plant Wealth Hall, the Cotton Museum, Ancient Egyptian Agriculture Hall, and halls covering the Greek, Roman, Coptic and Islamic periods, as well as the Syrian Hall and the Egyptian-Chinese Friendship Museum.

Farouk also called for a range of cultural, artistic and entertainment activities throughout the celebrations, targeting different age groups and Egyptian families.

The Agricultural Museum is one of the world’s largest agricultural museums, covering nearly 30 feddans and housing rare collections documenting the development of agriculture in Egypt from the Pharaonic era to modern times.

The Egypt Flower Exhibition operates year-round on an area of 15,000 square meters, featuring more than 80 exhibitors specializing in flowers, ornamental plants and landscaping.

It offers visitors an opportunity to enjoy green spaces and scenic views alongside a tour of the historic Agricultural Museum.

The flower exhibition is open daily from nine am to nine pm, while the Agricultural Museum’s halls are open to visitors until three pm.

World.title: PM reviews efforts to provide fertilizer supplies, regulate distribution to farmers
World.content:
Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly on Sunday, October 4, 2026, held a meeting to review efforts to provide agricultural fertilizers and the latest steps to regulate their distribution to farmers.

The meeting was attended by Finance Minister Ahmed Kouchouk, Agriculture and Land Reclamation Minister Alaa Farouk, Industry Minister Khaled Hashem, and officials from several relevant entities.

The Premier stressed the State’s commitment to supporting the agricultural sector, citing President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi’s continued directives to support farmers through an integrated vision that maximizes the sector’s resources and potential.

This support will help expand cultivated areas, diversify crops, particularly strategic ones, strengthen food security, meet domestic demand for various crops and increase agricultural exports, Madbouly added.

The Prime M1inister highlighted the government’s continued keenness to ensure the availability of all requirements for agricultural production, including the necessary fertilizers, in a way that boosts crop productivity and helps achieve further social and economic targets for both farmers and the State.

The meeting also tackled measures being taken in coordination with relevant entities to strengthen oversight of the agricultural fertilizer distribution system, ensuring that subsidized fertilizers reach eligible farmers and that the support provided for this purpose does not go to ineligible recipients.

It also followed up on efforts to supply fertilizers to farmers through agricultural cooperatives across the country, as well as measures to improve oversight of fertilizer distribution and allocation to eligible farmers, thereby enhancing transparency and efficiency.

World.title: Egypt unveils vision to develop human capital for expanding transport sector
World.content:
The Ministry of Transport reviewed the state’s plans to develop specialized human resources needed to keep pace with the rapid expansion of the transport sector and its growing infrastructure projects.

The ministry presented its vision during a World Bank-hosted workshop titled “Investing in Human Capital for the Future of Transport in Egypt: Moving Forward with the Vision of Establishing the Egyptian International University for Transport Engineering and Technology (ENUT),” attended by South Korea’s ambassador to Egypt.

The workshop explored cooperation with leading Korean institutions, including the Korea International Cooperation Agency (KOICA), Korea National University of Transportation (KNUT), Korea Maritime and Ocean University (KMOU), Korea National Railway and Hyundai Rotem, as well as international development partners.

The ministry said in a statement Sunday that Egypt has invested more than two trillion LE since 2014 to develop and modernize its transport system, covering roads, railways, public transport, ports and logistics networks.

Against the backdrop of continued expansion, the ministry is advancing the establishment of ENUT as a specialized institution combining academic education, technical and vocational training, applied research, innovation, and technology transfer, it added.

The university aims to prepare specialists capable of meeting the current and future needs of Egypt’s transport sector.

The project is being developed in cooperation with the World Bank, the Korea Green Growth Trust Fund (KGGTF) and Korean academic and technical partners.

It is intended to eventually make ENUT a regional center for transport education, training, applied research and capacity building serving Egypt as well as the Middle East and Africa.

World.title: Liberia: Naymote Demands Probe Into Alleged Political Favoritism Over Lofa’s India Training Slot
World.content:
MONROVIA — Naymote Partners for Democratic Development is calling for an independent investigation into the selection of Lofa County’s representative for an African-Asian Rural Development Organization (AARDO)-supported training program in India, amid allegations that a politically connected individual was selected while the county’s designated Development Officer was excluded.

Naymote said its concerns stem from a participant list showing that County Development Officers are representing other participating counties, while Lofa County is represented by an individual identified as a “County Technical Assistant”—a position the organization says it has not been able to verify within Lofa County’s current administrative structure.

According to Naymote, its preliminary inquiries indicate that Henry Bundoo, reportedly a Foya District Coordinator for Local Government Minister Francis Sakila Nyumalin’s political movement, is occupying Lofa County’s slot in the training.



Naymote said Francis Egu Lasanna, whom it identifies as Lofa County’s Development Officer, was instead left out.

The organization stressed, however, that the alleged political relationship between Bundoo and Minister Nyumalin, as well as whether that connection influenced his selection, has not been independently established.

Still, Naymote said the circumstances warrant scrutiny because County Development Officers have formal responsibilities for development planning, implementation, monitoring and reporting.

“Training intended to strengthen those functions should benefit officials who legitimately hold the relevant responsibilities and can apply the learning within county institutions upon return,” Naymote said.

The organization warned that if political considerations displaced the appropriate county official, Lofa County could have lost an opportunity to strengthen its development capacity.

“Such conduct would place personal political interests ahead of public responsibilities and undermine confidence in the Ministry’s commitment to accountable decentralization,” Naymote said.

Calls for Minister to Explain Selection

Naymote is calling on the Minister of Local Government to clarify Bundoo’s official appointment status, substantive duties and authority to represent Lofa County at the international training.

The organization is also demanding an explanation as to why the county’s Development Officer was not selected.

The Ministry, Naymote said, should verify that all participants are legitimate nominees and that their official responsibilities correspond with the objectives of the training program.

The group further called on the Office of the Ombudsman to investigate whether any conflict of interest, political favoritism or misuse of public authority played a role in determining Lofa County’s representation.

Naymote said any investigation should establish the facts, provide an opportunity for those implicated to respond and determine whether corrective measures or referral to other competent authorities are warranted.

“If improper influence is established,” Naymote said, “the President of Liberia and the responsible authorities should ensure appropriate accountability and restore the county’s access to the intended institutional benefit,” in coordination with AARDO and the Indian training hosts.

Political Connection Alone Not Proof of Wrongdoing

Naymote acknowledged that political association, by itself, does not constitute proof of wrongdoing.

But the organization argued that public authority should not be used to reward political loyalty at the expense of county development.

“Officials entrusted with decentralization must protect the interests of the communities they serve,” Naymote said.

The organization is also urging the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and other relevant government institutions to verify the official status and substantive responsibilities of nominees selected for internationally sponsored government training programs.

Naymote said it intends to seek clarification from AARDO and the relevant Indian partners through appropriate channels.

The organization commended the County Development Officers from Bong, Sinoe, River Gee, Rivercess, Margibi, Grand Bassa and Grand Gedeh counties who are participating in the training, urging them to use the opportunity to strengthen their knowledge, build professional networks and return better equipped to support county institutions.

Naymote said it remains committed to constructive engagement with the Ministry of Local Government, but stressed that a prompt, documented response and impartial investigation are necessary to protect the integrity of the training partnership, strengthen public confidence and safeguard Lofa County’s development interests.

World.title: Liberia: No Indictment After 47 Days as Justice Minister Denies Offering US$500K to Star Witness in Former Vice President Case
World.content:
Monrovia – When the Government of Liberia charged former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor in August, officials spoke with confidence. The state said it had the evidence. It said the case was strong.

By Rodney D. Sieh

Forty-seven days later, there is still no indictment.



Howard-Taylor was stopped at Roberts International Airport on August 19 before she could board a flight to Accra, where she was due to speak at a forum. She was charged with drug trafficking, money laundering and conspiracy linked to an alleged transnational narcotics network. She has denied every charge. Her bail request was denied, and she has since been moved from Monrovia Central Prison to house arrest.

Now, a question is circulating in legal and political circles in Monrovia: is the state’s case stuck because its most important witness won’t take the stand without being paid?

The man at the center

Almost every road in the state’s case runs through one man: Sheikh Bashiru Kante.

During the preliminary examination at the Monrovia City Court, the state’s first witness, acting Crime Services Commissioner Raphael A. Wilson, testified that Kante, himself an alleged co-conspirator, voluntarily surrendered his cellphone, and that forensic analysis found WhatsApp messages and audio recordings linking him to Howard-Taylor.

According to Wilson, the alleged cartel was led by a man identified as “Nicholas,” who met Kante in Dubai in 2021, and Kante later connected the group to Howard-Taylor. The charging documents say she received US$135,000 from people linked to the cartel, including US$75,000 allegedly channeled through Kante for her Jewel Star Fish Foundation.

In other words, the alleged introduction, the alleged money and the alleged recordings all come from Kante.

The US$500,000 claim

Sources close to the defense told FrontPageAfrica that the government, not Kante, initiated contact, and that the state has since built its case so heavily around him that it now cannot proceed without him.

According to those sources, Kante is demanding US$500,000 before he testifies. They say he wants to take the money out of Liberia, deposit it in a bank of his choosing, and only then return to take the stand. He reportedly claims he fears for his life from supporters of the former NPFL, the National Patriotic Party and the Congress for Democratic Change, and that he does not trust the government.

The sources say the government has refused, and the two sides are at a deadlock.

FrontPageAfrica could not independently confirm the claim. The government, through Justice Minister Betty Lamin Blamo has denied offering Kante US$500,000 or any payment to testify against the former vice president.

A witness with a past

Kante’s credibility has been questioned since the case began. A court record shows he was arrested in Maryland in the United States on April 20, 2022, on wire fraud and money laundering charges unrelated to narcotics. His name also surfaced in a 2022 controversy over a Liberian diplomatic passport he held despite having no formal diplomatic role. Then-President George Weah ordered an investigation, and Howard-Taylor’s office at the time denied arranging the passport.

In August, Bong County Representative Marvin Cole openly questioned Kante’s reliability. “You can’t have Sheikh passing all around going to night clubs drinking champagne and trying to blackmail other people by giving information,” Cole said on Sky FM. “How authentic that the information Sheikh is providing can be proven in court?”

“The Grand Jury is not sitting”

The government’s explanation for the delay is that the Grand Jury is not in session. Last month, prosecutors were expected to argue that Howard-Taylor could be held pending the Grand Jury term, which at the time was expected later in September. That term has come and gone without an indictment.

Her defense says the law offers a way around this. They point to Section 15.5 of the Criminal Procedure Law, which allows a Circuit Court judge, on application by the prosecution showing the public interest requires it, to summon fifteen people to serve as a special Grand Jury with the same powers as a regular one.

“If the government truly possesses the ‘overwhelming evidence’ it has repeatedly claimed,” one source close to the defense said, “then the public is entitled to ask a simple question: why has there been no indictment, and why does the entire case appear to depend on one witness?”

Legal experts consulted by The Analyst newspaper last week made a similar point, saying the absence of a Grand Jury indictment after 41 days of restraint was constitutionally significant.

What’s at stake

For the government, the case is a centerpiece of its crackdown on drug trafficking, coming after the seizure of four tonnes of cocaine valued at US$317 million in July.

For Howard-Taylor, a former senator, former vice president and former first lady, every day without an indictment is another day under restraint without formal charges from a Grand Jury.

And for the Liberian public, the question is simple. Either the state has the case it says it has, or it doesn’t. Until a Grand Jury sits, no one will know.

World.title: Liberia: NOCAL, Nigeria’s LADOL Sign Deal to Build Oil Shorebase in Buchanan
World.content:
Monrovia – The last time a major oil company drilled off Liberia’s coast, much of the money never touched Liberian soil.

By Rodney D. Sieh

When ExxonMobil drilled the Mesurado-1 well in late 2016, its operations were based out of Abidjan, in neighbouring Côte d’Ivoire. Supply boats, logistics, waste handling and technical support were all organized from across the border. In the end, the well came up dry and was plugged and abandoned, and Liberia was left with neither oil nor much to show from the drilling itself.



The National Oil Company of Liberia (NOCAL) now says it does not intend to let that happen again.

On Friday in London, NOCAL signed a Joint Development Agreement (JDA) with the Lagos Deep Offshore Logistics Base (LADOL), a Nigerian company that runs one of Africa’s largest oil and gas shorebases in Lagos. Under the deal, the two will work toward building and operating a logistics base in Buchanan, Grand Bassa County, to serve oil companies drilling offshore.

“We are determined to correct that narrative as we prepare for our next set of drilling programs,” NOCAL President and CEO Fabian M. Lai said. “Our goal is to ensure that the jobs, the contracts, the training, and the ancillary services that support our petroleum operations are performed by Liberian companies and create opportunities for Liberian citizens right here in Liberia.”

What the deal covers

LADOL will serve as technical lead partner, funding and conducting the feasibility study, coordinating engineering design, and partnering with NOCAL to build and run the facility. NOCAL says the study should begin within the next 45 days and run for six months.

It will look at land, waterfront and marine access, utilities, commercial viability, geotechnical and topographical surveys, and the early scoping of an Environmental and Social Impact Assessment.

The agreement also sets up a Joint Steering Committee to oversee progress and commits both sides to negotiating final project agreements. The two companies have also signed confidentiality and non-circumvention clauses.

LADOL Executive Chairman Sir Oladipo Ladi Jadesimi said the company sees itself as more than a financier. “We are not just investors; we are partners in building a sustainable future for Liberia’s oil and gas industry,” he said, adding that the shorebase could help ensure “Liberian businesses and workers are the primary beneficiaries of the country’s natural resources.”

Why now

The timing follows a burst of activity in Liberia’s offshore sector after years of quiet. In September 2025, the Liberia Petroleum Regulatory Authority signed four Production Sharing Contracts with Atlas/Oranto Petroleum for offshore blocks LB-15, LB-16, LB-22 and LB-24, an agreement that followed a recent deal with TotalEnergies.

More blocks are in play. Last month, Australia’s Bounty Oil & Gas agreed to acquire the company holding exclusive rights to the LB-32 offshore block, a right that stems from a letter of commitment issued by NOCAL in October 2025. That contract still has to be negotiated and go before Parliament for approval.

If any of these companies move to drilling, they will need a base on land. NOCAL is betting that if Buchanan is ready, they won’t need to look to Abidjan.

A long wait for oil

Liberia has been chasing an oil discovery for more than a decade. Before Mesurado-1, other companies had drilled off the coast, and Exxon’s well was seen at the time as the latest blow to Liberia’s hopes of emulating the exploration success of Ghana and Senegal. Exxon later pulled out of Block LB-13.

For residents of Buchanan, a port city that has watched iron ore and other resources pass through for decades, the question will be whether this project delivers real jobs for local people or becomes another promise on paper. The feasibility study, due in roughly seven months, will be the first real test.
