World.title: Nigeria: Nigerian Military Plane Crashes with 32 Onboard, Aviation Minister Says
World.content:
PREMIUM TIMES reported the crash on Monday morning, with the Nigerian Air Force saying the aircraft was travelling on a routine mission from Benin to Lagos.

There were 32 people on board a military aircraft that crashed in Ondo State on Monday, the Minister of Aviation, Festus Keyamo, said in a post on X.

PREMIUM TIMES reported the crash on Monday morning, with the Nigerian Air Force saying the aircraft was travelling on a routine mission from Benin to Lagos.

In his first official statement on the crash, Mr Keyamo said, "Preliminary information suggests that there were 25 passengers and 7 crew members on board."



Search and rescue operations are still ongoing, and the casualty figure from the crash has yet to be determined.

Read the minister's full statement below.

"I regret to inform the general public that Air Traffic Controllers have informed me of the disappearance of a military aircraft with tail number NGR 931, enroute Lagos from Benin at 0913 hours earlier today. All efforts to raise the aircraft on radio proved abortive.

"Subsequently information however confirmed that the military aircraft has crashed close to the Naval Base in Igbokoda, Ondo State. The wreckage has been located and search and rescue operations are ongoing.

Preliminary information suggests that there were 25 passengers and 7 crew members on board.

Whilst the control and regulation of military aircraft are completely outside the authority of the Ministry of Aviation, and Civil Aviation Authority, I have just spoken to the Chief of Air Staff, Air Marshal Sunday Kelvin Aneke and pledged our total cooperation and assistance in the search and rescue efforts ongoing.

Further information on this unfortunate incident will be made available subsequently.

World.title: Mozambique: Mozambique's Army Is Losing a Crucial Counter-Insurgency Battle
World.content:
analysis

Foreign training has strengthened the army, but abuses against civilians undermine the community support needed to defeat insurgents.

When terrorists attacked Cabo Delgado nine years ago on 5 October 2017, the Mozambique Defence Armed Forces (FADM) was taken by surprise, despite its three decades of experience fighting armed conflicts inside the country.

Until then, Mozambique had been largely spared the terrorist threats experienced by other African countries and beyond. The FADM had scant control over Cabo Delgado province and was unprepared for a rural guerrilla war imposed by local jihadists with external support. It lacked combat capability, logistics, modern military equipment, air combat assets and military intelligence.



The FADM has since benefitted from substantial external training and efforts to improve logistics and equipment. But this has yet to translate into results on the ground, where communities still suffer inadequate security and human rights violations at the hands of state forces. And it is in these communities that the FADM should be gaining the upper hand against insurgents.

Insurgents' seizure of district capitals and TotalEnergies subsequent suspension of its US$20 billion gas extraction project in 2021 forced the government to request external support, some of which benefitted the FADM.

The Southern African Development Community Mission in Mozambique (SAMIM) helped the FADM dismantle terrorist bases and neutralise leaders, restore state authority, strengthen maritime security and protect access routes within the province. The Rwanda Defence Force (RDF) helped recover territories key to the gas industry's logistics and trained the FADM in counter-terrorism, as did the European Union (EU), Algeria, United States (US) and other allies.

Of all these programmes, the EU's has had the greatest impact, channelling roughly €89 million into training and the acquisition of non-lethal equipment. The EU Training Mission in Mozambique trained over 1 600 military personnel, divided into 11 FADM Quick Reaction Force companies. The courses covered command and control, communication, civil-military cooperation, human rights and international humanitarian law.

Mozambique reactivated its military cooperation with Algeria, focusing on operational training, counter-terrorism and technical capacity building for army personnel. Specialised training of an FADM battalion currently underway in Algeria is expected to include tactical instruction, among other elements.

Through the US' Joint Combined Exchange Training programme, the FADM receives instruction in small-unit tactics, operational planning, combat medical care and civil protection.

These initiatives are gradually transforming the FADM's capabilities and increasing the survival rates of military personnel. However, inadequate logistics and equipment remain a major operational weakness, with much of FADM's gear originating from Russia and China. Military personnel report obsolete and non-functional weaponry, which has led to deaths on the battlefield, and insufficient transport for troops and for evacuating the injured.

In response, the Ministry of National Defence has built partnerships to secure logistics, supplies and equipment for the FADM. In March, an agreement was signed with India to supply defence equipment and transfer technology for the assembly and repair of aircraft, land vehicles and patrol vessels.

In 2024, a defence cooperation agreement with Turkey was ratified by Mozambique's Council of Ministers to develop an industry focused on military aviation and weapons, combat vehicles and the manufacture of naval assets.

The US is providing US$1.5 million for a new programme to strengthen Mozambique's capacity to manage and secure weapons and ammunition, and to reduce the risk of conventional weapons being diverted to criminal and terrorist groups.

However, the impact of these partnerships has yet to be felt on the ground. Since SAMIM's withdrawal in mid-2024, the FADM has independently led offensives, patrols along major roads, and established defensive positions to contain terrorists' advance. But weaknesses are showing.

Terrorist groups that had been confined to remote bases regained momentum and began attacks on major roads to steal food, abduct drivers and passengers, and demand ransoms. Joint police and FADM escorts were introduced, but the insurgents staged deadly ambushes, killing police officers, soldiers and civilians.

Human rights violations are another problem. Mozambican troops have repeatedly been accused of sexually exploiting displaced women, killing civilians suspected of collaborating with terrorist groups and committing war crimes against captured terror suspects. While the EU's training emphasises human rights, reports of civilians being killed by the FADM continue.

With training provided to the FADM by various countries, the problem of multiple military doctrines hinders a coherent approach to human rights. And Mozambique's political leadership has not clarified the matter. In his September speech marking the FADM's 62nd anniversary, none of President Daniel Chapo's recommendations addressed the need to respect human rights in counter-terrorism operations.

This is where Mozambique is losing the war against terrorism. As long as the FADM fails to gain the support of local communities in Cabo Delgado, the insurgents will keep thriving. They do not need to be militarily superior to government troops, as they are characterised by small, lightly armed bands practising guerrilla warfare.

Close 

To survive, they need to hide from government forces, which is made possible by the rough terrain, poor road access and distance from the centres of state power. And they benefit from local communities who agree not to report insurgents to government agents.

Effective counter-insurgency requires government forces to distinguish between active rebels and non-combatant community members. Rather than being targeted or killed by security forces, these community members should be encouraged to cooperate by reporting the insurgents' presence.

The recent establishment of a counter-terrorism centre offers hope that Mozambique can benefit from interagency coordination to better plan and conduct its counter-insurgency operations. But for this to happen, the FADM must reverse its culture of human rights abuses against communities affected by the insurgency and foster effective civil-military cooperation.

For permission to re-publish ISS Today articles, please email us. In South Africa, News24 has exclusive rights to republish ISS Today articles. In Nigeria, Premium Times has exclusive rights to republish ISS Today articles.

Borges Nhamirre, Researcher, Transnational Threats and Organised Crime, ISS

World.title: Nigeria: 28 Killed Despite Curfew in Plateau
World.content:
At least 28 people have been killed in a renewed wave of attacks across three local government areas of Plateau State despite a dusk-to-dawn curfew imposed by the state government on September 21 to restore peace and prevent further loss of life.

The affected areas, including Mangu, Bokkos and Barkin Ladi, have witnessed repeated attacks in recent weeks, leaving thousands of residents living in fear, disrupting farming and cattle grazing and forcing many people to abandon their livelihoods.

Daily Trust reports that the latest incident occurred yesterday where two people were killed and six others injured following an attack on Sunday evening on Fulani herders in a pick up vehicle around Total filling station in Bukuru, Jos South Local Government Area of Plateau State.



The latest attack occurred less than two weeks after gunmen attacked herders around Kassa community of Barkin Ladi, killing five and injuring one.

The state chairman of Miyetti Allah Cattle Breeders Association of Nigeria (MACBAN), Ibrahim Yusuf Babayo, who confirmed the incident in Jos yesterday said the gunmen attacked the vehicle around 5:30 while they were returning from the Cattle market to Bassa LGA of the state.

The chairman condemned the incident and called on the security agencies to track down those responsible and bring them to justice. He described the attack unprovoked and disturbing.

He said the insured victims have been rushed to the hospital, adding that one person was missing.

The spokespersons of Operation Enduring Peace and State Police command, Captained Polycarp Oteh and SP Alabo Alfred, didn't respond to inquiries from our correspondent as of press time.

Plateau had continued to witness attacks and killings despite the curfew imposed by the government.

In September alone, many people, including men, women and children, were reportedly killed, while houses and farmlands were destroyed and hundreds of cattle shot dead. The attacks have displaced families and disrupted economic activities across several communities.

Worried by the deteriorating security situation, the Plateau State government, through the Commissioner for Information and Communication, Joyce Ramnap, imposed an immediate dusk-to-dawn curfew on Barkin Ladi, Bokkos and Mangu on September 21.

The restriction of movement, which took effect that day, runs from 6pm to 6am daily until further notice. The government said the measure was intended to enable security agencies to stabilise the affected areas, protect lives and prevent a breakdown of law and order.

Security operatives were also directed to enforce the curfew and a ban on motorcycles in the affected areas.

However, the measure has failed to halt the killings, with several attacks recorded after its imposition.

The development has raised fresh concerns about the effectiveness of the security measures and the ability of security agencies to protect residents in the volatile communities.

More killings after curfew

Meanwhile, the attacks have continued despite the curfew and the visit of the Inspector-General of Police, Olatunji Disu, to the state on September 16 following killings in Mangu and other parts of Plateau.

During his visit, Disu said the police were committed to restoring peace and strengthening security operations in the state.

He assured residents that the police would continue to work with stakeholders to find lasting solutions to the crisis, stressing that sustainable peace required synergy and collaboration between security agencies and communities.

But fresh attacks were recorded in the affected communities.

On September 20, five Fulani herders were killed in Kassa community, Barkin Ladi, while transporting cattle from Bokkos to Jos South.

The following day, the state government announced the curfew.

On September 22, gunmen reportedly ambushed security operatives attached to Operation Rainbow along Gagshi Road, killing a police officer. Three Berom farmers were also reportedly killed at Rakok community in Barkin Ladi on the same day.

In Mangu, three vigilantes of Mwaghavul extraction were ambushed and killed at the Kyikyau-Gyambwas boundary.

Two Berom miners were killed at Gangare community, Barkin Ladi, on September 23 while carrying out mining operations.

The following day, a 27-year-old Fulani herder was killed, and 30 cattle reportedly rustled around Banka village in Mangu.

On September 25, three vigilantes, including a youth leader, were killed in Kassa community, Barkin Ladi. The attackers reportedly stormed the community around 1am and opened fire on the victims, who were said to be on duty protecting the area.

The killings prompted protests, with residents reportedly calling on soldiers stationed in the area to leave, expressing frustration over repeated attacks despite the presence of security personnel.

On September 26, five miners were killed and two others injured when gunmen ambushed them at Marit community in Barkin Ladi.

The violence spread further on September 27 when gunmen attacked a herding community in Lamor, Pushit District of Mangu. More than 20 cattle were reportedly killed, while several others were injured and more than 70 remained missing.

A Fulani herder was also killed around Rakung village in Barkin Ladi on the same day.

On September 28, three women working at a mining site in Rakum community, Barkin Ladi, were killed and another person injured after gunmen opened fire at the site.

A 14-year-old Fulani herder, Aliyu Ismail, was reportedly killed around Wereng community in Riyom Local Government Area on October 1.

The latest reported attack occurred on October 3 when two Berom men from Heipang District, Barkin Ladi, were shot dead at a mining site around Kuru Jenta, near the boundary between Jos South and Barkin Ladi.

Livelihoods paralysed

Beyond the deaths, the prolonged violence has severely affected economic activities, with farmers and herders suspending operations in parts of Mangu, Riyom and Barkin Ladi because of fear of attacks.

Residents said they were no longer able to freely access farms or grazing areas located far from their communities.

A resident of Dorowa Babuje in Barkin Ladi, Paul David, described the situation as chaotic.

"We cannot go to the farm freely like before because you don't know who is hunting for your life. We are no longer going to the farm as we used to. Farms that are far from the community cannot be accessed," he said.

A herder in Lugere, Barkin Ladi, Habibu Ibrahim, said grazing had also become difficult because herders risked being attacked or having their cattle rustled.

"We don't graze our cattle the way we used to because you can easily be attacked and killed. It is very difficult to move around because your life is at risk. We are being hunted by gunmen," he said.

Another farmer from Bokkos, Christopher Rafan, said the crisis had forced farmers to change their farming practices.

He said his cousin was killed while returning from the farm, adding that residents no longer planted tall crops such as maize and guinea corn close to communities because the crops could obstruct their view of approaching attackers.

He urged the government to intensify security in the villages, noting that some of the volatile rural communities were not covered by the curfew.

A herder in Riyom, Musa Abdullahi, also said grazing had become restricted because herders could no longer safely move long distances with their cattle.

A crisis with deep roots

The latest violence has further deepened longstanding tensions between Berom and Fulani communities, with leaders of the two groups trading accusations over responsibility for attacks on their members.

The rivalry, often complicated by farmer-herder disputes, land ownership and the longstanding indigene-settler divide, has claimed hundreds of lives and destroyed communities over the years.

The crisis also has an ethno-religious dimension dating back to the violent conflict that erupted in Jos in September 2001. The initial dispute later escalated into wider religious violence, leaving hundreds dead and many more displaced.

Since then, mistrust between Christian and Muslim communities has persisted, with accusations and counter-accusations often following fresh attacks.

The violence later spread into rural communities, particularly through farmer-herder conflicts, resulting in killings, destruction of property and displacement.

A committee set up by Governor Caleb Mutfwang and chaired by General Nicholas Rogers (retd.) to investigate the root causes of the crisis reportedly disclosed that about 11,000 people had been killed in Plateau over two decades.

Successive federal and state governments have established committees and introduced various initiatives aimed at ending the violence, but the attacks have continued.

Non-governmental organisations have also been working to complement government efforts through dialogue, mediation and community resilience programmes.

Close 

Organisations including the Centre for Humanitarian Dialogue, Youth Initiative Against Violence and Human Rights Abuse, CLEEN Foundation and Justice, Development and Peace Commission have facilitated inter-community dialogue, mapped conflict drivers and supported local peace structures.

The efforts have produced peace accords in some flashpoint areas, including Riyom and Barkin Ladi, where communities agreed on responsible grazing, early reporting of incidents and measures to curb criminality and drug abuse.

However, the latest attacks have shown the fragility of the peace efforts.

The Executive Director of YIAVHA, Pwakim Jacob Choji, said the government needed to invest more in social cohesion and community dialogue.

Choji said growing grievances against government were undermining public confidence and contributing to the security challenges.

The Director of the Civil Liberties Organisation, Steve Aluko, said the crisis could be resolved if the government addressed what he described as wrong profiling of criminal elements, weak enforcement of justice and inadequate security presence in difficult terrains.

He also advocated state policing and a regional security architecture that would combine intelligence gathering, analysis and appropriate deployment of security personnel.

The Vice Chancellor of Plateau State University, Bokkos, Professor Shedrack Best, identified inadequate youth participation in peacebuilding as one of the factors sustaining the crisis.

Best, a professor of International Relations and Peace Building, said many peace initiatives were targeted at traditional, religious and community leaders, while youths at the grassroots, who often bear the brunt of the violence, were left out.

He urged stakeholders to organise peacebuilding programmes in villages and directly involve young people from the affected communities.

He commended the Plateau State Peace Building Agency for taking peace initiatives to villages and local government areas.

With 28 people killed despite the curfew and security assurances, residents are now calling for stronger protection of vulnerable communities, while stakeholders continue to seek a lasting solution to the cycle of violence.

World.title: Burkina Faso: Women Weavers Give Faso Dan Fani Fresh Momentum
World.content:
Faso Dan Fani, Burkina Faso's distinctive woven cloth, is evolving with the growth of organic cotton, efforts to combat counterfeiting and improvements in weaving techniques. The women who have sustained this industry for generations are adapting to new quality requirements and seeking better returns for their work.

Early one Saturday morning in Koubri, near Ouagadougou, Sidonie Sawadogo prepares her loom for another day's work. She learned to weave in the 2000s, shortly after getting married, and made it her main occupation. Today, she is an influential member of the National Federation of Women Weavers of Burkina Faso (FENATI-BF).

At 50, weaving is her main source of income. It has enabled her to send her children to school and become financially independent.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"Weaving has enabled me to send my children to school and accomplish many other things. Over time, I have become independent, and I no longer need to wait for my husband's help to do anything."

To sell her products directly, Sawadogo opened a shop in Ouaga 2000, a commercial and diplomatic district of the capital, where she displays items made in her workshop.

"My cloths range from CFA 6,000 (about US 35). It depends on the quality and the design. Some designs require much more work than others."

After 22 years of weaving, Sawadogo has seen Burkina Faso's woven cloth gain value and improve in quality. She attributes this change to market pressures, better techniques and the quality of the yarn, much of which is produced by FILSAH, a Burkinabè company specialising in processing cotton fibre into yarn.

"The quality of the yarn directly influences the quality of the fabric we produce. The weave is more even and more durable."

She also highlights the importance of training and sharing skills. In the past, she says, techniques were more basic, and weavers did not always fully understand every stage of the process.

About 20 kilometres away, in Ouagadougou's 1200 Logements neighbourhood, Denise Kafando has been weaving since 1986. The work has helped her contribute to household expenses and support her husband. She, too, believes that weaving techniques and the quality of the cloth have improved.

She attributes some of this progress to the "buy local" policy, which has stimulated demand in Burkina Faso and beyond.

"Today, there are more orders, both nationally and internationally. Last week, I delivered an order worth CFA 4 million (about US6,900) to a localbank. In April, I delivered another worth nearly CFA2million (aboutUS3,500) to an NGO."

Counterfeiting threatens the industry

But counterfeiting is undermining this momentum. Despite measures taken by the ministry responsible for trade, including a nationwide ban on imports of weaving yarn and woven cloth in force since 24 September 2024, counterfeit yarn and cloth continue to reach the local market, weakening the position of Burkinabè weavers.

The problem persists. Repeated inspections by the Mobile Brigade for Economic Control and Fraud Prevention (BMCRF), following the import ban, have not yet stopped it. At a press conference held in Ouagadougou on 24 March 2026, the brigade, which operates under the trade ministry, presented the results of inspections carried out since October 2025.

During that period, it seized 319 pieces of counterfeit Faso Dan Fani cloth, 174 lots of cloth, more than 10,160 spools of imported weaving yarn and 2,108 pieces of imported woven cloth, with a total value of CFA 20,504,725. A fine of CFA 3,100,000 was also imposed, payable to the public treasury.

A month later, on 15 April 2026, customs officials announced that they had intercepted 31,200 counterfeit cloths imitating Koko Donda and Faso Dan Fani at Dakola, on the border with Ghana. Their estimated market value was CFA 156 million.

These products sell for much less than quality local cloth, attracting price-conscious consumers but also exposing them to lower-quality goods.

"When people go to the market, they want cheaper cloth. But they do not know that, generally, these cloths are counterfeit. When you put these counterfeit Faso Dan Fani cloths in water, they fall apart. Most people only realise they have been deceived after paying."

For Kafando, this unfair competition severely disadvantages local producers. She also questions the products' quality and composition.

"These cloths are made of rubber, and they make the skin itch. They cause illness in those who wear them."

Some of these products reportedly come from neighbouring Ghana, although that account requires qualification. Pauline Bafiogo, the current president of FENATI-BF, says the imported yarn is not manufactured in Ghana but passes through the country before entering the Burkinabè market.

With access to a seaport, which Burkina Faso lacks, Ghana has become a transit country for this counterfeit yarn. According to Bafiogo, the yarn originates in China.

"It is not Ghana that produces this counterfeit yarn. The yarn comes from China before reaching us here. But because Ghana has a port, the cloth passes through there before entering Burkina Faso," she explained.

The price of locally produced Faso Dan Fani presents another challenge. Kafando believes it must be considered alongside the work required to produce a handwoven cloth, from preparing and dyeing the yarn to weaving, as well as the cost of raw materials.

"We set a price that reflects the value of our work. We also pay a lot for yarn. We have asked for prices to be reduced, but we are told that cotton is expensive. If the price of yarn falls, the price of cloth will also fall, and we will reduce ours accordingly."

The promotion of "buy local", championed by Burkina Faso's president, Captain Ibrahim Traoré, has nevertheless helped expand the market. Faso Dan Fani has been incorporated into dress codes for courts, schools, universities and the military, increasing orders and opening new opportunities for producers.

According to Kafando, demand now extends beyond Burkina Faso's borders. Her cloth is ordered in Senegal and Ghana, which she sees as evidence of growing interest in the skills of Burkinabè women weavers.

"Internationally, people appreciate our cloth more than they do here at home. When the yarn is of better quality, the cloth can only be of better quality."

Organic cotton opens new opportunities for rural women

While weavers increasingly use locally produced yarn, particularly from FILSAH, organic cotton remains largely absent from their workshops. Yet in Koudougou, the Organic Cotton Ginning Company (SECOBIO-SA) processes certified fibre, most of which is exported.

According to Milogo Caro, SECOBIO-SA's managing director, 99% of the fibre produced by the factory is destined for international markets. Only 1% goes to Burkinabè craftswomen.

"We work with international partners to whom we supply our fibre. Nationally, we do not yet have a partner we work with."

Established in 2018 and brought into operation in January 2020, SECOBIO-SA emerged from a partnership between SOFITEX and the National Union of Cotton Producers of Burkina Faso (UNPCB). It supports growers in the west, centre and part of the east of the country.

Nearly 60% of the growers are women, according to Caro, partly because organic cotton can be cultivated on small plots.

"Organic cotton is grown on small areas, generally no more than five hectares. These are areas that women in villages can access."

SECOBIO supplies seeds and organic fertilisers. Its technical teams also train growers and support them throughout the growing season.

Certification sets standards for organic production

Certification requirements include the exclusion of chemical pesticides and herbicides. Ecocert carries out independent inspections during the growing season to check compliance with production standards, Caro explains. Certification is granted only after this process is completed.

"Independent inspections are carried out during the growing season by Ecocert to verify compliance with production standards."

In Koumbogoro, in Sissili province, 125 kilometres from Ouagadougou, Mamata Konaté has grown organic cotton since 2010. A member of the Assandani cooperative, she planted two hectares this year, which she tends using oxen and without chemical products. She uses inputs supplied through SECOBIO's support programme.

"For crop treatment, SECOBIO supplied us with the product for organic cotton, and I applied it using a sprayer."

Konaté continues growing the crop for the income it provides. She considers organic cotton easier to grow and says it offers an attractive yield compared with conventional cotton. Last year, she made a net profit of CFA 100,000 (about US$175), which enabled her to buy a few goats.

Close 

"With the profits from harvesting and selling the cotton, we can help our families meet household expenses."

Like Konaté, Safoura Nébié is a member of the Assandani cooperative. She has grown organic cotton for nearly 20 years. The income helps her pay for school supplies and fees, meet household needs and sometimes invest in other income-generating activities during the dry season.

"When the children start school, we can pay for their supplies and also help our husbands cover school fees."

The industry nevertheless faces difficulties. Nébié points to delays in collecting cotton after it has been placed in storage, leaving the harvest exposed to animals, as well as delays in payment.

"The main difficulty is the time the company takes to collect the cotton after it has been stored. Animals come and eat the stored cotton, which causes us losses."

Despite these constraints, Nébié, Konaté and around 100 women growers in the Assandani cooperative continue to place their hopes in organic cotton, which provides them with modest but regular income.

On paper, their production and the work of Faso Dan Fani weavers belong to the same value chain. In practice, the links remain weak: 99% of Burkina Faso's organic cotton fibre is exported, while weavers such as Sawadogo depend on locally produced yarn to meet demand.

Back in her Koubri workshop, Sawadogo continues preparing her loom, thread by thread. She has spent more than two decades refining her skills and turning them into a livelihood. The future of Faso Dan Fani may depend on the ability to build stronger connections between organic cotton growers and the women who turn yarn into cloth.

"Today's Faso Dan Fani cloth is of much better quality."

The challenge now is to ensure that a greater share of the value created by Burkinabè cotton, from the field to the finished fabric, remains in the hands of the women who produce it.

World.title: Rabbi who worked on Adam Brody's Netflix show slams actor over Gaza comments
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Adam Brody, who stars as Rabbi Noah Roklov in Netflix's "Nobody Wants This," recently made waves with his comments on the situation in Gaza, prompting criticism from a real-life rabbi who was a consultant on the show.

When asked about his stance on Israel and Gaza in a recent interview with GQ, Brody said, "Put me down as thinking it's a genocide. Put me down as wanting a free Palestine. It's awful that it's taken so much death and misery, but it does feel like it's reaching a breaking point that it should have a while ago."

Brody's remarks caught the attention of Rabbi Steve Leder, a Los Angeles-based rabbi who served as a consultant on the first season of "Nobody Wants this." Leder, who advised production on the show's portrayal of Judaism and Brody's role as a rabbi, posted a video to Instagram slamming the actor for his "flippant" remarks.

"The flippancy was adding insult to injury, in my opinion, and needed to be addressed," Leder told Fox News Digital about why he posted the video to social media. "That is a word and that is a geopolitical situation that warrants anything but flippancy."

'NOBODY WANTS THIS' STAR ACCUSES ISRAEL OF 'GENOCIDE'

Leder emphasized that the word "genocide" has a specific definition and that Brody's use of it to describe what happened in Gaza was inaccurate. He quoted the United Nations' definition of genocide, which says the term is meant to describe a situation in which specific acts are carried out "with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group."

"Israel's war is against Hamas. It is not against a nationality, it is not against an ethnicity, it is not a race, it is not against a religion," Leder told Fox News Digital. "There are many nationalities, ethnicities, races and religious people of various faiths living in Israel, comprising Israel's neighbors, and Israel has not and would not attack anyone for any of those reasons."

The rabbi said that his main issue with Brody's remarks was that the actor presented his opinion as fact.

"This is where I felt that Adam Brody went terribly wrong. He presented an opinion as a fact. And that is a mistake for any of us who are in the public eye," Leder said.

In the show, Brody plays a rabbi who falls in love with an agnostic woman played by Kristen Bell, which is loosely based on the real-life romance between "Nobody Wants This" creator Erin Foster and her husband, Simon Tikhman.

BILL MAHER RIPS MACKLEMORE'S GAZA STANCE, SAYS CELEBRITY 'MORAL CONFUSION' IS FUELING ANTISEMITISM

Brody is far from the first Jewish celebrity to decry Israel's actions in Gaza as "genocide." Hannah Einbinder of "Hacks" and "Broad City" star Ilana Glazer have also been vocal critics of Israel.

Leder told Fox News Digital that "they can say whatever they want as long as they acknowledge it's an opinion and not a fact."

The rabbi explained that in Brody's case he felt compelled to respond because of the role he played in the production of "Nobody Wants This," which was deeply tied to Jewish representation on screen.

Another element that added to the controversy over Brody's remarks is the fact that he plays a rabbi and has introduced many to Jewish culture through that role. Leder said it made the situation "doubly heartbreaking."

MS RACHEL SAYS SHE WON’T WORK WITH ‘PRIVILEGED’ PEOPLE WHO STAY SILENT ON GAZA

"Actors are not their roles, and we all understand that, they're acting. But in the minds of the public, in the mind of much of the pubic, it's sometimes hard to separate those two things," he said. "And when you have someone who is imagined — and I use that word deliberately — imagined to be an authority presenting opinions as facts, it's doubly painful."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Leder said public figures should stay away from discussing topics that they don't know enough about. In the video he released shortly after Brody's interview with GQ, Leder said, "If you know nothing about something, you should say nothing."

World.title: Abdul El-Sayed confronted on Soros ties after ridiculing politicians for taking corporate money
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed was challenged over his ties to billionaire Democratic mega-donor George Soros after criticizing his Republican opponent Mike Rogers for accepting money from corporations.

"There's a big difference there," El-Sayed said during an exclusive interview with "The Story" Monday.

El-Sayed’s graduate education was partially funded by the Paul & Daisy Soros Fellowships for New Americans and George Soros’ wealthy nephew, Jeffrey Soros, hosted El-Sayed at a Los Angeles fundraiser last month, according to footage reviewed by Fox News Digital.

As El-Sayed campaigns on a pledge to get "money out of politics," he was pressed by anchor Martha MacCallum on Monday about whether his relationships with wealthy donors undercut that message.

‘MONEY OUT OF POLITICS’ CANDIDATE ABDUL EL-SAYED SET TO FUNDRAISE WITH GEORGE SOROS’ NEPHEW IN CALIFORNIA

"When individuals want to give to my campaign, I welcome their support," he said, defending his relationship with the Soros family.

MICHIGAN SENATE HOPEFUL CALLS AIPAC DONATIONS 'LEGALIZED BRIBERY,' REMAINS SILENT ON OTHER DONATIONS

"You know what I don't do? I don't call corporations. I don't call AIPAC… Individuals who want to support a campaign, that's different."

Down to the studs, it was being transformed into the nerve center of the newest cable news channel.

During those first weeks, a ragtag crew of producers and writers and I were tasked with churning out practice newscasts to see how it would feel to do seven minutes of news at the top and bottom of every hour. It was a daunting task, as we were also creating a format and learning what worked and what didn’t. Pretty soon, we moved off-site to a rented studio to have greater access to cameras and equipment before the launch.

It made more than $100 million during its opening week. And I thought, "Wow! This cable network is bound for success if this is the kind of quality handiwork it puts out."

World.title: New Supreme Court term begins with justices stumped by climate change case
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court kicked off a new term Monday, with the justices wrestling with an attempt by oil companies to throw out lawsuits alleging they should pay damages for the impacts of climate change.

Although the case concerns a specific lawsuit the city and county of Boulder, Colorado, brought against Exxon Mobil and Suncor Energy, the ultimate decision could have broad ramifications for more than two dozen similar lawsuits brought by cities and counties around the country.

The justices — lacking a ninth member because Justice Samuel Alito recused himself — asked tough questions of both sides as they tackled broad legal questions raised in the case. Alito’s absence raises the possibility of a 4-4 split ruling that would leave the legal issues unresolved while allowing the Boulder case to move forward.

Boulder officials say they face increasing costs because of the impacts of climate change, including efforts to minimize risks from wildfires. Just this summer, Colorado has experienced extreme heat, drought and multiple fires.

The lawsuit, bringing claims under state law, says Exxon and Suncor misled consumers about the impact that greenhouse gases produced by their products would have on the climate.

The companies deny the allegations and warn that if the Boulder lawsuit and others like it are able to move forward to trial, they and other energy companies could face crippling damages in the billions of dollars. They also argue climate change is such an inherently national and international issue that it cannot be the subject of litigation in state courts.

There was some sympathy from the bench toward the oil companies and the potential for substantial damages.

00:00 00:00 Supreme Court weighs who can be sued for climate change costs 02:36

Chief Justice John Roberts, one of the court’s conservatives, wondered how many more cities and counties would launch similar lawsuits if the court allows the Boulder case to continue.

“Just to make sure I have a correct understanding. Presumably, if you prevail, the next day a municipality in every single state will file a lawsuit,” he told Boulder’s lawyer, Kevin Russell.

Although Boulder’s claims are based on consumer deception, Roberts also seemed skeptical that the lawsuit was anything other than what he called “an effort to reduce emissions.”

On the other hand, Roberts, in an exchange with the oil companies’ lawyer, Kannon Shanmugam, said litigation brought in state court against out-of-state companies over an alleged harmful product is commonplace.

Other justices also seemed conflicted. Liberal Justice Elena Kagan at one point compared climate litigation with the wave of lawsuits against tobacco companies and drug manufacturers that sold opioids, which were allowed to proceed.

The oil companies have pushed back on such comparisons, saying that in the tobacco and opioid litigation there was a much more direct connection between the product and alleged harm to consumers.

World.title: What to know about pneumonic plague after woman in Russia dies from mysterious illness
World.content:
The death of a 28-year-old woman who worked in an anti-plague laboratory in Russia is raising concerns about what caused her illness.

The woman died Friday, according to the World Health Organization, with no cause of death confirmed. A Russian official said the woman died of pneumonia of “undetermined” origin and did not link her death to her work at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East. The U.S. State Department said, however, that it’s monitoring reports of a fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague in the Irkutsk region, in southeastern Siberia, in coordination with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

“While the circumstances of this reported case remain unconfirmed, plague is a serious bacterial disease that is treatable with antibiotics, particularly when recognized and treated early,” a spokeswoman for the Department of Health and Human Services said in a statement. “At this time, there is no indication from available reporting of a broader threat to the United States.”

Key details aren’t known, including whether the woman was infected with plague at all and, if so, whether it was naturally occurring plague or bacteria studied in the lab. Scientists also don’t know how quickly her illness progressed and what treatment she received. Nearly 200 people who came into contact with the woman are under precautionary medical observation, according to Russian media.

“Maybe it’s going to come out that she died from something unrelated and it was just a coincidence” that she worked in an anti-plague lab, said Lisa Morici, a microbiologist and immunologist in the Tulane University School of Medicine.

Dr. Ashish Jha, the White House’s former Covid response coordinator, told NBC News in an interview, “If there were weapons programs, biological weapons programs in these labs, that would be much more concerning to me.”

“We need to understand that now,” he added.

The situation is still rapidly unfolding. But here’s what we know about the pneumonic plague, how it spreads and how dangerous it is.

What is plague?

Plague is an infection caused by Yersinia pestis bacteria. Known as the “Black Death” during the 14th century, the plague triggered several global pandemics over centuries before the discovery of antibiotics.

It presents in three main forms: bubonic, pneumonic and septicemic, according to the World Health Organization. All three are caused by Yersinia pestis, but they occur in different parts of the body.

Bubonic is the most common form, Morici said. It is primarily transmitted through bites of infected fleas or direct contact with infected rodents, which can cause painful, swollen lumps in the lymph nodes. It is usually not contagious.

Left untreated, however, it can spread to the lungs and become pneumonic plague, which can pass from person to person through respiratory droplets, Morici said.

Septicemic plague occurs when the bacteria grow and spread in the blood.

How does pneumonic plague spread?

Pneumonic plague can spread through the air when an infected person or animal coughs or sneezes.

The respiratory droplets don’t travel very far, maybe three to six feet, said Dr. Dave Wagner, director of the Pathogen and Microbiome Institute at Northern Arizona University. “They drop to the ground pretty quickly.”

It’s the rarest form of the disease, according to WHO.

Dr. William Schaffer, an infectious diseases expert at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, said close contacts are most at risk. Pneumonic plague isn’t something that spreads “distantly across a room, but to face-to-face contacts,” he said.

“It’s highly unlikely for most people to get the pneumonic form of the disease,” Morici said.

Covid, for example, spreads like wildfire through the air, traveling beyond six feet.

“It’s nothing like the Covid-19 pandemic,” she said.

How deadly is it?

While pneumonic plague is the rarest form of the disease, it’s also the deadliest.

“It’s the one that’s so frightening because it can kill so quickly,” Morici said.

It progresses remarkably fast, Wagner said. Symptoms typically appear within one to two days of exposure, and patients require treatment within 48 hours of showing symptoms to prevent fatal complications. Symptoms can include shortness of breath and coughing or blood in the phlegm.

Because of how rapidly it attacks the respiratory system, public health experts consider this strain the most likely candidate for a biological attack, according to Morici.

People with pneumonic plague are often quarantined, she said. Healthcare workers will often wear personal protective equipment, such as an N95 mask, or even a full body suit in case of accidental exposure.

“We’re using the strictest levels of biocontainment,” she said.

How is it treated?

Antibiotics are highly effective against plague, including pneumonic plague.

“This is why we don’t have big plague outbreaks anymore,” Wagner said.

Schaffner said there’s no evidence to suggest that the plague bacteria are evolving in a way to become resistant to antibiotics. “We will not turn 2026 into the Middle Ages, where the Black Death caused vast amounts of death throughout Europe. That will not happen.”

Wagner said he has no reason to believe this suspected case of plague is “going to take off and spread.”

“The plague that we have today is the same plague that was the scourge of humanity for so long during great pandemics,” he said.

Is the plague found in the U.S.?

About seven cases of plague are reported in the U.S. each year, according to the CDC. Most occur in rural parts of the Southwest, including Arizona, California, Colorado and New Mexico. These are areas where Yersinia pestis bacteria naturally circulate among wild rodents like prairie dogs and their fleas.

Most people are treated quickly with antibiotics and recover. Deaths from the plague in the U.S. are rare but do happen.

Last July, a man in Arizona died of pneumonic plague after he was exposed to sick cats. Within a week, the man went to an emergency department with shallow breathing, a fast heart rate, chest pain and a dry cough. Despite getting antibiotics and oxygen, the man died within eight hours of his admission to the hospital. Testing later showed he had pneumonic plague.

World.title: Ex-‘American Idol’ contestant Caleb Flynn sentenced to life without parole in wife’s murder
World.content:
A former Ohio music pastor and “American Idol” contestant has been sentenced to life without possibility of parole for killing his wife in their Dayton-area home earlier this year.

Caleb Flynn, 40, was found guilty of aggravated murder in the February shooting of Ashley Flynn, 37, a schoolteacher and volleyball coach. Flynn and their two daughters were home when police arrived.

Before issuing the sentence, Judge Jeannine Pratt said he would be punished because he posed a high risk of harm to the community.

“The layers of deceit, manipulation and cruelty are hard to fathom,” Pratt said Monday. “And you used your faith to manipulate the lives of others.”

Caleb Flynn reading his statement to the court Monday in Troy, Ohio, before being sentenced. Pool via NBC News

Flynn maintained his innocence Monday, crying and shaking as he read a statement to his family and Ashley’s.

“I loved her and loved her. She was my wife. She was beautiful and amazing in countless ways,” Flynn said. “I will continue to fight for my innocence as long as the Lord allows me to, since I did not kill my wife.”

To his two children, Flynn apologized and said they are his greatest joy in life. He thanked his parents for their love and kindness and said their support throughout the trial was “supernatural.”

“I never knew that love this fierce was possible until the moment that I held you for the first time,” Flynn said to his daughters. “Please know your daddy is so proud of you and loves you beyond what words can describe.”

Flynn’s daughters were not in court, but other family members read written statements from the preteen girls who were ages 9 and 11 when their mother was killed.

“I love you deeply with all my heart and it’s sad that you can’t love anyone but yourself,” read the letter from his daughter Alissa.

In her letter, his daughter Ava said photos and videos of her father on trial online have been inescapable.

“My heart aches to see you hurt, but then I think it was your choice,” she wrote. “It was your choice to have that affair.”

Both daughters implored their father to confess to murdering their mother. Along with their grandparents, uncle and aunt, who read statements in court, the girls said their faith has been helping them get through their grief.

Ashley Flynn’s sister, Kayla Keyt, said during her victim statement that her family could not overcome their sense of shock and despair after learning that Flynn betrayed them in such a violent and horrible way.

“We trusted you. We believed in you. We honestly would have laid down our lives for you,” Keyt said.

Prosecutors said Flynn’s wife was defenseless in bed when he shot her and then feigned a home invasion to mislead investigators.

Flynn frantically called 911 and said someone had broken in while he slept on the couch. He woke up to the sound of gunshots, he told investigators.

He said that a day before the killing, a man had come to their home and handed his wife an American flag while making a “weird sales pitch for America.”

But Flynn’s lover, Alleigha Botner, testified in court that he talked about hating his wife and having thoughts of killing her. Jurors heard AI-generated love songs that prosecutors say he made for Botner and some of the more than 100,000 text messages that authorities say they exchanged.

Miami County Prosecuting Attorney Paul Watkins read a statement to the court and shook his head as prosecutors said he endangered his children’s lives when he killed his wife while they were home.

“This case is about deliberate choices, the destruction of an irreplaceable life and the permanent devastation left behind,” he said.

“The defendant has never accepted responsibility or expressed genuine remorse for the life he ended,” Watkins added.

World.title: Plea agreement hearing set for ex-CIA officer found with gold bars
World.content:
WASHINGTON — A plea agreement hearing in federal court has been set for Tuesday in the case of an ex-CIA officer found with 303 gold bars worth $40 million at his home, according to court records.

David Rush, who has been accused of faking his lengthy professional record, has only formally been charged with one count of theft of public funds, accused of falsifying pay records. But two people familiar with the investigation have told NBC News that Rush is also accused of making up a false CIA program. Investigators believe there is likely more money or other items missing beyond what was seized by federal officials at his home, four people familiar with the investigation told NBC News.

Rush was placed on leave sometime before his arrest and eventually fired from the CIA. Court records show that the hearing Tuesday afternoon has been set before U.S. District Judge Michael Nachmanoff in Alexandria, Virginia.

A plea agreement would allow the government to avoid a lengthy trial which could bring further attention toward any mistakes the CIA made in the process and prevent the disclosure of additional information on the agency’s operations.

Rush has not yet entered a plea and has been held since his arrest. His attorney had no comment Monday. The prosecution and defense together had earlier requested additional time to work out a plea deal.

Rush’s case has also cast an unwelcome spotlight on the No. 2 at the Pentagon, Steve Feinberg, who had a close professional relationship with the former officer, sources told NBC News. Feinberg, through a Pentagon spokesperson, has denied the two had a close relationship.

Rush had worked on secret maritime programs at the Pentagon, NBC News reported in June. Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg was interviewed by the FBI as part of the investigation into Rush, but Feinberg has not been accused of wrongdoing and the bureau said in a statement he was not under investigation. There’s no indication Feinberg knew about Rush’s alleged fabrications. Several senior CIA officials were placed on leave over the management of Rush’s requests for money, NBC News reported in June.

The U.S. intelligence community’s inspector general is also investigating the circumstances that led to Rush’s arrest, which has raised questions among intelligence officials and U.S. lawmakers about how the CIA could have missed basic alleged falsehoods in Rush’s application, including about his academic and military records, NBC News reported last month.

World.title: How the shooting death of a Houston father is igniting Latino politics in Texas
World.content:
Pushing back

Lorenzo Salgado Araujo woke before dawn on a hot Houston morning on July 7, as he did most days. He had lived in the U.S. for decades without legal status but was in the process of getting a work permit. He had no criminal record.

He picked up workers in his white van and was driving to a jobsite when he was pursued by immigration agents in unmarked vehicles. An officer shot him, according to authorities, after they say he used his vehicle to ram them. It’s a story contradicted by witnesses in the van, but it’s one immigration authorities have told before in explaining how a traffic pursuit turned deadly.

This time, though, the family wasn’t having it. Salgado Araujo’s eldest son stood before cameras and delivered an emotional testimonial to his father that went viral.

“He was a hardworking family man who never wanted his name to be known by anyone outside of his family,” Ronaldo Salgado said at a news conference days after his father’s shooting, as his brother held up a photo of their father.

Ronaldo Salgado stressed that the story of his dad ramming government vehicles could not be true. Their father had always taught his kids that if law enforcement attempted to pull them over, they were to pull off the road, hand over their license and registration and act respectfully.

In the end, authorities admitted Salgado Araujo was not the intended target of the operation.

In an interview with NBC News, Ronaldo Salgado said as immigration arrests became more prevalent in 2025, they talked to their father about the procedure if he had an encounter, including calling his family, and that they’d contact their attorneys.

“Just remember, don’t sign anything. Call us,” Ronaldo Salgado said he told his father.

Sitting at Las Perras Cafe in Houston, where a makeshift altar to his father sits in the corner, Ronaldo Salgado recited the names of those who had been killed by immigration officers, including Renee Good, Alex Pretti and Ruben Ray Martinez, saying the country is not now safe because of their deaths.

“These are lives that are lost, and they need to be investigated, just like any other life lost. It needs to be investigated with the full cooperation of the agents involved and the agencies involved,” the son said.

Ronaldo Salgado at a makeshift altar to his father, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, at Las Perras Cafe in Houston. Natasha Korecki / NBC News

“All of this isn’t making us any safer. How is going after my dad going to work making the city safer?” Ronaldo Salgado said. “Criminals don’t wake up at 5 in the morning to pick up their crew and go to do a day of backbreaking labor. You don’t.”

In an unusual move, federal officials made public an FBI search warrant to get inside Salgado Araujo’s van after his death. Then, federal officials released a stinging detail: The bureau sought entry to look at baggies with crystals that they said resembled meth.

When he heard that, Ronaldo Salgado said he couldn’t help but break into a little smile: “Ohhh, they messed up.”

He knew what it was. And it would only make things worse for federal authorities. It was a homemade electrolyte mixture, mainly of salt, that his father later mixed into Gatorade for himself and workers to combat the triple-digit Houston summer heat outside.

The U.S. attorney’s office later confirmed that the mix was in fact not methamphetamine, surprising few who knew Salgado Araujo.

Ronaldo Salgado felt it was an effort to sully his father’s reputation and dampen public outrage.

The implication just added to community anger, viewed as a thinly veiled attempt at smearing the man immigration authorities killed.

“It really shook the community,” said Jasmine Khadem González, an immigrant rights organizer with the Houston Democratic Socialists of America. “A lot of us who are Latino, we have somebody in our family: If it’s not our father then it’s our uncle who has a very similar job. … To see somebody like that be targeted for just being on his way to work or for the color of his skin or for the kind of truck that he’s driving — because it’s associated with Latino men — to see somebody like that be targeted for doing a very everyday thing. For just existing.”

In the NBC News/Telemundo poll, 31% of Latino voters say they or someone close to them started carrying identification over concerns about ICE enforcement, while 27% say they know someone who has been deported or detained by ICE in the last two years.

Amy Zachmeyer, the executive director of New Economy for Working Houston, a group that helped organize community vigils and demanded accountability and transparency in the probe, said the Salgado family’s high-profile pushback kept authorities in check.

“They’ve shown incredible strength to be able to really defend their father,” she said.

Zachmeyer grew emotional as she spoke about the sons. “They never let a narrative set in that he was anything but a loving father, a Houstonian, a Texan, a hard worker.”

Anger reshapes local politics

Adrian Garcia, a Harris County commissioner, said Latinos are “feeling a lot of attack and disrespect.” Over the last year, he’s worked to reach out to those who don’t vote often. From his view, people now are willing to walk across broken glass to send a message to the Trump administration.

“The low-propensity voters that I’ve been speaking to absolutely have a great intensity to vote in this election, and they specifically speak to ICE enforcement. A lot of young kids: ‘I’m voting for my mom. I’m voting for my dad.’ I hear that a lot,” Garcia said.

More Latino registered voters than ever — 72% — rated their interest in the upcoming election as 10 out of 10 in the NBC News/Telemundo poll.

Garcia described the greater impact that fear of immigration enforcement has had across the Texas economy.

“This is not what our community deserves, and it is also what is impacting the things that we care about the most, the business, the economy. They’re hurting the industry,” he said. “They’re hurting those who work hard and play by the rules.”

Jareli Barrera, who works as a server at the popular Cielito Cafe in Houston, said she has never been so tuned into an election. Today, she said she’s helping others, including co-workers, to register to vote.

She cannot stand seeing the level of fear in her community, including among those who are citizens but fear being separated from family or an aggressive encounter.

“Republicans are probably going to lose. It’s not going to be the greatest thing for them at the end of the day,” Barrera said. “Most of these immigrants are the ones that are making the U.S. successful. They’re doing the hard work. … If everyone’s deported, who’s gonna do the hard labor? Who’s gonna construct? Who’s going to do all this cleaning that they don’t want to do?”

Since 2025, local activist groups have tried to work with the city of Houston to better protect Latinos as they watched intense enforcement operations in cities like Minneapolis, Los Angeles and Chicago upend life for residents and lead to encounters with immigration authorities that turned violent or deadly.

Jennefer Canales-Pelaez, a Houston-based senior policy attorney and strategist with the Immigrant Legal Resource Center, said Salgado Araujo’s death was a “culmination of years of Texas entrenching itself, entangling itself with ICE” and “illustrated to them the fear, the levels of persecution of justice that immigrant communities have been living with in Texas for a very long time.”

Before Salgado Araujo’s death, Canales-Pelaez was among those who worked to deter cooperation between Houston police and federal police agencies and pushed for greater transparency into immigration operations. Abbott, the three-term governor and a staunch Trump ally who is up for re-election in November, threatened to block $200 million in grants to Houston and other major cities if they didn’t change local rules that directed police forces not to hold individuals they encounter for longer time periods to assist ICE. The cities, including Houston, reworded their ordinances.

Houston Mayor John Whitmire, a centrist Democrat, told The New York Times last October that he kept his head down as other city and state leaders in the country grew combative with the White House over immigration operations. Whitmire said his city had avoided “turmoil” that others faced.

Whitmire initially declared his hands were tied after the shooting; the Houston Police Department had no jurisdiction to conduct an independent investigation. After community uproar, the city changed course. Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare has now launched a probe, with the county government approving the $2.5 million request to fund it.

“It ignited this flame and really showed other people that aren’t necessarily living this experience or working in this line of work, ‘Oh, this got to us,’” Canales-Pelaez said. “When the mayor told us that we weren’t going to be another Minneapolis, we weren’t going to be a Los Angeles, well, now we are. Someone’s dead. That really has sparked this rage, this collective, righteous anger.”

World.title: New information on FlyDubai cockpit flight; Russia continues attacks on Kyiv
World.content: New information on FlyDubai cockpit flight CBS News national security analyst Aaron MacLean joins "The Takeout" to discuss what we know now about the co-pilot who allegedly tried to bring down a FlyDubai plane headed for Israel, the Iran war and Russia's latest attacks on Ukraine.

World.title: Defense attorney says Letitia James should recuse herself from Cornell investigation
World.content:
An attorney for one of the seven men accused in the alleged sexual assault of a former Cornell University student at a fraternity house in 2024 is calling for Attorney General Letitia James to step down as special prosecutor.

Andrew Miltenberg, the attorney for Gillio Lopes, said he thinks James should recuse herself since she previously posted about the case on social media.

Gov. Kathy Hochul tapped James as special prosecutor in the case last week.

"Our concern is not political or personal. It is about confidence in the integrity and independence of this investigation," Miltenberg said. "Before she was appointed special prosecutor, Attorney General James publicly described what Jane Doe was 'forced to endure' as 'horrific and unacceptable,' said she was holding her 'in my heart and in my prayers,' and told her and 'all survivors,' 'We stand with you.'"

Miltenberg said there's nothing wrong with being compassionate toward someone who is making an allegation of sexual assault.

"The concern is that Attorney General James' words could be reasonably be understood as expressing a view about what occurred before she became responsible for independently evaluating the evidence and determining whether criminal charges are supported," Miltenberg said.

Both Hochul and James were asked about James' social media posts at a news conference to announce her appointment as special prosecutor.

Hochul said James "will follow the facts. She'll examine the evidence and go wherever it leads, and if the evidence supports charges, she will pursue them," adding that she had full confidence in her.

James said Friday she wouldn't be commenting about her social media post.

Miltenberg said that given James' social media post and the publicity around the case, "I believe the better institutional course is for Attorney General James to voluntarily recuse herself from this particular investigation and allow it to be led by a prosecutor who has made no prior public statements concerning the merits of these allegations."

"This is not an accusation that Attorney General James is corrupt, acting in bad faith or incapable of performing her duties professionally. Nor am I suggesting that a court has determined that she is legally disqualified. The point is much narrower: an avoidable question now hangs over this investigation, and voluntary recusal would remove it," Miltenberg said.

"Jane Doe is entitled to have her allegations investigated seriously, thoroughly and respectfully. Mr. Lopes is equally entitled to have the evidence concerning him evaluated individually, fairly and with an open mind," he said. "Publicity is not evidence. Repetition is not proof. This investigation should be about the facts and the law—not politics, social media or public pressure."

CBS News New York has reached out to James' office for comment about Miltenberg's statement and has not yet heard back.

Miltenberg has previously said his client "unequivocally denies the allegations against him."

World.title: Ex-"American Idol" contestant Caleb Flynn gets life sentence
World.content:
Caleb Flynn, a former "American Idol" contestant and pastor who was convicted last week of murdering his wife, a crime he tried to blame on an intruder breaking into their home, was sentenced to life without the possibility of parole Monday in Ohio.

Flynn did not take the stand in his defense during the trial, but he proclaimed his innocence before he was sentenced.

"I have unfortunately lied about a lot of things over the last couple of years, but as I stand here before God, who is my ultimate judge, I am not lying when I say I did not kill my wife," Flynn said. "I will continue to fight for my innocence as long as the Lord allows me to, as I did not kill my wife."

Miami County Common Pleas Judge Jeannine Pratt said the jury's guilty verdict in the case left her with "one clear and obvious conclusion."

"Your actions, Mr. Flynn, were abhorrent," Pratt said. "The layers of deceit, manipulation and cruelty that you have shown are quite honestly impossible to fathom, and frankly, sir, you used your faith to manipulate the lives of others."

Prosecutors said Flynn shot his wife, 37-year-old Ashley Flynn, twice in the back of the head while she was asleep in bed on Feb. 16. They alleged he then staged their Tipp City, Ohio, home to mimic a break-in and called 911 to claim an intruder was responsible for the murder.

Caleb Flynn had claimed he was in another room when his wife was killed.

Caleb Flynn reads his statement to the court before being sentenced in Troy, Ohio, Oct. 5, 2026, in this image taken from video. Pool Photo via AP

Flynn was found guilty of nine charges in total, including aggravated murder and three charges of murder, two charges of felonious assault and three charges of tampering with evidence. The aggravated murder charge is what carried the life sentence, and five other charges, including the three murder charges, were rolled into that sentence. Flynn was also sentenced to three years for each of the tampering with evidence charges, three years each for two separate firearm enhancements and another year for a third firearm enhancement.

Caleb Flynn texted, "I need her to die"

During the trial, Alleigha Botner, 24, who said she had an affair with the defendant, testified about the tens of thousands of text messages the two shared, including some in which he wrote he wanted his wife dead.

Botner testified to a roughly 18-month sexual affair with Caleb Flynn, whom she met when she was an intern at his church. She described how the two hid their messages, admitted to lying to the FBI at first, and explained how she lost her phone and work laptop just weeks before Ashley's death.

Asked how she feels about Flynn today, she testified, "I hate him."

In the texts, many of which were read in court, Caleb Flynn repeatedly said he wished Ashley Flynn was dead.

"I need her to die, to cheat again, to leave," Caleb Flynn wrote to Botner about his wife on Feb. 11, 2025, almost exactly a year before she was shot. FBI Special Agent Andrea Kinzig, who testified during the trial, said she found no evidence on Ashley Flynn's phone of her having an affair, as Caleb Flynn had told Botner, according to her testimony.

Weeks later, Caleb Flynn texted Botner, "I hate her as well and I want her gone." On March 24, 2025, Botner wrote, "What can I do?" and he responded, "Kill her."

Caleb Flynn once texted Botner, "I was up until 4 a.m. last night ... trying to think of ways to kill her and not go to jail. If I could literally kill her and not go to hell, I would do it in a heartbeat."

World.title: Coca-Cola reveals new flavors for Coke, Powerade and other brands
World.content:
Coca-Cola is refreshing its beverage lineup with a series of new fruit flavors.

The company said Monday that it will roll out "innovations" for its Coca-Cola, Fairlife, Mr. Pibb, Powerade and Topo Chico brands starting in 2027. Coca-Cola will showcase the new products at the National Association of Convenience Stores event in Las Vegas, Nevada, this week.

A Coca-Cola spokesperson said the company is also testing several new products in New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania to gauge consumer interest in a prebiotic version of Coca-Cola Zero Sugar, Sprite Zero Sugar and Fresca.

Coca-Cola fans will have two new flavors to try next year: Coca-Cola Cherry Lime is scheduled to debut in February, and Coca-Cola Strawberry Float will make its premiere in the summer.

The cherry lime product is a new spin on Coca-Cola Cherry, while the strawberry float version appears to be a nod to the popular dessert that blends soda and ice cream. Both come in sugar and zero-sugar options.

Other Coca-Cola beverage brands are also set to get a fruit-inspired refresh next year. Powerade will add watermelon and lemon-lime zero-sugar options in January 2027. Mr. Pibb, a spicy cherry soft drink, will debut "Mr. Pibb Black-Current" in the spring, while a "berry-forward" flavor will be offered for a limited time.

Topo Chico, a carbonated mineral water product, will launch a pineapple-coconut flavor in February, building on its existing lineup of fruit flavors, which include raspberry with lemon, passionfruit and tropical mango, among others.

Core Power protein shakes, sold under the Fairlife brand, will be available in banana and strawberry beginning in January, the first new flavors in almost a decade. Both will contain 26 grams of protein, while the banana flavor will also be available in a 42-gram version.

World.title: The iconic Arthur Read made his TV debut 30 years ago
World.content:
The iconic Arthur Read made his TV debut 30 years ago

toggle caption i WGBH Educational Foundation, WildBrain and Marc Brown Studios

This is part of a special series in which NPR looks back at its coverage of major news stories from the past.

Which long-running cartoon features this protagonist: he's got round ears, an iconic yellow sweater, and a snarky little sister?

If you immediately pictured an animated, 8-year-old aardvark, you've likely heard of Arthur Read, a character who made his TV debut 30 years ago on Oct. 7, 1996.

But before the bespectacled third-grader made his way onto our screens and into our hearts, Arthur's first home was in the world of books.

Here's a look at the beginnings of Arthur.

Sponsor Message

A Bedtime Story

The author of the Arthur books is Marc Brown, a writer and illustrator who was raised in Erie, Pa.

Although Brown was interested in art from a young age, after graduating from the Cleveland Institute of Art in 1968, he pursued a string of different jobs working as everything from truck driver to to short-order cook to assistant professor.

Brown says he got the inspiration for Arthur when his son Tolon asked for a bedtime story about a "weird" animal. The first weird animal that came to mind? An aardvark. From there, Brown wrote and illustrated his first picture book depicting an aardvark named Arthur. This animal, with its long anteater snout and small ears, starred in Arthur's Nose, published in 1976.

While working on the next book, Brown made a pivotal change to the character's design. The second book titled, Arthur's Eyes, featured Arthur getting a new pair of glasses. As Brown drew the glasses, he realized there was a problem.

Speaking to NPR's Linda Wertheimer in 1997, Brown said, "I was drawing Arthur, and I wanted him to face the viewer in the book. And I could not show his mouth because his — his nose was so long. And so I shortened it a little bit. And I thought to myself, gee, if there are two books about Arthur, well there might be a third book. Now how do you really want this character to look?"

Sponsor Message

So Brown spent more time redesigning Arthur's visage, making his face "a little rounder" and "a little more lovable looking." The result, Brown said, made Arthur "more human-like." As Brown published and sold more Arthur books, he was able to make a living writing books. Though they were not an immediate commercial success, Brown's picture books resonated with families, including Carol Greenwald's.

Like Brown, Greenwald was no stranger to bedtime story pleas from her two children. When her son was 3 years old, their neighbor gave them an Arthur picture book. After reading it a few times, Greenwald realized it was unique.

"After reading it for the seventh time," Greenwald told NPR in 1997, "I realized I wasn't tearing my hair out … There are so many books you read to your kids that they love to read, and you read them over and over again, and it makes you feel like you want to scream. But this particular book was not making me feel that way."

Greenwald also said she liked the way Arthur dealt with problems involving school, personal relationships and activities like reading. As a TV producer at the Boston-based public media station GBH, Greenwald raised the idea with her colleagues in the early '90s.

"We have a lot of research that tells us that a kid who watches a TV show based on a book is more likely to want to read that book, is more likely to want to read other books, and is even more likely to go to the library."

toggle caption i WGBH Educational Foundation, WildBrain and Marc Brown Studios

From books to television

Although Greenwald believed Arthur was ready to make his public television debut, Brown was less sure. Brown said he was hesitant to allow Arthur to make the multimedia leap, stating that he wanted to keep "control of the character."

But GBH's offer and the subsequent jump in book sales made Brown reconsider.

Sponsor Message

“I went from, you know, maybe selling two million books over a period of several years to selling two million books in a month,” Brown said. “And to me, that happening is just unimaginable…”





He worked closely with the show's writers and artists to preserve the essential little kid that is Arthur.

Produced by GBH and the Montreal-based animation studio Cinar, the first episode of the series premiered on PBS Kids on Oct. 7, 1996. Its storyline draws directly from the second picture book, "Arthur's Eyes," as Arthur "re-tells" the story of wearing glasses to school for the first time.

The premiere also brought the rest of the Elwood City animal community to life with sound and emotion. Every character is an animal, from Arthur's aardvark parents and sister D.W. (short for Dora Winifred) to the students in Mr. Ratburn's Lakewood Elementary class, including an athletic chimpanzee named Francine and Arthur's best friend, a bunny named Buster. One of the show's underlying themes of getting along with others in your community is present even in its joyful, reggae theme song, "Believe In Yourself" by Ziggy Marley and the Melody Makers as Arthur bops around Elwood City, interacting with family, friends, and trusted neighbors.

Shortly after the series premiere, Brown was asked whether Arthur would remain in third grade or be allowed the opportunity to grow.



“I don't think of Arthur as ever leaving third grade," Brown said. "I sort of think of Arthur as having this portrait in the attic that's aging. (laughs) But Arthur will stay forever in third grade.”





The legacy of a wonderful kind of day

True to his word, Arthur and his friends remained third-graders throughout the entire series' 25 seasons. As reported by the Los Angeles Times in 2022, Arthur aired over 250 episodes and seven television specials. The critically acclaimed series also won four Daytime Emmy Awards for outstanding children's animated program and one Peabody Award.

Sponsor Message

Although Arthur began as the star, the series evolved to focus on a diverse cast of other characters and their lives as they navigated relatable milestones for 8-year-olds such as developing asthma, learning with dyslexia, and living with diabetes. The principles of believing in yourself, valuing family and friendship, and loving reading carried from season to season.

But not all the characters' stories were celebrated. In 2019, Alabama Public Television refused to air an episode featuring a same-sex wedding between Arthur's teacher, Mr. Ratburn, and his partner, Patrick. As reported by the New York Times in 2006, when an episode of the spinoff "Postcards from Buster" featured a Vermont family with two moms, then-Secretary of Education Margaret Spellings wrote a letter to the then-president and CEO of PBS, Pat Mitchell, reminding her that the show received funding from the Department of Education. She added, "Many parents would not want their young children exposed to the life-styles portrayed in this episode."

When speaking to NPR in 2022, Brown said, "We, as adults, owe children the truth. They're trying to make a foundation on which they can build their lives, and if there isn't truth in that foundation, things get pretty shaky."

For 26 years, Arthur helped families build a foundation of truth and belonging with the animated, animal residents of Elwood City. The series finale titled, "All Grown Up," aired on Feb. 21, 2022. The characters were no longer children, but adults, each aged up 20 years and settled into their respective careers. And of course, Arthur became an author of graphic novels.

World.title: Dennis Hastert, longtime Republican House speaker who went to prison, dies at age 84
World.content:
Dennis Hastert, longtime Republican House speaker who went to prison, dies at age 84

toggle caption i Christian K. Lee/AP

Dennis Hastert, whose political legacy as Congress' longest-serving Republican House speaker was later fouled by allegations that he had molested high school athletes during his prior career as a teacher and wrestling coach, has died, a coroner said Monday. He was 84.

Hastert, who was speaker from 1999 until 2007, died Saturday of natural causes at his home while receiving hospice care, according to Kendall County Coroner Jacquie Purcell.
