When he was sentenced in 2016 to more than a year behind bars, the former history teacher became one of the highest-ranking American politicians ever ordered to prison.

In the late 1990s, Hastert was a little-known Illinois lawmaker with a reputation for congeniality that had helped him ascend the ranks of congressional leaders. When Newt Gingrich lost support because of ethics violations and the GOP's poor showing in an election, Republicans elected Hastert to succeed him. In his first weeks on the job, he presided over the House while the Senate conducted then-President Bill Clinton's impeachment trial.

Sponsor Message

After the GOP reclaimed the White House, Hastert helped pass then-President George W. Bush's legislative agenda, including massive tax cuts and a measure that amounted to a huge expansion of prescription drug benefits — the biggest change in Medicare in decades.

His legacy was suddenly thrown into doubt in 2015, when he was accused of evading banking regulations as part of a plan to pay hush money to conceal unspecified "prior misconduct." Nearly a year later, prosecutors filed papers that described what media reports had suggested for months: Hastert's alleged misconduct involved the sexual abuse of teenage boys on his wrestling team in the small town of Yorkville, west of Chicago.

During a 16-year coaching career, he led his team to a state championship and was named national coach of the year in 1976. But behind the accolades, prosecutors said, Hastert sexually abused at least four team members from 1965 to 1981.

The person Hastert was paying, identified in court papers only as Individual A, said the abuse occurred in a motel room when he was 14 on the way home from wrestling camp. Hastert allegedly touched other wrestlers in a locker room after saying he would give them massages. Two wrestlers said Hastert performed sexual acts on them.

Sponsor Message

Prosecutors also described a recliner where Hastert often sat in the locker room with a direct view of the stalls where the boys showered.

Hastert agreed to plead guilty to evading banking laws. In all, he paid more than $1.7 million out of $3.5 million that he had promised to Individual A, sometimes in lump sums of $100,000 cash.

At the sentencing hearing where he received 15 months behind bars, the visibly angry judge called Hastert a "serial child molester." A former wrestler struggled with his emotions as he told the court about his "dark secret" from adolescence.

In his own statement, Hastert said he was "deeply ashamed" and admitted that he "mistreated" some of his athletes. But he never referred directly to sexual abuse.

The public knew nothing about Hastert's past when Republicans lost seats in the 1998 midterm elections.

Hastert's path to the speaker's office was cleared when Louisiana Rep. Bob Livingston, who was considered a lock to replace Gingrich as speaker, resigned after acknowledging several extramarital affairs.

Hastert was aware of the personal pitfalls of holding the powerful position.

"You know, in this business, especially in a job like this, you can get your head someplace where it shouldn't be," Hastert said in a 1999 interview with The Associated Press. "But you come back home, and you're home. You're back where you've always been, and your feet are back on the ground."

Hastert said he lacked the appetite for higher office.

As the recount of the 2000 presidential election dragged on, Hastert's aides briefed him on the possibility that he might become acting president in the event of an Electoral College deadlock.

"I really didn't want to be president, temporary or otherwise," he wrote in his book. But he decided that he would not pass the office to the constitutional officer next in line if an Electoral College deadlock extended beyond Inauguration Day. In the end, the Supreme Court's 5-4 ruling ended the recount, and Bush moved into the White House.

Sponsor Message

Hastert's journey to Congress from his boyhood farm appeared to be the result of fate and luck.

In 1980, he finished third in an Illinois House primary. But the incumbent became fatally ill, and GOP leaders chose Hastert to take his place on the November ballot, where he won in a traditional GOP stronghold.

Hastert became a congressional candidate in 1986 and beat the Democrat with 52% of the vote, his smallest margin of victory in a congressional race.

In Washington, Hastert served quietly in House leadership, working closely with Gingrich and then-House Majority Whip Tom DeLay after Republicans took control in 1995.

Hastert became wealthy largely through a complex web of transactions that coincided with one of his own highway earmarks increasing the value of land he had purchased in his district.

He was forced to step down as speaker in 2007, when Democrats gained control of the House, and he resigned his seat later that year.

Born in Aurora, Illinois, Hastert earned a bachelor's degree in economics from Wheaton College in 1964 and a master's in education from Northern Illinois University in 1967.

In 2007, Wheaton named its newly created public policy center the J. Dennis Hastert Center for Economics, Government and Public Policy. After Hastert's indictment, the school removed his name in 2015. Other organizations abandoned associations with Hastert, and his portrait was removed from a hallway outside the House chamber.

Hastert lived his entire life in Chicago's suburbs, primarily in the Yorkville area. While growing up, he helped his father with the family feed business.

Survivors include his wife, Jean, and two adult sons.

World.title: Drones buzz overhead, troops hunker underground in Ukraine's hellish kill zone
World.content:
Drones buzz overhead, troops hunker underground in Ukraine's hellish kill zone

toggle caption i Andriy Andriyenko/Ukrainian 65th Mechanized brigade/Ukrainian military via AP

KYIV, Ukraine — The front line in the Russia-Ukraine war stretches the entire length of this country, from north to south. It has barely budged in four years and is sometimes compared to the static, deadlocked, trench warfare of World War I.

Yet straddling this front line is the kill zone, dominated by constantly evolving drone technology that's defining this conflict — and the future of warfare.

"This kill zone is a belt of territory which is full of Russian drones, Russian mines and also artillery. It's nonstop reconnaissance and surveillance," said Ukraine's Sr. Lt. Taras Myshak, the spokesman for Ukraine's 59th Separate Assault Brigade. He spoke with NPR on Zoom, just a few miles from the front line in eastern Ukraine.

Sponsor Message

Ukraine has a similar arsenal threatening the Russian forces that are dug in on the other side of the line.

The most important thing to know about the kill zone is that any sign of movement — just sticking your head out of a foxhole for fresh air — can get you noticed, and attacked, by the drones constantly buzzing overhead.

Myshak says even routine movements, like rotating troops in and out of this zone, is a nightmare.

"Not far from where we are talking today, we have a group that moved through the kill zone, and they will walk four hours just to go 1 kilometer," he said. "Because all the time they hear the drone, and they have to hide and wait. Then the drone passes, and they can move."

Nightfall doesn't make it any safer to move because the drones have thermal cameras that detect body heat and make it even harder to hide.

"In the night, it's even more dangerous," he said.

toggle caption i Iryna Rybakova/Ukrainian 93rd Mechanized Brigade/Ukrainian military via AP

A front line that barely budges

When Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, it advanced rapidly in conventional fashion with large columns of troops in armored vehicles. Later that fall, Ukraine's counteroffensive drove the Russians back in some places.

Sponsor Message

Since then, the two armies have settled in, and the front line has moved only incrementally, mostly with limited gains by Russia. This line now stretches more than 700 miles. On either side of the line, the kill zone is a band roughly 10 to 20 miles wide and dominated by drones.

"The kill zone is basically a product of drone warfare," said Rob Lee, a U.S. Marine veteran who now lives in Ukraine and monitors the war for the Foreign Policy Research Institute of Philadelphia.

Because Ukraine has far fewer troops and relies heavily on drones, it has a remarkably small presence on the front line.

Lee said that in many places, Ukraine has fewer than 10 soldiers per mile, in small groups, spaced out hundreds of yards apart.

"Those infantrymen are maybe two positions where it's two to four people," said Lee. "They're underground for the most part. They're trying to remain hidden."

These troops are not really trying to hold back advancing Russian soldiers, he added. They act more as spotters, relaying Russian movements to Ukrainian drone operators behind the front lines, who then track down the Russian intruders from the air.

Lee says the front line is so saturated with drones that it's virtually impossible for either side to pull together a large ground force without being detected and drawing fire.

Military vehicles like tanks and armored personnel carriers are even easier to spot and attack.

"Because of such a high density of drones, it became very difficult to bring vehicles near the front line at all," he said.

toggle caption i Genya Savilov/AFP via Getty Images

Neither army planned to fight this way.

Ukraine had no real drone industry at the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says the country will make 10 million this year.

Russia has ramped up its own drone production. It's expected to make more than 7 million this year, including jet-powered aircraft that are often evading Ukraine's defenses.

Sponsor Message

Starting from scratch

When Dima Putiata joined Ukraine's military four years ago, he knew nothing about drones and didn't think this was a manly way to wage war.

"When I saw that we have drones, I was not smart enough. I said, 'No, we don't need to have it. Let's fight like men.' I was a little bit maybe romantic in this way," said Putiata.

In addition to skeptics like Putiata, few Ukrainian troops were trained to use these new weapons.

"No one had drone operators," he recalled. "It's just, 'Oh, you're a driver? You can use it.' Or, 'Oh, can I use a drone? You can try.'"

By the time he left the military in May, Putiata, a sergeant, was commanding 26 drone crews in and around the kill zone in northeastern Ukraine.

Both sides have rapidly embraced the technology even if they don't know where it's headed next, he said.

"They understand how to use it here and right now, maybe not really understanding how to use it in the future," he noted. "My point is, you just need to keep going and adapting."

toggle caption i Iryna Rybakova/Ukrainian 93rd Mechanized Brigade via AP

Recognizing the role of drones

Two years ago, Ukraine became the first country to establish drones as an independent branch of its military.

This innovation now includes the widespread use of ground drones, which look like trollies and perform a wide range of tasks that have become too dangerous for troops.

The robots deliver food, medicine and ammunition to the front line. The robots can be loaded with machine guns that now carry out regular attacks.

The ground robots are also being used to evacuate wounded soldiers from the kill zone. But drone operators and combat medics have separate skills, and it turns out you need both.

"The drone operator doesn't know how to properly evacuate a wounded soldier, and the medic doesn't know how to operate a ground robot," said Lyuba Shipovich, a Ukrainian American who heads a private group, Dignitas, that trains troops on drones.

Sponsor Message

"So now we're trying to create combined program that will train both the medic and the robot operator," she said.

Media coverage tends to focus on long-range airstrikes that Russia and Ukraine are inflicting deep inside each other's territory.

But the vast majority of the fighting is in the kill zone, with drones now responsible for 80% of all casualties, according to Rob Lee and other military analysts.

Dima Putiata, the former Ukrainian soldier, says what started in this war has already spread to other conflicts.

"With drones, this is the cheapest flying munition that can be massively produced. You can destroy a lot of stuff," he said. "It's much cheaper than it used to be to have a war, unfortunately."

A kind of war, he predicts, that the world will see more often.

NPR's Hanna Palamarenko contributed to this story.

World.title: FBI arrests a woman accused of spying on Taiwan leader's family for China
World.content:
FBI arrests a woman accused of spying on Taiwan leader's family for China

BANGKOK — The FBI arrested a woman at Los Angeles International Airport as she was leaving the country and accused her of spying on the Taiwan president's family for China.

Wanying Zhang, also know as Heather, surveilled the Taiwanese president's son and his family for the Chinese government while in the United States, according to the FBI.

Zhang, 34, was arrested on charges for working for China as an unregistered agent, Assistant U.S. State Attorney Bill Essayli announced on social media. Zhang took photos and videos of her targets and sent license plate information to Chinese officials, he said.

Zhang was arrested as she was departing for a flight to China. Her nationality was not clear, and an attorney who represents her could not be determined. She was due to appear Monday in federal court in Los Angeles.

Taiwan's Presidential Office confirmed President Lai Ching-te's relatives were the targets, without specifying if it was the president's son, saying that "this is a classic case of transnational repression."

"Taiwan condemns in the strongest terms such barbaric acts — which disregard human rights and national sovereignty and aim to suppress, threaten, or even harm individuals advocating for freedom and democracy or their families — as such behavior should not be tolerated in the civilized world," spokesperson Karen Kuo said in a statement.

Sponsor Message

The Chinese Embassy in the U.S. did not immediately respond to a request for comment Monday and the Foreign Ministry in Beijing was closed for holidays.

Taiwan and China split after a civil war in 1949, but Beijing claims the island as part of its own territory. Lai, who was voted into office in 2024, has said that Taiwan and Beijing do not belong to each other and that the "People's Republic of China has no right to represent Taiwan."

China considers him a separatist and has called him a "destroyer of peace."

While in office, Lai has stepped up spending on defense for Taiwan, notably pledging to increase defense spending from 3% to 5% of the GDP, and pushing through a special budget for the construction of a T-Dome air defense system.

World.title: Imran Khan supporters march in Pakistan to demand his release after talks failed
World.content:
Imran Khan supporters march in Pakistan to demand his release after talks failed

toggle caption i Maaz Awan/AP

ISLAMABAD — More than 5,000 supporters of imprisoned former Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan began a dayslong march toward Islamabad on Sunday to demand his release, after talks between the government and the opposition fell through.

The looming showdown threatens to deepen Pakistan's political uncertainty at a time when the country is also grappling with a surge in militant attacks.

Khan is current Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's main political rival and has been imprisoned since 2023 on corruption and other charges that he and his party say are politically motivated. Despite his imprisonment, he retains a substantial and passionate support base, keeping him at the center of Pakistan's turbulent political landscape.

Sponsor Message

The demonstrators, traveling in a convoy of trucks, buses and cars, departed from Lakki Marwat district in the northwestern province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where Khan's party holds power. Organizers have planned overnight stops along the route as the caravan makes its way toward the capital. Sohail Afridi, the province's chief minister, and a staunch Khan supporter is leading the march.

Speaking from a specially designed container truck emblazoned with a large portrait of Khan, he expressed confidence in the movement's ability to press its demands and bring the political standoff into the heart of the capital.

Authorities have erected roadblocks, using containers, at the entrance to Islamabad and inside the city.

Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party, or PTI, and the federal government were in talks to postpone the march but failed to reach a resolution. Gohar Khan, the party's chairman, said negotiations remained deadlocked after two rounds.

Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi blamed Afridi for the failure of the talks, warning that he would be held responsible for any loss of life during the planned march.

Sharif's government urged postponement of the march, citing a surge in militant attacks by the Pakistani Taliban in the northwest. His government has accused PTI of sympathizing with the Pakistani Taliban, also known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan.

Sponsor Message

The organizers now vow to reach the capital after rallying with hundreds of thousands of Khan supporters.

Besides Khan's release, protesters are demanding his transfer to a hospital and permission for his family to visit him. Officials say he is in good health and receives regular family visits but maintain that meetings with the imprisoned former leader cannot be used for political purposes.

The march was originally scheduled for Sept. 27 but was postponed after party leaders said authorities blocked key approaches to Islamabad, including Attock Bridge, a major crossing for convoys from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

Previous protests by Khan's supporters have turned violent, including one in 2024 in which security personnel and civilians were killed.

Khan, a former cricket star, was ousted in a parliamentary no-confidence vote in April 2022. Sharif returned to office after the February 2024 election, which Khan's party says was rigged to deny it victory. The government denies the allegation.

World.title: SCOTUS hears major climate change case. And, Brazil's presidential race goes to runoff
World.content:
SCOTUS hears major climate change case. And, Brazil's presidential race goes to runoff

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

Investigators have found that the co-pilot who attempted to take control of a flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv last week aimed to crash it into Israel's Ben Gurion airport, according to a person familiar with the matter but not authorized to speak publicly. Authorities in the United Arab Emirates who are leading the investigation say the incident has been classified as a terrorist attack. They have not identified a clear motive, and the investigation is ongoing.

toggle caption i Erik Marmor/Getty Images

🎧 The co-pilot likely acted alone, according to the source. He carried out the attack with a crash axe, which is an emergency tool meant for breaking through panels or doors in the event of a crash. Israeli officials report that the co-pilot is from Oman. NPR's Kat Lonsdorf tells Up First that the co-pilot's origins have raised concerns about how he was allowed to fly in Israel, as the country prohibits pilots from nations with which it doesn't have diplomatic relations to fly in its airspace. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says Israel checks the backgrounds of pilots flying into the country, and this pilot must have gotten through a "loophole." While people in Israel are praising the passengers and the captain as heroes for averting disaster, a broader debate is emerging over government failures that allowed something like this to happen, Lonsdorf says.

Sponsor Message

A new Supreme Court term starts today with arguments in a significant climate change case. Boulder, Colo., is suing Suncor and Exxon Mobil, arguing that the companies misled the public about the harms of fossil fuels and caused costly disasters that cost the city time and money. This case could impact other states seeking to hold companies accountable for allegedly harming local communities.



🎧 The energy companies argue that this case should not be in state court, saying climate change is a global issue best addressed by the federal government, according to NPR's Carrie Johnson. Only eight justices will hear the case after Justice Sam Alito's surprising recusal last week, Johnson says. Alito has no stock in the two companies involved, but he has investments in other energy companies that could be impacted by the court's ruling. His recusal raises the risk of a tie, which would uphold the Colorado Supreme Court's ruling allowing the case to continue in state court.

Brazil's presidential race will go to a runoff later this month between left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and right-wing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro. In the tight first round, Bolsonaro, the son of Brazil's former far-right president, led with about 47% of the vote, while Lula followed closely with 45%.



Sponsor Message

🎧 Lula must close the runoff gap by attracting new voters, particularly among the millions who sat out yesterday's election, NPR's Carrie Kahn says. Winning over the 8% who supported other candidates will be challenging, as the people they backed are right and far-right candidates who will align with Bolsonaro. Disillusioned with politics, many Brazilians wanted new, younger candidates. Yasmin Soares, a Lula supporter, told Kahn that Bolsonaro's strong performance is scary and that the right brings hatred. Kahn says she heard similar sentiments from many Lula voters who fear a Bolsonaro conservative back in power.

Life advice

Penguin Random House/Lindsay Owens/NPR

Tech companies are "reinventing the rip-off," according to Lindsay Owens, head of the consumer advocacy group Groundwork Collaborative. She says corporations try to hide pricing schemes, such as using browsing data or a customer's geo-location to determine the cost of goods and services. In her book Gouged: The End of a Fair Price — And What That Means for Your Wallet, she uncovers these schemes and offers advice on how to protect yourself from being overcharged. In an interview with Life Kit, Owens explained steps you can take to get the best possible deal.

💸 Avoid shopping through retailer apps. When signed in, they might experiment with your data, potentially manipulating prices against you.

💸 Comparison shop by checking the product's price across multiple devices while logged in, logged out and with and without incognito mode.

💸 Regularly clear your browsing data and cookies to protect your information. Consider using a VPN to conceal your location, which may help avoid higher charges.

💸 Try shopping the old-fashioned way in person, but keep in mind that big-box retailers and grocery stores are increasingly using electronic shelf labels to change prices at any time.

For more advice on how to avoid being ripped off, listen to this episode of NPR's Life Kit. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.

Sponsor Message

Behind the story

by Andrew Limbong , Society & Culture Reporter

Harper

In a town not far from Barbara Kingsolver's house in southwestern Virginia is a historic marker noting Marion, Va., as "the birthplace of modern Mountain Dew." I came across it on the drive down I-81 to interview the Pulitzer-Prize winning author. It took me by surprise — I didn't expect such a momentous event here, in Appalachia. After all, isn't this the middle of nowhere?

There's some quibbling — the drink's roots trace back to Knoxville, Tennessee, which is why the word "modern" is in the designation. But it's here, in Marion, where the Dew truly realized both its potential and its propensity for change.

When I first encountered Kingsolver's work (The Poisonwood Bible, in high school AP English class), I was more partial to Mountain Dew Code Red — the version most associated with hardcore gamers. That didn't end up being my life, though.

Contested memories, an overlooked and condescended-to town, expectations of the future that go awry, how things change (but do they, really?) — we get into all of that in my interview with Kingsolver about her new novel, Partita. It's about a young classical pianist from Appalachia who has the chops to really make it, until her life gets upended. Kingsolver grew up loving classical music, and even went to college on a music scholarship. But that didn't end up being her life, either.

Give the full interview a listen in NPR's Book of the Day podcast feed.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i Akilah Townsend for NPR

Contemporary art world titan Theaster Gates is taking his career in a new direction by acquiring Pickard China, the last remaining manufacturer of fine china in the United States. Philadelphia's historic Academy of Natural Sciences closed just short of its 200th birthday last week amid an intense effort by local residents, politicians and scientists to save it. The U.S. Coast Guard says searchers have found debris off Nantucket, Mass., from a Canadian air ambulance that disappeared Saturday while carrying six people from Bermuda to Boston.

Sponsor Message

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen. Majd Al-Waheidi contributed.

World.title: FlyDubai attacker intended to crash plane into Tel Aviv airport, investigation finds
World.content:
FlyDubai attacker intended to crash plane into Tel Aviv airport, investigation finds

toggle caption i Jack Guez/AFP via Getty Images

TEL AVIV, Israel — An ongoing investigation into last week's midair attack on a FlyDubai plane has found that the co-pilot who tried to take control of the flight intended to crash it into Israel's Ben Gurion International Airport, a person familiar with the matter but not authorized to speak publicly told NPR.

The plane was flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv and was intending to land at Ben Gurion midmorning on a busy weekday. The co-pilot attacked the plane's captain midflight with an axe and attempted to take control of the plane.

Sponsor Message

It is believed that the co-pilot likely acted alone, the source said.

Authorities in the United Arab Emirates — which is leading the main investigation into the incident, with help from Israeli officials — and in Israel have deemed the attack an attempted terrorist attack, although the motive is still being investigated.

The commercial flight had 172 people on board, according to the airline, the majority of whom were Israeli. All passengers and crew were safe and accounted for after the plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. They were flown to Tel Aviv late Wednesday.

Investigators said that the co-pilot carried out the attack with what's called a crash axe — a lightweight emergency tool stored in the cockpit to break through panels or jammed doors in the event of a crash.

The aviation tracking site Flightradar24 said data shows at one point the plane descended more than 14,000 feet, or nearly 3 miles, in under 30 seconds — way faster than normal.

The pilot was able to open the cockpit door during the attack, and passengers rushed in and subdued the attacker, while another pilot who happened to be on board helped land the plane, according to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who spoke to the injured pilot as he was recovering in the hospital.

Sponsor Message

Both the pilot and the co-pilot are alive and have been transferred to the UAE for questioning.

Attacker is an Omani national

The co-pilot is from Oman, according to Israeli officials. Omani and Emirati officials have not confirmed that publicly.

The detail of his nationality is raising questions in Israel about how he was allowed to fly a plane heading to Ben Gurion, as Israel does not allow pilots from countries it doesn't have diplomatic relations with to fly in its airspace. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Fox & Friends that Israel checks the background of pilots flying routes into the country, and that the attacker must have gotten through a "loophole."

Officials from Israel's Ministry of Transportation and security services have traded accusations over the lack of oversight and vetting of the pilot. Meanwhile, several of Netanyahu's political opponents have said the security breach is a failure on the prime minister's part and have called for a larger investigation.

Netanyahu announced late Sunday that there will be a formal examination into the security situation around "foreign civil aviation into Israel," but did not provide further details.

A politically tense time in Israel

National elections in Israel — which will determine whether or not Netanyahu will remain prime minister — are just weeks away. It's the first such national election since the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, which sparked the war in Gaza.

Polls in Israel show that the race is tight, and analysts say the FlyDubai attack would likely not change Israelis' attitudes on how they will vote.

Netanyahu has been campaigning largely on the idea that he alone can protect Israelis from the external threats that Israel faces, while his opponents have pointed to what they see as major security failures under his leadership — including the Oct. 7 attack.

World.title: Nobel medicine prize goes to 3 scientists for research into brain activity
World.content:
Nobel medicine prize goes to 3 scientists for research into brain activity

toggle caption i Pontus Lundahl/TT News Agency via AP

STOCKHOLM — The Nobel Prize in medicine was awarded Monday to three scientists working on the mechanisms the brain uses to switch on, or off, the activity of individual nerve cells.

Karl Deisseroth, 54, Peter Hegemann, 71, and Georg Nagel, 73, have carried out research into light-gated ion channels and optogenetics. They are based at universities in Germany and the United States.

toggle caption i Eugene Hoshiko/AP

The Nobel committee lauded their work, writing on X that the method "is now being used in laboratories around the world to reveal the brain's mysteries."

The Nobel Assembly said Deisseroth is based at Stanford University in California, while Hegemann is at Humboldt University in Berlin and Nagel at the University of Würzburg in Germany.

Sponsor Message

Thomas Perlmann, the secretary of the medicine committee, said he was able to reach all three winners by phone Monday.

The prize was announced at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, kicking off Nobels week.

The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million).

Last year, the prize went to three scientists researching the immune system.

Monday's medicine prize is followed by the physics prize on Tuesday, chemistry on Wednesday and literature on Thursday.

After Friday's peace prize is awarded, the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced on Oct. 12.

The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organization.

World.title: Cornell protesters demand university president resign over handling of alleged frat-house gang rape
World.content:
Student at 'Justice for Survivors' demonstration says conversation has been 'vindicating'

Campus sexual assault not just a Cornell problem, says student | Duration closed caption 7:05

Students at Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., are protesting the school's handling of an alleged gang rape at the Chi Phi fraternity in 2024. A third-year student at the protest told the CBC's Katie Nicholson she had a similar experience of sexual assault and that it's a systemic problem on many campuses.

World.title: Crown says DNA evidence helped ID man now on trial for decades-old sex assaults against children
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This story contains details of sexual assaults against children.

For three decades, the brutal cold case confounded police.

An unidentified attacker had violently tied up three children as young as eight in southern Ontario parks between 1992 and 1995. He sexually assaulted each of them and got away every time.

At a court in Brampton, Ont., on Monday, prosecutors told a jury how DNA evidence had finally linked each attack to Richard Neil, now 67.

As Neil's trial got underway, Crown attorney Shazin Karim went into graphic detail about the attacks — involving urination and anal penetration — and how they were reported to police at the time.

The victims were an eight-year-old boy, a 10-year-old boy and a 15-year-old girl, Karim said.

"They were children," she said, underlining to the jury some of the evidence "may be difficult to hear."

One of the three attacks was in September 1994, when a 10-year-old boy was sexually assaulted by a man in Brampton's Norton Place Park. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

Neil has pleaded not guilty to the 17 charges he's facing, including kidnapping, sexual assault causing bodily harm and administering a stupefying drug.

Karim told the jurors investigators had first identified him as a suspect in recent years thanks to genetic genealogy analysis conducted in the U.S.

The investigative technique — which involves comparing crime scene DNA to genetic data voluntarily submitted to direct-to-consumer genealogical services — was unavailable to police in the 1990s.

Karim said police later uncovered further evidence that positively identified Neil as the assailant.

According to the Crown's opening statement to the jury, Neil's fingerprints matched those lifted by police from a bag and a bottle carried by the attacker all those years ago.

Lawyer Leo Adler, left and his client, Neil, are seen in a sketch at the Ontario Superior Court of Justice in Brampton on Monday. (Pam Davies/CBC)

His DNA also matched samples recovered from each of the three crime scenes — Brampton's Norton Place Park, Idlewood Park in Kitchener and Wildwood Park in Oakville — the Crown said.

Neil wore a dark suit jacket and white buttoned shirt in the courtroom, seated next to his lawyer Leo Adler. The accused appeared to glance over at jurors during Karim's opening statement.

According to an indictment filed in the Ontario Superior Court of Justice, Neil is also accused of making "a video tape recording constituting child pornography" on the date of the Oakville attack on the girl.

The victims' identities are covered by a publication ban.

Karim told the jury employment records show Neil worked at Canada Post in Waterloo at the time of the assault in neighbouring Kitchener in 1992.

What's more, the prosecutor said when police seized Neil's electronic devices following his arrest in 2024, they found photos and videos pointing to an "interest" in urine drinking.

Karim said the victims' accounts of what happened is not contested. But she said the defence disputes the allegation that Neil was the assailant.

The trial continues.

World.title: 'Heartbreaking reality': Crew, passengers of downed medical transport jet are likely dead, company says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The decision by the U.S. Coast Guard to end the search for the crew and passengers of a medical transport jet out of Hamilton means it's likely that the four Canadians and two Bermudians on board didn't survive, says the company that operated the jet.

Latitude Air Ambulance issued a statement late Sunday night, saying hope of finding survivors from the downed Gulfstream G100 aircraft, which is named Heartbeat 104, appeared to be gone.

"It is with profound sadness that we acknowledge the decision by the United States Coast Guard to conclude active search and rescue operations and transition to recovery efforts," Latitude said in its statement.

"Given the information shared by authorities and the conclusion of the search and rescue phase, we must now face the heartbreaking reality that the four members of our Latitude team, our patient and the patient's family escort, who were aboard…are presumed to have died."

The Bermuda Police Service on Monday released the names of the two Bermudians presumed dead. They identified 66-year-old Marilyn Lavonne Bean and her 41-year-old son, Sergio Wayne Lottimore, as those missing. The identities of the Canadian flight crew have not been released yet.

The Transportation Safety Board of Canada (TSBC) also announced on Monday that it will lead the investigation.

The agency said early indications are that something might have gone wrong with the jet's electrical system.

The Coast Guard and National Guard had used fixed wing aircraft, helicopters and ships to search a huge area of 11,500 square kilometres since about 2 a.m. Saturday when the Coast Guard said it was contacted by the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration that contact had been lost with the Gulfstream aircraft. The jet, which had flown out of Hamilton, was travelling from Bermuda to Boston with a patient and a family member along with the crew.

Sunday morning, the Coast Guard said debris from the jet had been found off Nantucket. Sunday night, the Coast Guard decided to end the search.

"Suspending a search is not an easy decision," Rear Adm. Matthew Lake, commander of the Northeast District, said Sunday night. We express our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones affected by the tragedy and our gratitude for our partner agencies who helped support search efforts.

Debris was recovered by U.S. Coast Guard

Sunday morning, Lake said the Coast Guard was in the process of working with Massachusetts authorities to get some craft out in the area that are equipped with sonar to be able to do some detection on the seabed floor. He said the water was about 80 to 90 feet deep in the area.

Latitude said its thoughts are first and foremost with the families, loved ones, friends, and colleagues of the people on the jet.

"Our four crew members were valued members of the Latitude family. They dedicated themselves to providing care to people at some of the most difficult moments in their lives, and they were carrying out that mission when this tragedy occurred," the company said.

"We are grieving their loss deeply and will continue to support their families and our employees through the difficult days ahead.

"We extend that same care and compassion to the family and loved ones of our patient and family escort," Latitude said. "We ask that the privacy of all of the families involved be respected as they grieve."

The company said it will continue to cooperate fully with the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board, the Transportation Safety Board of Canada and all other relevant authorities as recovery efforts and the investigation proceed.

"Determining the circumstances and cause of an aviation accident is a careful and methodical process, and we will not speculate about what occurred," the company said.

Hamilton Mayor Andrea Horwath said she was "heartbroken by the tragic loss of life."

"My heart goes out to the families and loved ones of those who were aboard, and to the entire Latitude team as they mourn the loss of their colleagues and friends," she said in a statement on Monday. "Latitude is part of our Hamilton community, operating out of Hamilton International Airport. On behalf of the city of Hamilton, I extend my deepest condolences to everyone affected by this tragedy."

Latitude said it was "deeply grateful to the United States Coast Guard and to the air traffic controllers, search and rescue crews, first responders, government agencies and others in Canada, the United States and Bermuda who worked tirelessly in the search" for those aboard the jet.

"Their professionalism, determination, and compassion will never be forgotten."

'Unimaginable loss': Latitude Air Ambulance president

Peter Byl, president of Latitude, said the tragedy is an "unimaginable loss for our Latitude family and for everyone who loved the six people" aboard the jet.

"Our focus now is on supporting their families, supporting our people and assisting the authorities. We will honour our colleagues by remembering the care, professionalism, and commitment they brought to their work every day."

The company said it may provide further relevant information when it is confirmed by the appropriate authorities and can be shared with respect for the families involved.

Reached by CBC News on Monday, Byl said it is a "profoundly difficult time for the families and loved ones of the six people aboard Heartbeat 104, as well as for everyone at Latitude.

"Any further public communication will be guided by confirmed information from the appropriate authorities, the progress of the investigation, and the privacy and needs of the families involved."

The TSBC said, as per international agreements, investigations should be led by the state of registry — in this case, Canada.

The agency said it will be assisted by the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board, and in the coming days will deploy investigators to assist in the search for and recovery of the missing jet.

The TSBC said in a news release that the Gulfstream jet was approaching Boston when the crew reported electrical difficulties. The aircraft subsequently descended rapidly and contact with air traffic control was lost south of Nantucket, the agency said.

Bermuda's Premier David Burt said the country's worst fears have been realized after holding out hope for the best. In a separate statement, Bermuda Health Minister Kim Wilson said it is an "incredibly difficult time for all those affected, and I know many people across Bermuda are holding them in their thoughts and prayers."

She also offered thanks for the Canadian crew who flew to her country to help a family in need.

"We... recognize the dedicated crew who came to Bermuda to provide a service that has supported many families during some of life's most difficult moments," she said. "For that, we are deeply grateful."

World.title: The mental health of young men is declining. Experts warn it could get worse
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canadian men and boys are facing an escalating societal crisis as their rates of depression, anxiety and addiction rise. For The National, CBC's Omar Dabaghi-Pacheco investigates the roots of the struggle and whether a new federal mental health strategy goes far enough.

On the surface, Nick Cholmsky looked like a thriving teenager.

Growing up in Ottawa, he says he was athletic and heavily involved in basketball, had friends and a close relationship with his family.

But underneath all that he says he was deeply depressed. The symptoms began in middle school and became much worse by Grade 11.

At 16, he had begun entertaining suicidal thoughts.

Nick Cholmsky, who grew up in Ottawa, experienced depression as a teen. He says online messaging encourages boys and men to stay silent about their psychological struggles. (CBC)

Even as his depression and anxiety grew stronger, Cholmsky believed he couldn’t say anything, because "being a man" meant pushing negative thoughts down, and that any sign of weakness would cause him shame.

"Looking back, so much of that [congenial attitude] was for sure just a performance, me acting the way I thought I was supposed to act as a man," said Cholmsky, now 21.

There’s a common problem everywhere and it’s how men and boys are feeling. And they are not feeling great. - Federal Health Minister Marjorie Michel

Earlier this year, the federal government reported on a wide range of data showing that the mental health of young men has deteriorated since 2012. Between 2012 and 2022, the number of men aged 15 to 24 who self-reported mood disorders increased from 11 per cent to 16 per cent, while self-reported generalized anxiety disorders increased from four per cent to 10 per cent.

Those who reported their mental health as "very good" or "excellent" plummeted from 70 per cent to 52 per cent in that same time period.

A separate report shows that men are three times as likely as women to kill themselves and that it's the second-leading cause of death in boys aged 15 to 34 (after unintentional injuries).

"There’s a common problem everywhere and it’s how men and boys are feeling. And they are not feeling great," federal Health Minister Marjorie Michel told CBC News.

"There is a lot of anxiety [about] their role as men and boys."

Social media use, gambling major issues

Research implicates a variety of factors in men’s depression, most prominently social isolation, social media use and online sports betting.

Data from the Canadian Medical Association Journal shows a huge rise in young men calling helplines with gambling addictions. (Health Canada reports men are three times more likely than women to have a gambling problem.)

Canada legalized single-event sports betting in 2021. In 2022, Ontario became the first province to allow private companies to operate alongside government-regulated industry.

A separate report released this month by the Institute for Clinical Evaluation Sciences (ICES) showed that since 2022, emergency room visits for gambling disorders had doubled — largely with young men showing up in a psychological crisis, such as suicidal ideation or psychosis, as a result of gambling losses.

"The gambling stats didn’t surprise me at all when I heard them," said Cholmsky. "I saw kids in middle school gambling."

WATCH | Investor and podcast Scott Galloway on male potential: Scott Galloway on male potential | Duration closed caption 1:10 U.S. investor and podcaster Scott Galloway talks to CBC News about the impacts of the manosphere and the loss of 'off-ramps to the middle class,' and how young men are being impacted.

Whether the stress is the result of gambling or something else, Cholmsky says online messaging encourages boys and men to stay silent.

"When I was going through some of my worst mental health times, I was online a lot and it was really the height of Andrew Tate," Cholmsky said.

The U.S.-born Tate is one of the best-known influencers in the manosphere, famous for espousing strict rules for being an alpha male, such as maximizing fitness, maintaining control over relationships and emotions and making as much money as possible.

He retains a large following despite being in U.S. detention on multiple criminal charges, including sex trafficking.

"[Tate's] message, and a lot of that manosphere messaging for boys, is 'be a man, be tough, make lots of money,'" Cholmsky said.

There are also trends like "looksmaxxing." Influencer Braden Peters, also known as Clavicular, has amassed a huge following telling young boys sometimes to smash their own faces with hammers to be more conventionally beautiful. His content has more than 40 million likes. Peters was charged with rape last month.

Experts warn dangerous role models like this can have real-world impacts.

"The manosphere is radicalizing young boys who don’t know where they fit — and that should concern us all," said John Oliffe, Canada research chair in men’s health promotion at the University of British Columbia.

Oliffe says this was "amplified" by the earliest parts of the COVID-19 pandemic when global lockdowns increased isolation and the loss of social connection. Vulnerable teenagers often found themselves lost online.

"There continues to be a whole world of pain in some of that unregulated content," Oliffe said.

John Oliffe, Canada research chair in men’s health promotion at the University of British Columbia, says the radicalizing effects of the manosphere should worry us all. (Nav Rahi/CBC)

Adam Kunder, a 33-year-old former firefighter who lives in Toronto, says he also felt he needed to keep his problems quiet. He suffered mental health issues and hit "rock bottom" before beginning to find help in the summer of 2024.

"As a man, you think you are supposed to be strong, push any bad feelings down, suppress depression or sadness or fear," he said.

Kunder says he has lost multiple friends to suicide and says you never would have known they were suffering.

Gender roles and 'toxic masculinity'

Kunder said the world is changing in ways that are becoming confusing for many men.

The emphasis on women's parity in the labour force and society, as well as a greater acceptance of non-traditional gender identities, has upended expectations.

"At one point we knew we were supposed to be the provider and protector, and the idea of ‘toxic masculinity’ wasn’t a thing," he said. "I think men are really trying to figure out what it means to be a man in today’s world."

WATCH | Why manosphere influencers appeal to young men: Why ‘manosphere’ influencers are appealing to young men | Duration 1:30 Critic Amil Niazi joins Commotion with Elamin Abdelmahmoud to discuss Louis Theroux: Inside the Manosphere, a documentary about the online world of toxic masculinity, and examine the rising popularity of "manosphere" influencers among young men.

Oliffe pointed to other troubling patterns for young men.

"There are increasing lower rates of boys heading to universities, and very serious challenges in male-dominated industries such as construction, that as a society, we should not ignore."

Oliffe said that while the trades offer good careers, they often see high rates of substance use and mental health issues, as the necessary physical labour and harsh working environments can "heighten these risks."

Oliffe said that in the last decade, there has been "low government investment in men's mental health."

"I think the theme of silence is a very regrettable period in history, where on one side we talked about equity and inclusion, and then in effect ostracized 50 per cent of the population," Oliffe said.

Health Minister Michel said that when she brought this issue to the federal cabinet, she was met with some resistance. Some colleagues told her it took "courage" to broach the mental health of boys and men, given it could even be politically risky to talk publicly about the issue.

"I said 'courage'? This is not courage. We are ministers of health, it is our job to take care of the entire population," she said.

"Men don't know how to ask for help. And when they are struggling, they don't know how to express it."

Government strategy to come by early 2027

The federal government will soon l aunch its first-ever mental health strategy for boys and men.

The agency told CBC that some of what they hope to invest in will be "mentorship, peer support, sport and recreation," while "promoting healthy relationships, positive social norms and safer online environments."

Toronto resident Adam Kunder says he feels it's his duty 'to show up for men who are suffering and to hear them out and just let them know it’s all OK.' (CBC)

For Robert Whitley, a men’s health expert and professor of psychiatry at McGill University in Montreal, part of the problem is the way society now views masculinity.

"Traditional masculinity has been denigrated in the popular mind whether it's through the media, through influencers, through commentators," he said. "The problem sometimes is a lack of masculinity."

He says there's a need for positive male role models.

"I’ve said many times before, it’s not a crisis of masculinity, there’s a crisis of mentorship," said Whitley.

For example, data from Statistics Canada shows only 25 per cent of teachers across elementary and high school systems in Canada are men. And at the organizations that step in to fill the mentorship gap — like the Big Brothers and Big Sisters of Canada — 70 per cent of volunteers are women.

"We're getting young men who are getting to the age of 18, 19, 20, who have never had a male role model in their lives," Whitley said.

Kunder and Cholmsky both say their mental health began to recover after they started asking for help, and they're now working to be role models for other young men.

"I feel like it’s my duty in a way to show up for men who are suffering and to hear them out and just let them know it’s all OK," said Kunder, who coaches and works with other men.

Last month in Ottawa, Cholmsky was awarded top 21 under 21 for his work in mental health advocacy and challenging "harmful stereotypes around masculinity and mental health."

"We all need to be doing our part to talk about this stuff," he said.

World.title: Southern Manitoba First Nations condemn newspaper for column questioning deaths at residential schools
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A column questioning the deaths of children at residential schools has led the Southern Chiefs' Organization to condemn the Winnipeg Sun and express concern that the newspaper's CEO is running for mayor of the Manitoba capital.

That candidate, Kevin Klein, apologized Monday for the column after initially disavowing responsibility for its publication.

On Oct. 4, the Sun published a column entitled "Grave misdirection: Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence," suggesting the deaths of Indigenous children at residential schools have been mischaracterized.

"Each death is a tragedy, but none is evidence of an atrocity," the column states, citing as examples the death of one child from bronchitis and another by lightning.

The National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation documented the deaths of at least 4,200 Indigenous children over the course of 165 years at Canada's residential schools. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada defined the deaths and widespread abuses within residential schools as cultural genocide.

The publication of the column four days after the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, also known as Orange Shirt Day, led to a formal statement of condemnation from the Southern Chiefs' Organization, which represents 33 Anishinaabe and Dakota First Nations in Manitoba.

Grand Chief Jerry Daniels is seen in a file photo. The SCO leader condemned the Winnipeg Sun article on Sunday. (Justin Fraser/CBC)

"Survivors and their families should not be forced, yet again, to prove what happened to them or defend the children who never came home," SCO Grand Chief Jerry Daniels said in a statement. "Thousands of children died while attending residential schools. Children were forcibly removed from their families and Nations, stripped of their languages and cultures, and subjected to systems of abuse, neglect and assimilation.

"These are not allegations or political talking points. They are part of Canada's documented historical record."

The co-author of a book about residential school denialism called the column disgusting because, he said, it perpetuates the notion the deaths of thousands of children who were forcibly removed from their families is less horrific because many died of disease, malnutrition and neglect as opposed to murder.

"A lot of people will say, oh, it was just tuberculosis. Lots of kids died of tuberculosis in the early 20th century," said University of Manitoba history professor Sean Carleton, the co-author of Truth Before Reconciliation: Confronting Residential School Denialism.

"That, in fact, is true, except for the fact that, you know what spreads tuberculosis faster? Overcrowding, poor nutrition. Lack of proper sanitation, overwork. All of these issues that were known to be systemic to the residential school system."

Carleton said the column perpetuates what he describes as far-right misinformation about First Nations making claims about mass graves or clandestine murders.

"This is a distraction tactic. It's an attempt to move the goalposts, to make it extremely difficult for Indigenous nations, to explain the complicated nuanced understanding of what we already know, thanks to church and state records, that at least 4,000 children died in these institutions for a variety of different reasons," he said.

Column shouldn't have run: Klein

As criticism of the column mounted Sunday, the editor-in-chief of the Klein Group, the company that owns the Winnipeg Sun, dug in her heels. Heather Klein defended the column in a followup entitled "Disagreement is not denial."

The Southern Chiefs' Organization also criticized her husband, Klein Group CEO Kevin Klein, who is one of 12 running for Winnipeg mayor in this month's civic election.

Daniels called it "deeply concerning" someone seeking public office provided a platform for someone to use residential schools and the deaths of First Nations children as the basis for political commentary.

"Winnipeg is home to a large and vibrant First Nations population. Anyone asking to lead this city has a responsibility to understand the history of residential schools and the ongoing responsibilities of reconciliation," Daniels said.

On Monday, Klein said the column in the Sun should not have run and said it lacked sufficient research.

"I wasn't happy with it. If I had been in charge, I would not have ran that column. I would not have approved that column," Klein said prior to a campaign announcement outside the Granite Curling Club in Winnipeg.

"But I am not involved in those decisions. So that mistake was made, and it was a mistake," he said.

"I apologize to the Southern Chiefs' Organization or any member of the community that was offended by that, but that's not my column. Those are not my words, and I did not approve that."

Kevin Klein speaks during an Oct. 2 campaign announcement. He said in a Sunday statement he is not responsible for the content of the Winnipeg Sun while he runs for mayor. (Prabhjot Singh Lotey/CBC)

In an earlier statement, issued Sunday, Klein said he is not responsible for the content of the Winnipeg Sun while he runs for mayor.

"From the day I entered the race for mayor, I stepped away from every editorial decision at the Winnipeg Sun, and I have kept that commitment. The paper stands on its own," his statement said.

Heather Klein alone is responsible for the content, the candidate said in his statement, adding he does not assign stories, edit copy, approve pieces or stop them from running.

"Any suggestion otherwise is reckless and without foundation," he said.

Other mayoral candidates criticize Klein

Several mayoral candidates also criticized the newspaper CEO-turned-candidate.

Mayoral candidate Noah Redden said in a statement there is a difference between upholding freedom of speech and tolerating hate speech.

Redden called residential school denialism inflammatory and said Klein needs to explain to Winnipeg's Indigenous population why his newspaper echoed attacks on residential school survivors.

Incumbent mayoral candidate Scott Gillingham told reporters Sunday he's spoken to enough Indigenous families in Winnipeg to hear first-hand the impact of residential schools.

"What is not deniable in my mind is the impact, the lasting, devastating impact of residential schools on our country," said Gillingham, who attended TRC Day events in an official capacity on Wednesday.

Klein said Friday he did not attend TRC Day events but called the national holiday important.

"Canadians ought to know what took place in the residential school system and what it has meant for Indigenous families and communities ever since," Klein said Sunday in a statement.

"The wrongs of the past should not be forgotten. As a father and a grandfather, I cannot begin to imagine the pain those families carry."

World.title: Avengers: Endgame once again beats Avatar as highest-grossing movie of all time
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Marvel's Avengers: Endgame recaptured its title this weekend as the highest-grossing movie of all time (not accounting for inflation). With a gross of $2.9255 billion US, the Disney title narrowly superseded James Cameron's biggest release, Avatar, at $2.9237 billion US.

The shift follows Endgame's recent re-release in theatres, and represents the second time it has overtaken Avatar at the box office. Hitting theatres late last month with four additional minutes, the slightly recut version of Marvel's superhero super-collage debuted to $86 million US at the global box office ($26 million US domestic), according to parent company Disney.

The film was re-released as an anticipatory tee-up to Avengers: Doomsday, the next in the Marvel Cinematic Universe's cycle of big-budget team-up films. Due to release Dec. 18, that movie will reintroduce a number of familiar faces, including stars like Robert Downey Jr. and Chris Evans.

It is a chance for the MCU to recapture the cultural zeitgeist after disappointing recent entries — like Thunderbolts* and Captain America: Brave New World — whose new leading characters failed to capture audience interest.

Among re-releases, only 1997's Star Wars: A New Hope ($35.9 million US) and 2011's The Lion King ($30.2 million US) have opened higher than Endgame in domestic cinemas. That release set its own record in 2019 — it was then that the Marvel film's total gross overtook Avatar, the intergalactic film about war between Na'vi and humans, shortly after its release.

This image released by Marvel Studios shows a scene from Avengers: Endgame. (Marvel Studios/Disney)

It was a historic achievement; Cameron had actually individually held the record since 1998, when Titanic became the all-time highest-grossing film. While the ocean-liner epic reached its gross of $1.84 billion US via markedly lower ticket prices, Avatar's ascendance was still shocking, surging to the top spot in 2010 after just 39 days in theatres.

But when Endgame finally broke his streak in 2019, Cameron did not appear to be a sore loser.

“Oel ngati kameie,” the Canadian New Zealand director shared on X (then Twitter) at the time , using a phrase from his film's fictional language. “I see you, Marvel. Congratulations to Avengers: Endgame on becoming the new box-office king.”

But after a 2021 re-release in China, Cameron's Avatar beat Marvel once again, catapulting to a gross of over $2.8 billion US. Endgame directors Joe and Anthony Russo then took to social media to congratulate Cameron, writing in a post, “Passing the gauntlet back to you.”

An unpredictable box office

The latest record flip-flop comes at a uniquely unpredictable time for the box office. Hollywood had its best summer on record this year, posting $4.76 billion US in domestic ticket sales, according to analytics firm Rentrak .

But it came along with a slew of poor performers, like Steven Spielberg's return to sci-fi filmmaking, Disclosure Day, and the Spielberg-style nostalgia dinosaur flick The End of Oak Street, which similarly failed to pull audiences in despite strong reviews and famous faces like Anne Hathaway and Ewan McGregor.

Then the Jacob Elordi-led apocalypse film The Dog Stars let down 20th Century Studios, bombing with roughly $8 million US domestic in its opening weekend against a reported $80-million US production budget. Tom Cruise's Digger saw perhaps the A-lister's biggest flop of his career, opening with a shocking $8 million US domestically against a reported budget of between $125 million US to $180 million US.

That is on top of a dismal year for studio Warner Bros., none of whose offerings surpassed $100 million US in the domestic box office.

World.title: Cold reality: Canadian troops struggle in Alaska as military relearns Arctic warfare
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A series of internal Department of National Defence documents suggest Canadian troops were ill-prepared and occasionally ill-equipped for the harsh conditions they faced last winter during a major training exercise with American forces in Alaska.

The evaluation reports, obtained by CBC News, show the military has a lot to learn and a long way to go to rebuild its capability to defend the Arctic.

The training involved over 400 members of the 3rd Battalion Royal Canadian Regiment (3RCR) which was folded into a much larger U.S. Army brigade during Exercise Global Response in February at the Joint Pacific Multinational Readiness Center, north of Fairbanks, Alaska.

The Carney government has committed to an almost year-round presence in the Far North and the reports indicate, among other things, that troops will need to learn to rely less on technology and more on basic skills in order to fight and survive, according to defence experts.

Separate Canadian and American evaluations were prepared and both show a litany of concerns that raise questions about how prepared troops and their equipment are to fight in harsh conditions, where the temperatures plunge below –30 C.

"Throughout their stay in the waiting area the Coy [Company] consistently demonstrated a lack of preparations needed to live in Arctic conditions," said an undated Canadian evaluation, which assessed individual companies within the battalion.

WATCH | Former chief of the defence staff on Canada's Arctic plan: Carney's $35B plan is 'a start' for Arctic security: former Canadian top soldier | Duration closed caption 7:57 Retired general Tom Lawson, former chief of the defence staff for the Canadian Armed Forces and the chair of the board at the CDA Institute, joins Power & Politics to break down how much Prime Minister Mark Carney's $35-billion announcement in Yellowknife can bolster Arctic sovereignty.

The report was critical of a recent initiative which allowed the regiment to purchase off-the-shelf civilian equipment to augment military cold-weather gear — something that created problems.

"This was evident when observing soldiers attempting to remedy issues with a Coleman stove and lanterns or watching them attempt to set up a 10-man tent," said the evaluation, obtained by CBC News. It said that among some Canadian units there was a "lack of emphasis on basic winter soldiering skills."

In an interview, Lt.-Col. Aaron Corey, the commander of 3RCR, disagreed and said his troops trained for winter conditions for a year before the Alaska training deployment.

"Every soldier to go up on that exercise had to be a cold weather operator qualified," Corey said.

"All of our leaders from the sections and up, we received cold weather leader training and then we had Arctic operations advisers that were sprinkled into the battalion as well."

He added the battalion "put a lot of effort into preparations for this exercise in the year preceding it and to get back to a level of winter warfare — or Arctic warfare — that we haven't seen in a few years."

Members of Mike Company, 3rd Battalion Royal Canadian Regiment are seen at the training exercise last winter. (Pte. Felix Chagnon/Department of National Defence)

Canadian soldiers have wrestled with the problem of fighting in extreme cold for decades, and even prepared for the possibility of Soviet attack across the polar region during the early Cold War.

The Alaskan exercise reports did note that despite the challenges — and as many as 30 troops suffering various levels of frostbite — the battalion was successful in the exercise by capturing its training objectives.

Corey said troops learned valuable lessons, most notably how they have to slow down and take the weather into account, more so than when they are on operations in other parts of the world.

"We had the enemy and the weather, which was a greater enemy in most cases," Corey said. "So we had to slow down. We had to make sure that our troops had warming cycles. We had to slow down because the kit and equipment you're carrying is heavier. We had to slow down because there's more energy being exerted as you fight your way through the muskeg or up the mountains."

The Ottawa Citizen previously reported on the frostbite casualties. The documents obtained by CBC News, however, paint a broader picture of the challenges faced by the regiment.

One document noted how "several gaps emerged regarding the medical team's understanding of their required tasks" during the exercise.

The medics thought they were only on standby to treat real casualties, not participate in the training scenario, said an undated evaluation prepared for the health services branch. On three occasions some of them were seen using personal phones for long calls, giving away their positions to the enemy.

It was also noted that the medical team was only given a four-hour professional development seminar on Arctic medicine principles rather than a five-day U.S.-led course at the Arctic medicine simulation centre.

Chief Warrant Officer Robert McSpadden, the regimental sergeant major for 3RCR, said he found the medical team to be outstanding, especially when it came to treating the frostbite casualties. He said he couldn't speak to the training decisions.

The Canadians also ran into problems with the rapid cold weather draining batteries for their drones, leaving in some cases only 10 minutes of flying time. There were problems with communications because of the absence of satellites so far north.

The separate American assessment, prepared by the Ted Stevens Center for Arctic Security Studies and published online, noted how U.S. units experienced similar difficulties. It pointed to basic preparation problems such as a lack of snowclearing equipment and a shortage of fuel to keep engines running in order to prevent them from freezing.

Retired colonel Pierre Leblanc, who served in the Far North in command positions in the late 1990s, said it's been almost a generation since Canadian troops were present in large numbers in the Arctic and many skills will have to be relearned.

WATCH | Canada's Armed Forces preparing to defend northern border: Who’s defending Canada’s Arctic? | Duration closed caption 4:56 For Radio-Canada/RAD, Julia Pagé and director Frédéric Lacelle go to the Arctic to join the Canadian Rangers on patrol in extreme conditions to see first hand how armed forces are preparing to defend the northern border.

"It's a different world," said Leblanc, who noted the unpredictability of the weather and the vast distances made it the most challenging place to operate he'd ever encountered.

He used the example of having to dispatch a repair team to a North Warning System radar location during his tenure.

It was supposed to be a simple job, lasting only a few hours. The team was stuck there for 21 days, Leblanc said.

Today's high-tech, web-enabled, satellite-tethered military needs a serious back-to-basics approach in a place where technology can't be counted on, he said.

"If you rely too much on it, you're going to very quickly have a problem. Have to be able to work with very, very basic systems," said Leblanc.

Rob Huebert, an Arctic defence expert at the University of Calgary, said the Canadian military in the 1950s and 60s was expert at training and fighting in the Far North.

There was, at the time, the capacity to move more than 1,000 troops and their equipment at short notice anywhere in Canada.

For example, in February 1950, more than 5,000 Canadian and American troops took part in Exercise Sweetbriar along the Alaska Highway between Whitehorse and Alaska, specifically testing how combined forces could move, fight and sustain themselves in Arctic conditions.

Canadian troops subsequently trained for the possibility of Soviet airborne attacks in the North, while the military experimented with clothing, vehicles, communications, mobility and survival techniques. In the 1970s, the Canadian Airborne Regiment practised its own parachute assaults at places including Coral Harbour and Inuvik.

Huebert acknowledged the increase in winter exercises that the Carney government has enabled through its increase in defence spending. But he says they are a smaller scale.

"You can't just simply say, we know how to do this with small units and we can magically do it with big units," Huebert said.

It's also a mindset problem, he added.

Several years ago the country's former top military commander, retired general Walt Natynczyk, quipped that if the Russians ever invaded Canada's Arctic, the first thing he'd do is launch a search and rescue operation.

"I really think that that was a very unfortunate comment," said Huebert, who added it established the notion that troops wouldn't have to fight in the Far North.

"The Russians know how to fight in the North. We would be much better off if General Natynczyk, at that time, had actually said there are growing signs that the Russians are not the friends that we thought they were."

World.title: Alleged NATO spy case brings 'some serious lessons' for Canada, public safety minister says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree says "gaps" in Canada's security screening need to be addressed following the arrest of a Canadian NATO intern in Belgium on espionage charges.

Anandasangaree faced an hour of grilling from MPs on the House of Commons public safety and national security committee on Monday, who are probing how the intern gained security clearance from Ottawa to work at the military alliance.

Belgian authorities arrested the intern on July 24, alleging she was spying on behalf of a third country and of being a member of a criminal organization. Sources have told Reuters and other media that the suspected third country is China.

The minister said he asked the RCMP and CSIS to review what happened and is going through their recommendations.

"There will obviously be some serious lessons that come out of that process," he said.

Anandasangaree said there are some 200,000 screenings done every year by government departments, with the support of CSIS and the RCMP.

"By and large, it is an unimpeachable record. Of course, there are gaps here, and I recognize that there are gaps," he testified.

"And that's what I think we need to improve on."

However, the minister provided few answers about what those gaps are and what he's considering changing going forward.

While Belgian courts do not publicly identify defendants in criminal investigations until their trial, a CBC News investigation identified the accused spy as Biwei Zhang, a systems engineer with a background in economics who was an intern at NATO's Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe (SHAPE) in the southern Belgian city of Mons. She also uses the name Claire Zhang professionally and Catina Zhang on her Facebook profile.

WATCH | Minister acknowledges 'gaps': Minister acknowledges security screening process has 'gaps' | Duration closed caption 0:40 Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree told the House of Commons public safety and national security committee on Monday that there are gaps in Canada's security screening that are being looked at following the arrest of a Canadian NATO intern in Belgium on espionage charges.

In 2023, the Public Service Commission of Canada found Zhang had committed fraud by applying for a position at the Canada Border Services Agency under two different names and emails, failing to later clarify whether she submitted multiple applications.

The Canadian Security Intelligence Service (CSIS) told the committee that working for NATO usually requires at least a secret level clearance if not higher.

GAC had security clearance authorization in this case

Much of the questioning revolved around how the intern was cleared after the fraud finding.

"If someone is willing to lie to get a job with the federal government, how are we not more cautious?" asked Conservative MP Rhonda Kirkland during one of her rounds of questioning.

The minister and senior bureaucrats who appeared in front of the committee on Monday often responded that they were limited in answering specifics of the case because there's an ongoing investigation.

Opposition MPs grew increasingly frustrated as the committee went on, calling out what they said was a lack of accountability on an important national security file.

Speaking in French, Bloc MP Claude DeBellefeuille told the minister and other witnesses she sees "gross incompetence" and "weaknesses" across multiple departments in this case.

MPs did hear from bureaucrats about how the Treasury Board sets security screening policy for the government but it's up to the individual department's deputy head to sign off on an employee's clearance.

In this case the final authorization landed with Global Affairs Canada, witnesses testified.

Vanessa Lloyd, deputy director of policy and strategic partnerships at CSIS, said her agency found "opportunities for improvements" in the process.

Case is 'disgraceful': Conservative MP

The committee's probe was triggered by the Conservatives and Bloc Québécois, who argued it's necessary to find out whether Canada had missed warning signs or red flags.

"It is a shame and I think it's actually disgraceful, dare I say minister, that it was Belgium that figured out a Canadian was spying rather than Canada," said Conservative MP Frank Caputo, the party's public safety critic.

WATCH | Questions raised about Canada's security screening: Canadian NATO spying suspect raises questions about country’s security screening | Duration closed caption 10:35 A CBC News investigation has identified Biwei Zhang as the Canadian woman recently arrested on suspicion of spying at NATO’s military headquarters in Belgium. According to her online resume, Zhang previously worked for both the Canadian Space Agency and Statistics Canada prior to her NATO internship. The case has raised questions surrounding Canada's security screening process for sensitive government roles.

"Was this an intelligence failure? Yes, it was. Did Canada's international standing suffer because of this? Yes.… How did this happen? We have no answer."

Based on online information, Zhang also previously worked as an economist at Statistics Canada and as a systems engineer at the Canadian Space Agency.

The Chinese Embassy in Canada told CBC News it firmly opposes "baseless speculations" that Zhang was acting on behalf of Beijing.

She remains in custody in Belgium.

World.title: Afternoon front page: ‘Gaps’ in government security; prof sues Lethbridge university for $3M; and more
World.content:
Article content

It’s another announcement from Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith. And it’s about the same West Coast pipeline they’ve announced before. This time it’s been designated a project of “national interest.” Still undetermined is whether it’s of interest to investors and shippers.
