World.title: El Jalapeño: Guanajuato residents mistake arrival of French acrobats for third ‘French Intervention’
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

GUANAJUATO, Guanajuato — Civic vigilance reached a 160-year high in the historic capital of Guanajuato on Saturday evening after local residents, observing a group of French performers scaling public buildings and suspending high-tension ropes across historic plazas, mistakenly believed the French Republic had launched a third military intervention in Mexico.

Members of the Paris-based Chaillot National Theater, who arrived in the city to perform a collaborative aerial circus piece titled “Vértigo” for the 54th International Cervantino Festival, were met with suspicious glances and immediate defensive maneuvering from municipal historians, local shopkeepers, and neighborhood watch organizers who recalled that previous French arrivals had resulted in imposed monarchies and six-year occupations.

“We saw men in fitted performance gear deploying cables across Plaza Allende and securing anchor points near the Cervantes Theater,” said local historian and retired educator Don Héctor Morales, who admitted to briefly scouring his cellar for period-appropriate artillery. “Naturally, given the diplomatic history of 1838 and 1862, we assumed the French government was once again attempting to collect unpaid bakery debts or institute an unconstitutional monarchy. It turned out they were just balancing on a wire to live ambient jazz.”

The diplomatic confusion mounted when highliner Jean-Claude Moreau walked across a slackline suspended decades above the cobbled streets, an act interpreted by several onlookers as an attempt to establish aerial dominance over the state’s historic center. Public concern was only eased when municipal officers confirmed that France was merely participating as the festival’s invited guest nation to celebrate 200 years of mostly peaceful diplomatic relations.

The production, which combines contemporary dance, live music, and aerial arts, required local authorities to release a clarification confirming that highliners hanging mid-air were engaged in artistic expression rather than strategic reconnaissance. Organizers assured the public that despite the visible presence of French acrobats hovering near historic architecture, no foreign princes would be installed in Chapultepec Castle as a result of the performance.

World.title: Brazil Stocks Jump 7.7% to Record 206,912 After Vote
World.content:
Avenida Faria Lima, São Paulo's financial district. Photo: Mauro Cateb via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

MARKETS · BRAZIL

Runoff · Sunday, 25 October Flávio Bolsonaro vs Lula: what happens next First-round results, how the runoff works, the key dates and who backs whom, in one guide. Read the runoff guide →

Key Facts — The country Brazil is Latin America’s largest economy and a major exporter of oil, iron ore and soybeans. Its main stock index, the Ibovespa, tracks the most traded shares on B3, the São Paulo exchange.

— Why it matters Americans hold Brazil mainly through US-listed shares of Petrobras, Vale and Itaú, and the iShares MSCI Brazil fund (EWZ). Monday showed how money prices a possible change of government.

— Why now Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the conservative Liberal Party (PL) candidate, led Sunday’s first round with 47.03% to President Lula’s 45.16%, per the electoral court (TSE). The runoff is on 25 October.

— What happened On Monday 5 October the Ibovespa closed at a record 206,911.89 points, up 7.70%. The central bank’s final PTAX rate was 4.9859 reais per dollar, 4.6% below Friday.

— The numbers At the 4 p.m. ET close, EWZ rose 12.57% to US$42.99 and the Petrobras ADR 11.59% to US$24.16. Friday closes: US$38.19 and US$21.65.

— What it means for you Brazilian holdings are worth more in dollars, while Brazil trips cost about 4% more. One real was worth about 20 US cents at Monday’s close, against 19.2 cents on Friday.

— Still open Whether the rally survives the 25 October runoff. Exporters such as Suzano and Embraer traded lower on Monday, because a stronger real shrinks their earnings in reais.

— Prediction markets Polymarket gives a quarter-point cut in Brazil’s Selic rate in November a 73% chance (5 October, 4:22 p.m. ET). Polymarket puts Flávio Bolsonaro’s chance of winning at 83% and Kalshi at 83% (Lula: 17% and 17% ), as of 5 October, 4:20 pm ET ; prices are bets, not polls.

Brazil stocks closed at a record on Monday, the first session after Flávio Bolsonaro led Sunday’s presidential first round. The Ibovespa, São Paulo’s benchmark index, rose 7.70% to 206,911.89 points, its first close above 200,000.

For US investors the gain was bigger, because the real rallied too. The iShares MSCI Brazil ETF (EWZ) rose 12.57% in New York, and the dollar fell 4.12% against the real.

Flávio, a conservative senator and son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, faces President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the runoff. Lula leads the left-wing Workers’ Party (PT) and seeks a fourth term.

How the Real and the Ibovespa Moved on Monday

The Ibovespa closed at 206,911.89 points, up 7.70% from Friday’s 192,114.55, InfoMoney reported. During the session it traded above 209,000 points for the first time, according to G1, CNN Brasil and InfoMoney.

It was the largest daily rise since 24 March 2020, when the index gained 9.69% during the pandemic rebound, B3 closing data show. The previous closing record was 198,657.33 points, set in April.

The spot dollar closed down 4.12% at 5.0022 reais per dollar, Terra and Money Times reported. During the day it fell as low as 4.954 reais per dollar.

The central bank’s final PTAX reference rate was 4.9859 reais per dollar, 4.6% below Friday’s 5.2238. It was the first PTAX below five since 14 May, central bank data show.

Measured in dollars, the Ibovespa rose about 12% on the day, from about 36,800 to about 41,400. That is roughly the gain a US investor in the index would see.

The dollar's official PTAX rate fell 4.6% on Monday after the first round, closing below five reais for the first time since 14 May. Source: Banco Central do Brasil.

Friday’s positioning is in Ibovespa Jumps 2.6% to 192,115 on Vote Eve | Brazil Market Report, Oct 2. Our overnight report, Brazil Runoff Set; Ibovespa Entered Vote at 192,115, has the last prices before the count.

Petrobras, Itaú and Vale in New York

Brazilian shares listed in the US moved hours before São Paulo opened and held their gains to the 4 p.m. ET close. The Petrobras ADR rose 11.59% to US$24.16.

An ADR, or American depositary receipt, is a US-listed certificate for a foreign share. Itaú Unibanco’s ADR closed 15.42% higher at US$9.92 and Bradesco’s 18.48% higher at US$4.32.

Vale, the iron ore miner, lagged with a 2.98% gain to US$14.17. EWZ, the main US fund for Brazil stocks, closed 12.57% higher at US$42.99.

EWZ gains include the currency move, Valor noted, so they run ahead of the index in reais. A stronger real lifts the dollar value of every Brazilian share at once.

In São Paulo, state-linked names led the large caps in the morning. At 10:30 a.m., Banco do Brasil was up 12.82% and Petrobras preferred shares 6.47%, per Valor.

Why Investors Moved, and Where the Risk Sits

Investors read the result as raising the odds of a change of government and tighter public spending from 2027. Polls had expected Lula to finish first, Investing.com noted.

The right also gained in Congress. The Liberal Party (PL), the Bolsonaro family’s conservative party led by Valdemar Costa Neto, won 19 Senate seats on Sunday.

Capital Economics, a London-based research firm, said a Flávio win would bring better prospects of fiscal tightening and reform.

Interest-rate futures fell sharply. The January 2031 contract dropped 97 basis points to 13.02% by 9:20 a.m., hitting B3’s daily limit, Valor reported.

Lower long-term rates ease borrowing costs for the government and for companies. Not every share rose, though.

Exporters such as pulp maker Suzano, planemaker Embraer and motor maker WEG traded lower, InfoMoney reported. A stronger real cuts their revenue once converted from dollars.

History offers a guide and a caution. In 2022, after Jair Bolsonaro beat the polls in the first round, the index jumped 5.54% the next day, B3 data show.

The central bank’s PTAX dollar rate fell 3.8% that day. Lula still won the runoff four weeks later.

What It Means for You

For US holders of Brazil stocks through EWZ or ADRs, Monday added to a strong run. The Ibovespa had already gained 4.7% in the week to Friday 2 October.

For travellers, the move works the other way. At Monday’s close the rate was 5.00 reais per dollar, against 5.22 on Friday, so Brazil costs roughly 4% more.

US firms that buy Brazilian goods also pay more in dollars if the real holds. Brazil’s exporters of soybeans, iron ore and oil earn fewer reais per dollar sold.

What Is Not Known

The bigger unknown for Brazil stocks is the 25 October runoff. Flávio leads by about 2.2 million votes, but a two-point gap leaves room for Lula to recover.

Flávio’s fiscal plans are not yet clear, CNN Brasil noted, even as markets price in tighter spending. Some analysts warned of euphoria without a fiscal basis.

Nor is it known how the central bank will read a stronger real. The Selic, Brazil’s policy rate, stands at 13.75% after a quarter-point cut on 16 September.

More: Brazil news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket’s “Bank of Brazil decision in November?” market, bets put a quarter-point Selic cut at 73% on 5 October at 4:22 p.m. ET. A cut of 50 points or more stood at 13.9%, and no change at 8.5%.

Over the past day, no change lost about 11 points and the larger cut gained about 10. It is a thin market, with about US$42,000 traded.

The central bank’s Monetary Policy Committee (Copom) meets on 3 and 4 November, nine days after the runoff. A stronger real lowers import prices, which can leave room to keep cutting.

Why did Brazil stocks rise after the first round?

Investors read Flávio Bolsonaro’s lead as raising the chance of a change of government and tighter spending. The Ibovespa closed above 200,000 points for the first time on 5 October.

How much is the Brazilian real worth in US dollars?

At Monday’s close on 5 October, the rate was 5.00 reais per dollar, down 4.12% on the day. One real was worth about 20 US cents.

When is Brazil’s presidential runoff?

It is on Sunday 25 October 2026, between Flávio Bolsonaro and Lula. The central bank’s next rate decision follows on 4 November.

World.title: Guatemala Recaptures 2 Fraijanes Escapees in Mexico
World.content:
Police officers on motorcycles at an intersection in Guatemala City on 3 September 2018 (file photo). (Photo: tian2992, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

SECURITY · GUATEMALA

Key Facts — The country Guatemala, Central America’s most populous nation, borders Mexico and is a major source of migrants to the US. Gangs and drug routes shape its security agenda with Washington.

— Why it matters The US designated Barrio 18 a Foreign Terrorist Organization in September 2025. The Fraijanes II escape of 20 of its members became Guatemala’s biggest prison scandal in years.

— Why now The arrests came on Monday 5 October, a week before the first anniversary of the escape, confirmed on 12 October 2025.

— What happened Mexican and Guatemalan forces caught two Barrio 18 escapees, alias “Smoking” and “Liro Spyder”, in Benito Juárez, Quintana Roo, the municipality of Cancún, on 5 October, Guatemalan prosecutors said.

— The numbers Of the 20 escapees, 10 are now back in custody, one was found dead and nine remain at large, Interior Minister Marco Antonio Villeda said on 5 October.

— What it means for you Leaders of a US-designated terrorist group were hiding in a resort area popular with US visitors. Their capture shows cross-border police cooperation working.

— Still open When Mexico hands the two men back, whether they first face charges there over seized guns and drugs, and where the other nine fugitives are.

Two Fraijanes escapees from the Barrio 18 gang were caught on Monday near Cancún, Mexico, Guatemalan authorities said. Barrio 18 began in Los Angeles and has been on the US list of Foreign Terrorist Organizations since September 2025.

The two men fled Guatemala’s Fraijanes II maximum-security prison with 18 other gang members in an escape confirmed in October 2025. Nine of the 20 are still at large, Interior Minister Marco Antonio Villeda said.

Who Was Caught and Where

Guatemala’s Public Prosecutor’s Office (Ministerio Público, MP), the independent national prosecution service, announced the arrests on 5 October. It named the men as Rudy O., alias “Smoking”, and Esvin H., alias “Liro Spyder”.

The Interior Ministry, which runs the National Civil Police (PNC), gave their full names. They are Rudy Augusto Ortiz Morales and Esvin Estuardo Herrera Ardiano, AGN reported.

Both were found in the municipality of Benito Juárez, whose seat is the resort city of Cancún. Each had an Interpol red notice, an international request to locate and arrest a wanted person, issued over the escape.

The prosecutors said suspected marijuana, firearms and ammunition were found on the men when they were detained. The operation joined the MP, the PNC’s Transnational Anti-Gang Centre and Mexican security forces.

No charges over the seized items have been announced. Both men are presumed innocent of any new offence unless a court rules otherwise.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

A Year Hunting the Fraijanes Escapees

Guatemala’s Prison System confirmed on 12 October 2025 that 20 Barrio 18 members had escaped from Fraijanes II, east of Guatemala City. Police chief David Custodio Boteo said all of them led local gang cells, Prensa Libre reported.

Early investigations suggested the men slipped out over the previous two months with help from prison staff, the paper added. Charges against the guards are still moving through the courts, as covered in Guatemala Judge Changes Fraijanes Guards’ Charges Again.

Barrio 18 members from the Fraijanes II escape still at large, by date of official count. Source: Guatemala Interior Ministry, National Civil Police and Prison System figures reported by AGN.

The number at large has fallen in steps. AGN, the state news agency, put it at 16 in late October 2025. It was 13 in January and 11 at the end of March.

Monday’s two arrests bring it to nine. Ten escapees are back in custody and one was found dead, Villeda said.

“Smoking” first escaped Fraijanes II in 2022 by leaving another person in his place. He then lived in Mexico until his arrest there on 8 February 2025.

Mexico deported him to Guatemala after that arrest, Prensa Libre reported in October 2025. AGN also reported that one of the escapees had previously been returned by Mexican authorities.

What Villeda and the US Role Add

Villeda took over the Interior Ministry in late October 2025, about two weeks after the escape became public. He thanked Mexico on Monday and said “borders do not end an investigation”.

“We have nine to go, and the search does not end until we find the last one,” he told AGN. He added that the government is working so that an escape like Fraijanes II does not happen again.

One of his first steps as minister was to ask the US for help. A team from the FBI’s Joint Task Force Vulcan, which targets violent gangs, began working with Guatemalan police in November 2025.

That team withdrew in December and its return was set for July 2026, Villeda said in June, according to La Hora. He blamed the exit on poor cooperation from the former attorney general, Consuelo Porras.

Her successor, Attorney General Gabriel Estuardo García Luna, now leads the MP. Monday’s official statements did not say whether US agencies took part in the Quintana Roo arrests.

The Interior Ministry has offered 150,000 quetzales (about US$19,600) for information on each fugitive since 13 October 2025, AGN reported. Tips go to the hotlines 110 and 1561.

What It Means for You

For US readers, the case is about a group Washington treats as terrorists. The State Department announced the designation on 23 September 2025. It cited gang attacks on police, officials and civilians in Guatemala, Honduras and El Salvador.

The designation makes giving material support to the gang a federal crime and blocks its assets under US jurisdiction. Gang leaders moving between Guatemala and Mexico are a direct concern for US border and counter-gang policy.

For travellers, nothing in the official accounts points to a threat to visitors in Cancún. The arrests instead show Mexican and Guatemalan police sharing intelligence and acting on red notices.

The president’s wider security record is covered in Who Is Bernardo Arévalo, Guatemala’s President in 2026.

What Is Not Known

It is not known when the two Fraijanes escapees will reach Guatemala. Prosecutors said they are coordinating “extradition or handover” under the law, and gave no date.

Mexican authorities have not publicly detailed the operation. It is also unclear whether the men will first face Mexican charges over the guns and drugs reportedly seized.

Officials did not say how long the pair had been in Quintana Roo or who helped them. The location of the nine other fugitives has not been disclosed.

Who are the Fraijanes escapees caught in Mexico?

They are Rudy Augusto Ortiz Morales, alias Smoking, and Esvin Estuardo Herrera Ardiano, alias Liro Spyder, both Barrio 18 members. They were caught in Benito Juárez, Quintana Roo, on 5 October 2026.

How many Fraijanes II fugitives are still at large?

Nine of the 20 Barrio 18 members who escaped remain at large, Interior Minister Marco Antonio Villeda said on 5 October 2026. Ten have been recaptured and one was found dead.

Why does the US care about Barrio 18?

The US State Department designated Barrio 18 a Foreign Terrorist Organization in September 2025. Material support to the gang is a federal crime, and the FBI has helped Guatemala hunt the escapees.

World.title: Chile Rain Alert Covers Santiago Through 7 October
World.content:
Pedestrians on a rainy night at Avenida Departamental and Avenida Haydn in Santiago (file photo, May 2012). (Photo: Javier Vieras, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

WEATHER · CHILE

Key Facts — The country Chile, a long Pacific nation of nearly 19 million people and the world’s largest copper producer. Most Chileans live in the central valley around the capital, Santiago.

— Why it matters Santiago is Chile’s main gateway for US flights, and the nearby Andes hold big copper mines and ski resorts. The state geology service sees a moderate chance of mudslides around the capital.

— Why now A frontal system fed by an atmospheric river, a narrow band of moist Pacific air, reaches central Chile from Monday night, 5 October, forecasters say.

— What happened The national weather service issued alert AA174/2026 at 11:25 on Monday 5 October for moderate to heavy rain in Coquimbo, Valparaíso, the Santiago region and O’Higgins.

— The numbers The alert expects 25 to 55 mm of rain, about 1 to 2.2 inches, from early Tuesday 6 to Wednesday 7 October. Separate warnings mention gusts of up to 70 km/h, about 43 mph.

— What it means for you Visitors to Santiago, Valparaíso or the mountains should expect wet roads, storms and snow at altitude on Tuesday and Wednesday. Check airline and road updates before setting out.

— Still open How much rain finally falls, whether flights, mines or schools are disrupted, and whether the disaster agency raises its preventive alerts.

Chile’s national weather service issued a Chile rain alert on Monday 5 October for four central regions, including the capital, Santiago. It forecasts up to 55 mm of rain, about 2.2 inches, between early Tuesday and Wednesday afternoon.

For US travellers and investors, the storm hits the main air gateway and Andean valleys with copper mines and ski resorts. A TV forecaster called it the most important rain of the southern spring so far.

What the Weather Service Announced

The Dirección Meteorológica de Chile (DMC), the state weather service run by the civil aviation authority, issued alert AA174/2026 at 11:25 local time. That was 10:25 a.m. US Eastern time on Monday.

The alert covers moderate to heavy rain from the early hours of Tuesday 6 October until Wednesday 7 October in the afternoon. Radio Agricultura and BioBioChile both reported its terms on Monday.

Expected totals vary by region. Coquimbo, in the semi-arid north of the zone, may see 25 to 40 mm, about 1 to 1.6 inches.

Valparaíso and the Santiago Metropolitan Region could each receive 30 to 50 mm, about 1.2 to 2 inches. In the Santiago region, the city’s valley may get 30 to 40 mm, and the coastal hills up to 50 mm.

O’Higgins, the farming region south of Santiago, has the highest range, at 30 to 55 mm. On the DMC’s scale, an alert sits above a lower-level warning, known as an aviso.

The DMC has also issued avisos for wind and storms, BioBioChile reported. Winds of 40 to 60 km/h, with gusts up to 70 km/h, may hit parts of the country.

Another aviso warns of thunderstorms, possible hail and strong local gusts between Coquimbo and Biobío, from Tuesday to Thursday 8 October.

Expected rain under the weather service alert issued on Monday 5 October, from early Tuesday 6 to Wednesday 7 October. O'Higgins has the highest range, up to 55 mm. (Chart: The Rio Times, data: Dirección Meteorológica de Chile)

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Preventive Alerts and Mudslide Risk

Senapred, Chile’s national disaster prevention and response service, declared a preventive early alert for the Santiago region on Sunday 4 October. T13 and TVN reported the step that evening.

This is the lowest level of Senapred’s alert system. It means closer monitoring and coordination of emergency services, not evacuations.

The forecast behind it points to 1 to 39 mm of rain and 30 to 60 cm of mountain snow. That is about 12 to 24 inches of snow.

It also expects winds of 25 to 60 km/h and a freezing level between 2,200 and 3,700 metres. Below that line, precipitation falls as rain.

Sernageomin, the state geology and mining service, rated the mudslide risk as moderate in the coastal hills, valley and foothills. It rated the chance as low in the high Andes.

Senapred also declared a preventive alert for mainland Valparaíso, Epicentro Chile reported. In Biobío, further south, Diario Concepción said the agency kept its own preventive alert in place on Monday.

How the Storm Should Unfold

Gianfranco Marcone, a meteorologist on the T13 channel, expects the first light rain in Santiago on Monday night. He said Tuesday should bring about 60% of the total, with 25 to 45 mm in places.

Wednesday and Thursday should be more unstable, with bursts of rain, sunny spells, hail and lightning, he said. He rated the atmospheric river at category 1 to 3 and saw no category 4 or 5 event.

Meteored, a private forecaster using European and US weather models, projects heavier totals further south. It sees close to 100 mm by Friday in the Andean foothills of Ñuble and the mountains of Biobío, ADN Radio reported.

Those private figures are model estimates, not part of the official alert. The DMC alert stops at O’Higgins.

What It Means for You

If you are flying to Santiago while the Chile rain alert is in force, check with your airline before leaving for the airport. Allow extra time for city traffic, as heavy rain often slows the capital’s roads.

Mountain trips need more care. Fresh snow may affect Andean roads but extends a strong season after Chile’s Valle Nevado Hits 315 cm Snow, Fuels Ski Comeback.

For investors, the rain falls over central Andean copper districts such as El Teniente, the state miner Codelco’s operation in O’Higgins. Whether mining will be affected is not yet known.

For the central valley, the storm also brings welcome water after years of drought. Senapred advises people to shelter in solid buildings during thunderstorms and to keep away from rivers.

What Is Not Known

It is not known how much rain will finally fall, since forecasts still differ by region and by model. Coquimbo, at the northern edge, carries the most uncertainty, BioBioChile reported, citing Meteored.

It is not yet known whether flights, schools or mines will be disrupted. It is also unclear whether Senapred will raise its preventive alerts to a higher level.

Which areas does the Chile rain alert cover?

The weather service alert covers parts of Coquimbo, Valparaíso, the Santiago Metropolitan Region and O’Higgins. It runs from early Tuesday 6 October to Wednesday 7 October in the afternoon.

How much rain is expected in Santiago?

The alert forecasts 30 to 40 mm, about 1.2 to 1.6 inches, in the valley where the city lies. The coastal hills may get up to 50 mm, and Senapred’s earlier regional forecast ranges from 1 to 39 mm.

Is it safe to travel to Chile this week?

The alerts are preventive and do not restrict travel. Expect wet roads, storms and mountain snow on Tuesday and Wednesday, and check airline and official updates.

World.title: Guatemala Issues Fuel Tax Exemption Rules on 5 October
World.content:
Fuel storage tanks and a tanker-truck loading bay at a Puma Energy terminal in Guatemala, photographed in 2012. (Photo: Jonathan Glynn-Smith, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

ECONOMY · GUATEMALA

Key Facts — The country Guatemala is Central America’s most populous country and uses the quetzal, at Q7.64 to the US dollar on 2 October 2026. Bernardo Arévalo, a centre-left reformer, has been president since January 2024.

— Why it matters Fuel costs feed into transport, food and freight prices. The rules decide whether a tax break of up to Q9.05 (about US$1.18) a gallon reaches buyers, the energy ministry estimates.

— Why now Decree 22-2026 suspended value-added tax (VAT) and the IDP fuel levy from Thursday 1 October. The rules to enforce it were only published on Monday 5 October.

— What happened On Monday 5 October the energy ministry published Government Agreement 164-2026 in the official gazette, Diario de Centro América. The gazette said it takes effect the next day.

— The numbers Estimated saving per gallon at 1 October reference prices: premium Q9.05 (about US$1.18), regular Q8.33 (about US$1.09), diesel Q6.45 (about US$0.84), the energy ministry said.

— What it means for you Visitors, US companies and hauliers should get fuel receipts that show the exemption. Fuel bought tax-free may not be exported, a rule aimed at resale across borders.

— Still open The actual cost to the treasury, how many stations comply and what happens to pump prices when both taxes return after 31 December 2026.

Guatemala fuel tax exemption rules were published on Monday 5 October as Government Agreement 164-2026 in the official gazette. They make every petrol station report its prices daily and print the tax saving on each receipt.

For US readers, the rules decide whether a tax break of up to Q9.05 (about US$1.18) a gallon reaches drivers, firms and visitors. That figure is the energy ministry’s estimate for premium petrol at 1 October reference prices.

The agreement puts the machinery behind Decree 22-2026, which Congress passed and President Bernardo Arévalo signed on 30 September. Arévalo is a centre-left reformer elected on an anti-corruption platform.

The decree suspends VAT and the IDP fuel levy on premium, regular and diesel until 31 December. The Ministry of Energy and Mines (MEM), which regulates the fuel trade, issued the rules. The gazette says they apply from Tuesday 6 October, while Prensa Libre and La Hora reported 5 October.

What the New Rules Require

Each seller must file a daily report for every service station, listing the final price of premium, regular and diesel. The prices go into the ministry’s fuel trade statistics system, the Sistema Estadístico de Comercialización de Hidrocarburos.

The ministry must publish each report on its website the following day. Energy Minister Erwin Barrios told Congress on 2 October that the system already held about 2,170 registrations.

Electronic invoices must now state that the VAT and IDP exemptions were applied. They must also show the value of the saving on each gallon sold, the gazette reported.

Card companies are drawn in as well. Operators must work with stations so that no tax is withheld on card payments for fuel, Prensa Libre reported. Small taxpayers are the exception.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Guatemala markets Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Who Checks the Price at the Pump

Every Monday, the ministry’s General Directorate of Hydrocarbons will send a list of stations that failed to report. It goes to Diaco, the consumer protection office of the Economy Ministry.

Diaco will compare the prices stations display with the prices on their invoices. Its task is to confirm that the full tax saving is passed on to the buyer, AGN reported.

Stations that break the rules can be sanctioned under the Consumer Protection Law, the gazette report says. The ministry also plans its own field checks on quality and quantity.

.84" data-lazy-src="https://www.riotimesonline.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/rt-chart-guatemala-fuel-tax-exemption-rules-2026-1.png" /> .84" /> Estimated saving per gallon from the VAT and IDP exemption at 1 October 2026 reference prices, converted at Q7.64 per US dollar. Source: Ministry of Energy and Mines, via AGN.

How Much Drivers Save per Gallon

The energy ministry estimated the saving at Q9.05 (about US$1.18) a gallon for premium and Q8.33 (about US$1.09) for regular. Diesel buyers save about Q6.45 (about US$0.84).

Part of the gap is the IDP levy itself. It stands at Q4.70 (about US$0.62) a gallon for premium, Q4.60 (about US$0.60) for regular and Q1.30 (about US$0.17) for diesel.

The rest is VAT, charged at 12 percent under Article 10 of the VAT law, as published by the tax authority SAT. The first week of the exemption is covered in Guatemala Premium Petrol Falls to US$4.74 a Gallon.

Companies face one catch. The tax authority (SAT) has said fuel bought tax-free gives no VAT credit, as reported in Guatemala SAT Says Tax-Free Fuel Earns No VAT Credit.

The Cost to the Treasury

The rules tell the Finance Ministry to adjust the budget where needed. It must also cover any shortfall in revenue that the law earmarks for specific uses.

That money will come from funds not yet programmed in the 2026 budget. Sources already assigned to those uses are not to be touched, Prensa Libre reported.

The agreement bans exporting premium, regular or diesel that was bought tax-free, under any customs regime. Sellers must also keep an opening stock count and file monthly inventory reports.

After 31 December, they must keep reporting tax-free stock each month until it is sold. The reports let officials track tax-free stock that is still sold once the exemption ends.

What It Means for You

Under the Guatemala fuel tax exemption rules, travellers and US companies should check that receipts show the exemption. The daily price list should let buyers compare stations before they fill up.

For investors, the scheme is a short, targeted relief measure rather than a standing subsidy. It ends on 31 December 2026 unless Congress extends it.

The export ban matters on Guatemala’s land borders with Mexico, Belize, Honduras and El Salvador. It keeps tax-free fuel from leaving the country for resale.

What Is Not Known

No tally of the revenue actually lost since 1 October had been published by Monday. Nor has the Finance Ministry said which unprogrammed funds will cover the gap.

It is not yet known how many stations report every day, or whether Diaco has fined any seller. The first weekly list of non-reporting stations is due under the new rules.

How far pump prices fell because of the tax, rather than world oil prices, has not been measured. Whether the break will be extended past 31 December is also open.

What do Guatemala’s new fuel tax exemption rules require?

Every petrol station must report its pump prices daily to the energy ministry, which publishes them the next day. Electronic receipts must state that VAT and the IDP fuel levy were not charged.

How much cheaper is fuel in Guatemala under the exemption?

The energy ministry estimated savings per gallon of Q9.05 (about US$1.18) for premium, Q8.33 (about US$1.09) for regular and Q6.45 (about US$0.84) for diesel, at 1 October reference prices.

How long does the Guatemala fuel tax exemption last?

Decree 22-2026 runs from 1 October to 31 December 2026. After that, sellers must keep filing monthly reports on tax-free stock until it is used up.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Colón Firms 0.4% Against Dollar on Monday
World.content:
Shoppers on a pedestrian shopping street in downtown San José, Costa Rica, where shops price goods in colones. (Photo: Wayne77, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

MARKETS · COSTA RICA

Key Facts — The country Costa Rica, a stable Central American democracy popular with American visitors and retirees, lets its currency, the colón, float. The Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR) runs Monex, the wholesale dollar market.

— Why it matters The dollar has lost about 8 percent against the colón this year. Monex averaged 497.07 colones per dollar on 2 January, BCCR data show.

— Why now The dollar rose 3.1 percent from this year’s low of 446.80 colones on 17 September to 460.45 on 1 October. Analysts link it to a US rate rise.

— What happened Monex averaged 457.03 colones per dollar on Monday 5 October, down 1.64 from Friday, BCCR data show. It was the second fall in a row.

— The numbers Dealers matched 291 trades worth about US$68.7 million on Monday, BCCR data show. That is three times Friday’s US$22.6 million.

— What it means for you At Monday’s average, US$1,000 buys about 457,030 colones. Costa Rica costs dollar earners about 9 percent more than in early January.

— Still open Whether the September rebound has peaked and how far US rates rise. The BCCR has not signalled a move from its 3.00 percent rate.

The Costa Rica exchange rate eased for a second day on Monday 5 October, with the dollar averaging 457.03 colones on Monex. That is the central bank’s wholesale currency market in San José.

For Americans who earn in dollars and spend in colones, each dollar now buys slightly less than at last week’s peak. The move follows a 3.1 percent rebound that began after a US rate rise in September.

What Monex Showed on Monday

Monex, short for Mercado de Monedas Extranjeras, is run by the Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR). Banks and other dealers trade dollars there in one daily session, from noon to 1 p.m. local time.

On Monday the weighted average was 457.03 colones per dollar, BCCR data show. That is 1.64 colones, or 0.4 percent, below Friday’s 458.67.

Trades ranged from 456.20 to 460.00 colones per dollar. The last deal of the session was struck at 456.40.

Volume was heavy, with 291 trades worth about US$68.7 million. That was three times Friday’s US$22.6 million and double Thursday’s US$34.4 million.

The BCCR’s reference rates in force on Monday stood at 455.71 colones to buy and 462.08 to sell per dollar. The Finance Ministry and the broadcaster Telediario published the same figures.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Costa Rica markets Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

A Rebound From This Year’s Low

The dollar fell to this year’s lowest Monex average on Thursday 17 September, at 446.80 colones. It then rose in almost every session, reaching 460.45 on Thursday 1 October.

That was the highest average since early June, BCCR data show. Friday 2 October then brought the first fall after five straight rises, La Nación reported.

The rebound followed a quarter-point rate rise by the US Federal Reserve, the newspaper Diario Extra reported on 3 October. Higher US rates make dollar savings more attractive.

Carlos Valerín, a currency market specialist, told the paper the Fed’s move was the main driver. He also cited talk of a second or even third US increase.

The BCCR held its own policy rate at 3.00 percent on Thursday 24 September. Its board cited oil supply disruption in the Middle East and tighter global money conditions for longer.

Róger Madrigal, the BCCR’s president, told Diario Extra that a wider rate gap favours savings in foreign currency. He said it could prompt capital outflows and move the exchange rate.

The earlier stage of the move is covered in Costa Rica Dollar Climbs 2.7% From Record Low. Monday’s session extended Friday’s easing rather than resuming the climb.

The dollar's Monex average fell to 446.80 colones on 17 September, peaked at 460.45 on 1 October and eased to 457.03 on Monday 5 October. (Chart: The Rio Times, data: Banco Central de Costa Rica)

A Strong Currency, With Two Sides

Even after the September rebound, the colón remains far stronger than at the start of the year. On 2 January the Monex average was 497.07 colones per dollar.

A strong currency has a stabilising side. It cheapens imported goods and fuel. The central bank expects inflation to move towards its 3 percent target over the medium term.

It also carries risks. The BCCR said on 24 September that activity has slowed. Firms in the special export regimes, such as free zones, are growing less quickly.

Oil near US$100 a barrel adds to the country’s need for dollars to pay for fuel imports, Diario Extra noted. That demand tends to lift the dollar.

For the central bank’s wider view of the economy, see Costa Rica Central Bank Sees No Broad Job Market Hit.

What It Means for You

For American visitors and retirees, Monday’s average means US$1,000 converts into about 457,030 colones. That is about 3,420 colones (about US$7) less than at the 1 October peak.

The bigger change is over the year. Rents, hotel bills and wages priced in colones cost dollar earners about 9 percent more than in early January.

US companies in Costa Rica’s free zones pay local wages in colones, so a strong currency raises their costs. Exporters face the same squeeze, since they earn dollars and pay many costs in colones.

Investors holding colón bonds gained from the currency’s strength this year. A sustained rebound in the dollar would erode part of that gain in US$ terms.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether the September rebound has run its course or merely paused. Two sessions of easing are too few to call a turn.

The path of US interest rates is the main open question. Valerín pointed to talk of further Fed increases, which would favour the dollar.

The BCCR has not signalled a change to its 3.00 percent rate. Its board said it would adjust the rate when economic conditions require.

Oil prices are the other wild card for the Costa Rica exchange rate. Cheaper crude would ease dollar demand for fuel, while a new spike would add to it.

More: Costa Rica news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

What is Monex in Costa Rica?

Monex is the wholesale foreign-exchange market run by the Central Bank of Costa Rica. Banks and dealers trade dollars there daily from noon to 1 p.m., and its weighted average is the main daily exchange-rate figure.

Why did the dollar rise in Costa Rica in September?

The rebound followed a quarter-point rate rise by the US Federal Reserve. The Central Bank of Costa Rica held its rate at 3.00 percent on 24 September. Local analysts also cited oil prices near US$100 a barrel.

How many colones does US$100 buy today?

At Monday’s Monex average of 457.03 colones per dollar, US$100 equals about 45,703 colones. Banks quote slightly different buying and selling rates at their counters.

World.title: Cuba Power Shortfall Hits ETECSA Internet on Monday
World.content:
Cubans connect to the internet on their phones at a public Wi-Fi spot in Havana. (Photo: Othmar Kyas, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

TECHNOLOGY · CUBA

Key Facts — The country Cuba is a one-party communist state of about 10 million people, 90 miles from Florida. ETECSA, the state-owned Empresa de Telecomunicaciones de Cuba, is its only phone and internet provider.

— Why it matters Nauta is how many Cubans get online at Wi-Fi spots and at home. Transfermóvil is the main app for paying phone bills and topping up credit.

— Why now ETECSA posted the notice on its social media pages on the morning of Monday 5 October 2026. Power cuts had topped 2,000 megawatts on most days for weeks.

— What happened On 5 October ETECSA said power problems had knocked out several systems, cutting Nauta browsing and Transfermóvil payments. Mobile data still works, the company said.

— The numbers In the 18 September grid collapse, over 80% of mobile radio-base sites and almost 70% of telecom cabinets went down. Internet traffic fell 58% (ETECSA, 24 September).

— What it means for you Relatives in the US may find family harder to reach and top-ups slower to confirm. ETECSA’s bonus for top-ups sent from abroad runs from 5 to 10 October.

— Still open When the services return, how many provinces are affected, and whether bonus top-ups will be credited on time. ETECSA gave no timetable.

An ETECSA outage on Monday 5 October cut the Nauta internet service and the Transfermóvil payment app in Cuba. The state phone company blamed “energy problems” that had shut down several of its systems.

For Cuban Americans who call, message and send phone credit to relatives, it means another day of patchy contact. ETECSA said mobile data kept working but gave no time for a full repair.

What ETECSA Said

ETECSA published a short notice on its social media pages on Monday morning. CiberCuba linked it to the company’s official Facebook page. It said that “different systems and technological equipment” were down because of power problems.

The company listed three effects. Browsing through Nauta was disrupted, Transfermóvil payments failed, and customers could not manage the services linked to both.

Nauta is ETECSA’s internet account system. Cubans use it at public Wi-Fi spots, in internet rooms and through Nauta Hogar, the home connection.

Transfermóvil is a payment app that works over ETECSA’s network. People use it to top up mobile and Nauta credit and to pay phone and internet bills.

ETECSA said its specialists were “evaluating alternatives” to restore the services. It also warned that other institutions could see their own services affected, without naming them.

The notice was reported the same day by the Cuban outlets CiberCuba, Periódico Cubano, Cuba Noticias 360, CubitaNOW and Asere Noticias. None could say how many users or provinces were hit.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why the Grid Keeps Hitting Phones

Cuba’s telecoms depend on a power system that has been failing for months. The state grid operator, Unión Eléctrica (UNE), publishes a daily estimate of the load it must cut.

From 3 September to 2 October, 23 of 28 comparable days ended with over 2,000 megawatts unserved. Infobae drew the count from UNE’s daily notes. The cut reached 2,059 megawatts on 1 October and 2,130 on 2 October.

Monday’s outlook was no better, as set out in Cuba Grid Operator Forecasts 1,920 MW Blackout Monday. When power fails, mobile masts and street cabinets lose supply unless they have batteries or generators.

ETECSA itself spelled out the damage on 24 September in a statement carried by the state news site Cubadebate. It said availability of mobile and fixed services had fallen in recent months.

In the grid collapse of 18 September, over 80% of mobile radio-base sites and almost 70% of telecom cabinets went offline. Internet traffic dropped 58% against similar periods, the company said.

Share of ETECSA's network knocked out in the 18 September nationwide grid collapse, and the fall in internet traffic. (Source: ETECSA statement, 24 September 2026, via Cubadebate)

The same statement said it was “not viable” to keep expanding the access network without power backup. ETECSA has paused new masts, cabinets and Wi-Fi sites for now.

What Is Still Working

There is a partial cushion. ETECSA says mobile data stayed up on Monday. Apps such as WhatsApp may still connect where a phone has signal and credit.

The company is also moving its sites to solar power. By late September, the main centres of 64 municipal seats had solar backup. Most progress was in Pinar del Río, Villa Clara, Matanzas and Granma.

ETECSA admits that this capacity does not always last 24 hours. Users quoted by Periódico Cubano said data also fails when local masts lose power.

Frustration runs high because of prices. ETECSA sharply raised data prices in May 2025, a move Cubans call the “tarifazo”, and many now ask where that revenue went.

What It Means for You

For families in the United States, the ETECSA outage matters most for staying in touch. Calls over mobile data may still work, but relatives who rely on Wi-Fi spots or home Nauta may be offline.

ETECSA courts top-ups paid from abroad with regular bonus offers. Its current bonus, running from 5 to 10 October, gives 25 gigabytes extra and unlimited early-morning browsing to people who receive them.

Recipients of two or more top-ups in that window also get domestic minutes and text messages for ten days. ETECSA has not said whether Monday’s fault will delay crediting these bonuses.

Travellers heading to Cuba should expect patchy internet and plan offline maps and backups. For wider context, see Cuba Explained 2026: The Economy, the Exodus, the System and What to Watch.

What Is Not Known

By 3 p.m. Havana time on Monday, ETECSA had not announced that Nauta and Transfermóvil were back. It has not said when the ETECSA outage will end. It also gave no figure for the number of users, provinces or sites affected.

The company did not name the other institutions whose services might suffer. Nor did it say whether the fault is only a power cut or whether equipment was damaged.

It is also unclear how long mobile data can hold up during the ETECSA outage if blackouts deepen tonight. That depends on fuel for generators and on how much solar backup each site has.

What did ETECSA announce on 5 October 2026?

ETECSA said power problems had interrupted several of its systems. Nauta internet browsing, Transfermóvil payments and related services were affected, while mobile data kept working.

Why do blackouts in Cuba cause an ETECSA outage?

Mobile masts and telecom cabinets need electricity. In the 18 September grid collapse, more than 80% of radio-base sites went down, according to ETECSA.

Can relatives in the US still send top-ups to Cuba?

ETECSA’s bonus for top-ups sent from abroad runs from 5 to 10 October. The company has not said whether Monday’s fault will delay crediting them.

Sources: CiberCuba, quoting ETECSA’s Facebook notice, 5 October 2026; Periódico Cubano, 5 October 2026; Cuba Noticias 360, 5 October 2026; CubitaNOW, 5 October 2026; Asere Noticias, 5 October 2026; Cubadebate on ETECSA’s statement, 24 September 2026; Cubanet, 24 September 2026; 14ymedio on the 2025 ETECSA price rise, 5 October 2026; Infobae on UNE blackout data, 4 October 2026.

World.title: Venezuela Edges Past US in Spain Crude Sales in August
World.content:
Repsol’s oil refinery in A Coruña, in northwest Spain, at dusk. Spain is one of the European buyers of Venezuelan crude. (Photo: Gregorio Puga Bailón, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

ENERGY · VENEZUELA

Key Facts — The country Venezuela holds the world’s largest proved oil reserves. Acting president Delcy Rodríguez has run it since US forces captured Nicolás Maduro in January, with oil sales under US licences.

— Why it matters Europe is a second outlet for Venezuelan barrels beside the US Gulf Coast. Spain, home of oil company Repsol, is now one of its biggest European buyers.

— Why now Cores, Spain’s strategic oil reserves agency, published its August crude import figures on Monday 5 October 2026.

— What happened Spain imported 641,000 tonnes of Venezuelan crude in August, 11.2% of its total. It bought none in August 2025, Cores says.

— The numbers Venezuela ranked third in August, just above the US on 632,000 tonnes. From January to August Spain took 2.32 million tonnes, up 211.9%.

— What it means for you US crude lost ground in one European market: its August sales to Spain fell 26% year on year. US pump prices are not affected by this shift alone.

— Still open Whether the flow holds after September, when tanker data showed Venezuelan sales to Europe falling to about 86,000 barrels a day.

Spain imported 641,000 tonnes of Venezuelan crude in August, edging past US oil, official data published in Madrid on Monday show. Venezuela ranked third among Spain’s suppliers, a year after selling it nothing.

For US readers, the figures show Venezuelan barrels returning to Europe under the US licensing system that followed Maduro’s capture. They also show American crude losing a little ground in one of its European markets.

What the August Figures Show

Cores, the agency that holds Spain’s strategic oil stocks, reports to the Ministry for the Ecological Transition. It publishes import data by country each month. Its August bulletin was dated Monday 5 October 2026.

Spain imported 5.7 million tonnes of crude in August, up 11.0% from a year earlier. The oil came from 13 countries and covered 30 grades.

Nigeria was the largest supplier with 1.04 million tonnes, or 18.1% of the total. Mexico followed with 648,000 tonnes and Venezuela with 641,000 tonnes, or 11.2%.

The United States came fourth with 632,000 tonnes, 11.1% of the total and 26.0% less than in August 2025. Libya and Brazil completed the top six.

Spain bought no oil at all from Venezuela in August 2025, the Cores table shows. That makes the year-on-year comparison for the month meaningless, so the agency left it blank.

Spain's six largest crude suppliers in August 2026, thousand tonnes. Source: Cores, crude imports by country, published 5 October 2026.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Venezuela markets Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

A Year of Rising Shipments

From January to August, Spain imported 2.32 million tonnes from Venezuela, up 211.9% on the same period of 2025. That equals 5.8% of all crude Spain bought this year.

The Energy Post, an industry site, reports that this is the highest January to August total since 2006, citing Cores records. The Rio Times has not checked that historical series.

The United States remains Spain’s largest supplier for the year so far, with 5.61 million tonnes and a 14.0% share. Mexico, Nigeria, Libya and Brazil follow it.

Venezuela still accounts for only 3.8% of Spain’s imports over the past 12 months. August alone supplied more than a quarter of this year’s total.

Repsol and the US Licences Behind the Flow

Madrid daily La Razón links the rise to agreements between the Trump administration and Rodríguez to revive Venezuela’s oil industry. Venezuelan oil sales now depend on licences from the US Treasury.

Repsol, the Madrid-based oil company, is the main Spanish link. It holds 40% of Petroquiriquire, a joint venture with state oil company PDVSA, which owns the other 60%.

In June the two firms signed a memorandum to explore new areas on Lake Maracaibo’s eastern shore, Caracas outlet El Cooperante reported. PDVSA president Héctor Obregón said it could add about 20,000 barrels a day.

Repsol chief executive Josu Jon Imaz said at the signing that the company would keep investing in Venezuela. Repsol is also studying a partial sale of an offshore gas field, as covered in Eni and Repsol Weigh Partial Sale of Perla Gas Field.

A Weaker September for Europe

Venezuela’s crude exports fell to 1.08 million barrels a day in September from 1.19 million in August. Maracaibo daily Panorama reported this, citing tanker data.

Shipments to Europe dropped to about 86,000 barrels a day from 260,000, the same data show. Sales to the United States rose to 629,000 barrels a day from 553,000.

Higher freight costs drove part of the shift, Panorama said. Commodity traders Vitol and Trafigura pressed PDVSA for bigger discounts, delaying some cargoes.

US firms are also moving deeper into Venezuelan energy, as shown in Baker Hughes Signs Venezuela Gas Deal on 5 October. Most of Venezuela’s oil still heads north rather than to Europe.

What It Means for You

For US investors, Spain’s data show Venezuelan heavy crude competing with American oil in Europe. US crude sales to Spain fell 26% in August, though the US still leads for the year.

For US drivers, nothing changes from this alone. Spain’s imports are a small slice of world oil trade, and the larger Venezuelan flow still goes to US refiners.

For anyone following sanctions, every cargo depends on Washington. A change in US licensing policy would hit these flows faster than any market move.

What Is Not Known

Cores does not say which companies imported the Venezuelan crude or at what price. It also does not say how the cargoes were paid for.

It is not known whether September volumes to Spain held up, since Cores will publish that data next month. Neither Repsol nor PDVSA had commented on the August figures by Monday evening.

How much Venezuelan crude did Spain import in August 2026?

Spain imported 641,000 tonnes of Venezuelan crude in August 2026, 11.2% of its total crude imports, according to Cores. It imported none in August 2025.

Did Venezuela overtake the United States as a supplier to Spain?

In August only, yes. Venezuela supplied 641,000 tonnes against 632,000 from the United States, but the US remains Spain’s largest supplier for January to August.

Why is Venezuelan crude reaching Spain again?

Venezuelan oil sales resumed under US licences after Nicolás Maduro was captured in January. Repsol, which holds 40% of the Petroquiriquire venture with PDVSA, is the main Spanish link.

Sources: Cores, crude imports by country, August 2026; El Cooperante; La Razón; Panorama; The Energy Post.

World.title: Dominican Republic Deficit Reaches US$3.2 Billion
World.content:
The Palacio del Congreso Nacional in Santo Domingo, where lawmakers are studying the 2027 budget bill (file photo, June 2021). (Photo: Peteremueller, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

PUBLIC FINANCES · DOMINICAN REPUBLIC

Key Facts — The country A Caribbean economy of about 11 million people, a short flight from Miami. Tourism, remittances and free-zone exports to the US drive its growth.

— Why it matters Interest on public debt is the fastest-growing claim on the budget. That shapes the risk on Dominican dollar bonds held by foreign investors.

— Why now On Monday 5 October two Dominican papers published budget office (Digepres) data to 25 September. The same day the opposition PLD attacked the 2027 budget bill.

— What happened Revenue reached RD$987.1 billion (about US$16.4 billion) and spending RD$1.18 trillion (about US$19.6 billion). The deficit was RD$191.2 billion (about US$3.18 billion).

— The numbers Debt interest reached RD$234.9 billion (about US$3.90 billion) by 25 September, 75.5% of its full-year budget (Digepres via Diario Libre).

— What it means for you Spending is close to plan. Bondholders will watch interest costs and the 2027 deficit target as Congress studies the bill.

— Still open Whether Congress changes the 2027 bill, and how the Finance Ministry answers the PLD’s figures.

The Dominican Republic fiscal deficit reached RD$191.2 billion (about US$3.18 billion) between 1 January and 25 September, official budget data show. The gap is driven by interest on the public debt.

For US investors who hold Dominican dollar bonds, that interest bill is the number to watch. On Monday the main opposition party warned that the 2027 budget leaves even less room.

The figures come from the General Budget Directorate (Digepres), the Finance Ministry office that records state revenue and spending. Diario Libre and elDinero reported them on Monday 5 October.

What the Budget Office Recorded

Accrued revenue reached RD$987.1 billion (about US$16.4 billion) by 25 September. Spending totalled RD$1.18 trillion (about US$19.6 billion), Diario Libre reported from the Digepres records.

Current spending, such as wages, transfers and interest, took RD$1.04 trillion (about US$17.3 billion). Capital spending on investment was RD$135.9 billion (about US$2.26 billion).

The deficit equals about 2.2% of gross domestic product (GDP), elDinero reported. It is 67.1% of the RD$284.9 billion (about US$4.74 billion) planned for the whole of 2026.

By 25 September about 73% of the calendar year had passed. On that measure the Dominican Republic fiscal deficit is running slightly behind plan, not ahead of it.

Share of the current full-year 2026 central government budget recorded from 1 January to 25 September 2026. Source: General Budget Directorate (Digepres) data via Diario Libre and elDinero.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on the Dominican Republic markets Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Interest Is the Heaviest Line

Debt interest reached RD$234.9 billion (about US$3.90 billion) by 25 September. That is 75.5% of the RD$311.0 billion (about US$5.17 billion) set aside for interest this year.

Without interest the accounts show a primary surplus of RD$43.7 billion (about US$726 million), or 0.5% of GDP, elDinero reported. In other words, the state covers its day-to-day costs but borrows to pay its creditors.

Investment lags. Only 61.1% of the capital budget had been used, against 75.5% of the interest budget, Diario Libre noted.

How the interest bill overtook school spending is set out in Dominican Republic Debt Interest Passes Education Spending by 18 September. Another large outlay is covered in Dominican Electricity Subsidy Hits US$1.47 Billion.

The Opposition Targets the 2027 Budget

On Monday the Dominican Liberation Party (PLD) held a press conference on the 2027 budget bill. The PLD, a centrist party founded by Juan Bosch, ruled from 1996 to 2000 and 2004 to 2020 and is now in opposition.

Its vice-president, Temístocles Montás, a former economy minister, led the event. The bill was sent to Congress by President Luis Abinader of the governing Modern Revolutionary Party (PRM).

Montás said the bill plans central government revenue of about RD$1.51 trillion (about US$25.1 billion). He put the 2027 deficit at about RD$327.3 billion (about US$5.44 billion), or 3.4% of GDP.

He said a 2024 Finance Ministry plan had aimed for a 2027 deficit of about 2.4% of GDP. Interest of about RD$351.3 billion (about US$5.84 billion) would equal 3.7% of GDP, he added.

The party added a RD$44.6 billion (about US$741 million) transfer to the central bank. About RD$26 of every RD$100 collected would go to these two items, it said. El Nacional and El Nuevo Diario carried the figures.

The PLD also said education would get about 3.8% of GDP, below the 4% set by law. The party called for spending discipline and better tax collection rather than new taxes alone.

The bill, worth about RD$2.04 trillion (about US$33.9 billion), is before a joint commission of both chambers of Congress, El Nacional reported.

What It Means for You

For bond investors, the data show a government that stays close to its budget but pays more each year to its creditors. The central bank also tightened policy last week, as reported in Dominican Republic Central Bank Raises Rate to 5.50%.

The peso has weakened by about 2.7% against the dollar since the end of August, central bank reference rates show. A weaker peso raises the local cost of interest on dollar debt.

For American visitors and businesses, nothing changes for now. Neither the data nor the PLD statement involve new taxes, fees or travel rules.

What Is Not Known

The reports did not compare the deficit with the same period of 2025. It is also not clear how much of the interest bill falls due in the last quarter.

The Finance Ministry had not publicly answered the PLD’s figures in the reports available on Monday. The joint commission has not said when it will report on the 2027 bill.

The PLD’s GDP shares are its own calculations from the bill and are not independently confirmed. Conversions use the central bank reference rate of 2 October, 60.17 pesos per US dollar.

How large is the Dominican Republic fiscal deficit in 2026?

Budget office data show a central government deficit of RD$191.2 billion (about US$3.18 billion) from 1 January to 25 September 2026. The full-year plan is RD$284.9 billion (about US$4.74 billion).

Why does debt interest matter so much in the Dominican Republic?

Interest reached RD$234.9 billion (about US$3.90 billion) by 25 September. Without it, the accounts would show a primary surplus of about 0.5% of GDP.

What did the opposition say about the 2027 budget?

On 5 October the PLD said the 2027 bill plans a deficit of about 3.4% of GDP. A 2024 plan had aimed for 2.4%. It also said education falls below the legal 4% of GDP.

Sources: General Budget Directorate, Digepres (weekly execution report to 25 September); elDinero (Digepres data, 5 October); Diario Libre (Digepres data, 5 October); El Nacional (PLD on the 2027 budget); El Nuevo Diario (PLD statement); De Último Minuto (PLD, education share); Central Bank of the Dominican Republic (reference exchange rates).

World.title: Costa Rica Job Losses Mount as Major Companies Cut Operations
World.content:
Job creation has struggled to gain momentum in Costa Rica, while business closures and corporate restructuring have resulted in the loss of at least 6,000 jobs over the past three years. Multinational companies across several economic sectors have moved all or part of their operations out of Costa Rica, closed plants, or reduced their local workforces during this period.

According to experts, the trend is partly linked to a slowdown in foreign direct investment (FDI) in some of the most dynamic free-trade-zone sectors, particularly advanced manufacturing and modern services. Agro-export companies, meanwhile, have faced higher production costs and pressure from the exchange rate.

Standard Fruit Company Costa Rica, for example, shut down operations at two banana plantations in the Caribbean and laid off 111 employees, citing the impact of the Costa Rican Central Bank’s (BCCR) exchange rate policy. In May of that same year, the company laid off another 412 workers, again pointing to the effects of the declining dollar exchange rate on its operations in Costa Rica.

The following year, Qorvo Inc., a U.S. company specializing in semiconductors and radio-frequency solutions, shut down its Costa Rican operations after 29 years, resulting in the loss of approximately 300 jobs. In July, technology giant Intel announced plans to reduce its global workforce by 15%. In Costa Rica, the company closed its Assembly and Test plant in San Antonio de Belén and transferred those operations to Asia. The move is estimated to have resulted in at least 1,500 job losses.

The layoffs continued this year. In January, Viant Costa Rica, a multinational medical-device manufacturer, announced the elimination of approximately 900 positions from its local workforce. Amazon later announced plans to cut 16,000 jobs worldwide, a restructuring that also affected Costa Rica. About 1,000 local employees were reportedly laid off in May.

In June, TicoFrut, one of Central America’s largest agro-industrial companies specializing in orange and pineapple processing, announced the dismissal of 600 workers as part of a restructuring process prompted by economic difficulties. A month later, U.S. technology company Microsoft announced 4,800 job cuts globally. Its Costa Rican operations were also affected, with the local workforce estimated to have decreased by at least 400 employees.

Also in July, Boston Scientific, one of the world’s leading medical-device manufacturers, announced a restructuring plan that includes workforce reductions and affects its operations in Costa Rica. Western Union followed in September, announcing a downsizing of its operations center here.

Not all of these job losses can be attributed to conditions specific to Costa Rica. Several stem from broader corporate restructuring, cost-cutting measures, and operational decisions affecting companies worldwide. However, companies operating under Costa Rica’s free-trade-zone regime have repeatedly warned that the exchange rate has become a significant challenge.

Many of these companies generate revenue in U.S. dollars while paying a substantial portion of their operating expenses in colones, meaning a stronger local currency can reduce their revenues in colón terms while increasing the relative weight of domestic costs

World.title: Fruit, Roadside Traditions and the Seasons of Guanacaste
World.content:
I’m not good with exact dates. Ask me when my boys were born or when I got married and you’ll see an uneasy look begin to spread across my face. I do better with the fluidity of the seasons. They seem to come and go without the requirements of fixed dates. After years of driving around Guanacaste for my job, I’ve come to recognize some signs of the seasons unique to the area.

Perfectly Acceptable Litter Season

We are in the thick of acceptable litter season right now. This season is based on a fruit called mamón chino. Known as rambutan in other parts of the world, this wild-looking fruit is native to Southeast Asia. It’s a 2-inch red ball of soft spikes. To eat it, one must stick their fingernail through the red shell and peel it away, revealing what appears to be a massive pale green grape underneath. The delicious soft fruit surrounds a big seed in the middle.

In Costa Rica, mamón chino isn’t grown in Guanacaste. It comes from the wetter climates of the country. Personally, I’ve seen it growing on farms in the province of Limón. It’s made available to the consumers of Guanacaste via roadside stands with little tables topped with a huge pyramid-style pile of fruits.

For a few thousand colones, drivers receive an enormous bag of fruit. Here’s the important part, the fruit should be eaten by all of the passengers of the vehicle, while driving, and everyone should toss the peels out of the crack of their open window. If you look at the shoulder of any road in Guanacaste right now, you won’t have to travel far until you spot this spikey, fruit-based litter on the side of the road.

Dudes in Trees Season

How long has it been since you’ve seen an adult man in a tree on the side of the road? For me, it’s only been a few months, as dudes in trees season ended a little while ago. This season is also fruit-based. The main character here is a fruit called jocote. These fruits start out as inch-long green ovals that eventually mature to a bright shade of red. Edible at both stages, they grow on a small, straggly, quite climb-able tree that’s often used as a living fence on the side of the road.

This season is highlighted by men, and I only point out that it´s men because that’s what I’ve observed, climbing the trees to obtain the precious fruit. Sometimes a lady is involved, but normally she’s waiting at the base of the tree with a bag. While driving by, I like to picture the man saying, ‘I’ll get the fruits for you, my love,’ before ascending the tree.

I should point out that dudes in trees season aligns perfectly with men chucking sticks at trees season. The only difference is the desired fruit. For the latter, the fruit being sought-after are mangoes. Mangoes grow on trees that can be quite enormous and are thus unclimble-able, requiring the men to throw perfectly aimed sticks at the fruit baring branches to get their prize.

Christmas Season

You’d think you’d know the timing of this season from personal experience, but in Guanacaste you’d be wrong. It indeed begins in December, before Christmas, when a little Guanacasteco town decides to get together and decorate the central plaza for the holidays. The go-to decoration is a giant Christmas tree made of a cone of welded rebar wrapped with green agricultural fabric, locally known as serán, and then decorated with Christmas ornaments. The trick is, the holidays come and go, and nobody bothers to take the tree down.

As I drive through tiny town after tiny town, no less than 75% of them are celebrating Christmas year-round. I started really paying attention while driving lately, with thoughts of this article in my head, and the big cone Christmas tree is by far the most common, though I have noted a giant, sparkling star, a series of big plastic reindeer followed by Santa’s sleigh, and, my personal favorite, a palm tree at the edge of the plaza decorated with Christmas balls and garland. It’s always Christmas in Guanacaste.

About the Author

Vincent Losasso, founder of Guanacaste Wildlife Monitoring, is a biologist who works with camera traps throughout Costa Rica

World.title: Canadian arrivals in Costa Rica jump 24% as travelers skip the US
World.content:
Canadians who have turned away from vacations in the United States are showing up in Costa Rica in record numbers, and they are staying long enough to change the math of our tourism economy. Figures from the Costa Rican Tourism Institute (ICT) show 232,949 Canadians arrived in the first eight months of 2026, up from 187,781 in the same period last year. That is a 24.1% increase and the fastest growth of any major market.

Canada’s share of all visitors climbed from 9% to 10.6%. Arrivals from the United States, which still supplies well over half of all tourists, rose just 2.7% over the same months. What’s driving it is no mystery as Canadian travel to the United States has fallen sharply since early 2025 amid trade disputes and political tension between the two countries, and the winter travelers who once filled Florida condos have been looking elsewhere.

Connie Salazar, executive director of the tourism promotion group Proimagen has said Canadians who favored the Florida coast no longer want to go there and that Costa Rica has proven a natural fit with its beaches, nature and wellness offerings. Costa Rica moved quickly to catch that demand. The ICT’s air connectivity team spotted the opening as Canadian traffic to the United States and parts of the Caribbean dropped, then traveled to Canada with airport authorities to pitch the airlines directly.

Carriers responded with more frequencies and new routes. Air Canada, WestJet, Air Transat and Porter now all fly here and Air Transat and Porter have converted seasonal flights into year-round service. In December Air Canada will launch a Vancouver-Liberia route, Air Transat will connect Quebec City with San José and Porter will add four weekly flights between Toronto and Juan Santamaría International Airport. By high season travelers will be able to fly nonstop from seven Canadian cities.

What makes this market so valuable is not only how many Canadians come but how long they stay. ICT data show the average Canadian visitor spends 14.9 nights in the country and about $203 (₡93,000) per day. That works out to roughly $3,000 (₡1.4 million) per person per trip. Applied to the 45,000 additional Canadians who arrived through August, the growth alone represents something on the order of $135 million (₡62 billion) in new spending. It is a rough estimate, but it shows the scale.

A visitor who stays two weeks or more behaves differently from one on a five-day resort package. Long-stay travelers rent houses and condos, shop at local supermarkets and ferias, hire guides, eat at neighborhood sodas and move around the country. Their money reaches small businesses and communities that rarely see the short-stay crowd. Many are retirees and remote workers escaping the northern winter, and the rules favor them, since Canadians can remain in Costa Rica for up to 180 days as tourists.

Some of those who return year after year go on to rent long term, buy property or apply for residency, which carries the benefit well beyond hotels and tours. The gains so far are concentrated in Guanacaste. Daniel Oduber Quirós International Airport in Liberia received 71% of all Canadian air arrivals in the first four months of the year, a 32% jump over 2025, and Canadians now account for roughly 26% of tourist arrivals there.

Hotels, vacation rentals, restaurants and tour operators along the northern Pacific coast are the most direct beneficiaries. The challenge for the rest of Costa rica is to draw those long stays south and inland. There is also a strategic benefit since with Americans making up close to six of every 10 visitors, Costa Rica’s tourism business has long been exposed to a downturn in a single market. A growing Canadian base, along with steady gains from Europe, spreads that risk.

Canadian demand remains weighted toward the winter months, though the move to year-round flights by two carriers suggests that is starting to change. Tourism officials are not yet declaring victory as air arrivals slowed in June, which the ICT attributed to geopolitical tension and higher jet fuel costs and the institute has said it is watching the second half of the year with caution.

The strong colón, trading near ₡460 to the dollar, makes Costa Rica a more expensive destination than it was a few years ago, a cost that weighs on visitors who earn Canadian dollars. And part of the current surge depends on a political mood in Canada that could shift. For now the trend favors Costa Rica with airlines are adding seats rather than cutting them and the ICT has stepped up promotion in Toronto, Montreal and other cities.

First time visitors to Costa Rica during a winter away from Florida may keep coming back even if relations with Washington improve. If they do, those who arrived because of a boycott could become one of the steadiest sources of Costa Rican tourism.

World.title: Costa Rica Beats Haiti 2-0 as Bryan Ruiz Finishes Interim Run Unbeaten
World.content:
Costa Rica beat Haiti 2-0 last night at Estadio Ricardo Saprissa, closing its Concacaf Nations League group stage with a second consecutive victory under interim coach Bryan Ruiz. Carlos Mora and Andrey Soto scored inside the first 21 minutes as La Sele completed Ruiz’s two-match assignment with five goals scored and none conceded. The former captain’s future remained unresolved after the final whistle.

Costa Rica finished fourth in Group A with six points, behind Curaçao, Haiti and the Dominican Republic. Curaçao and Haiti advanced to the quarterfinals, while Costa Rica will enter the preliminary round of qualifying for the 2027 Gold Cup. La Sele’s place in League A was already secure before kickoff after Trinidad and Tobago drew 1-1 with Curaçao, allowing Costa Rica to focus on ending a difficult campaign with a win at home.

Mora opened the scoring in the sixth minute, heading in a corner from Ronald Matarrita. The left back helped create the second goal too. Yerlan Sosa sent a long pass across the field to Matarrita, who set up Soto for a left-footed finish into the far corner in the 21st minute.

With Keylor Navas in goal and Celso Borges in midfield, Costa Rica protected its early advantage. Haiti controlled the ball at times but struggled to create scoring chances. In the second half, La Sele stayed organized in defense and looked for chances to counterattack without sending too many players forward.

Supporters at Saprissa chanted “olé” as Costa Rica moved the ball during the first half, showing their appreciation for a team that had opened the competition with two straight defeats. Costa Rica began its Nations League campaign with a 4-3 loss to Curaçao on Sept. 24, followed by a 2-0 defeat to Haiti in Jamaica on Sept. 27. Ruiz’s first match in charge produced a 3-0 win over Nicaragua in Managua on Oct. 1 and Sunday’s result gave La Sele a measure of revenge against Haiti, although it could not repair the damage to its quarterfinal hopes.

After the match, Ruiz said he had completed his assignment but had not decided whether to stay on permanently. He said he had not sought the role and would let discussions about his future take their course. Coaching Costa Rica remained an ambition, but any decision would depend on what was best for the country and his family.

Ruiz said he expected to take Monday off and return Tuesday to his work with Alajuelense’s under-20 team. He also repeated his preference for a Costa Rican coach to lead the national side and emphasizing the need for someone who could earn the players’ trust while demanding more from them.

Ruiz urged the players to carry that improvement back to their clubs, saying commitment and consistent performances would be key to building the national team. Costa Rica will play two qualifying matches in March 2027, one at home and one away. The winner on total goals will advance to the 2027 Gold Cup.

World.title: Costa Rica Landfill Plan in Mora Faces New Land-Use Challenge
World.content:
A decades-long fight over a proposed waste project in Picagres has flared again after the Mora municipal administration issued a new land-use certificate for Parque Industrial Jateo, prompting residents, local officials and lawmakers to question whether the project should be allowed to move forward.

Residents and members of the Mora Municipal Council toured the area Saturday, Oct. 3, with lawmakers and legislative advisers. The visit focused on the roads that would be used by garbage trucks and the environmental conditions around the proposed site in Cordel, a community in the district of Picagres.

Among those joining the visit were Álvaro Ramírez Bogantes, leader of the opposition National Liberation Party in the Legislative Assembly, and Frente Amplio lawmaker Vianey Mora Vega, who represents San José province. Ramírez questioned whether the existing roads could handle the volume and weight of truck traffic associated with the project, while Mora raised concerns about water sources and nearby ecosystems.

The controversy was revived after it became known that the municipality had issued a land-use certificate for Parque Industrial Jateo. That certificate does not by itself authorize construction or allow the waste facility to begin operating, but opponents say the decision is significant because the lack of a valid municipal land-use document has been one of the major obstacles facing the project for years.
