Against this backdrop, the European Union has reached out to Armenia. It has launched measures to support the Armenian economy and give exporters additional opportunities to access the EU market. In July, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced in Yerevan that the EU could introduce autonomous trade measures for Armenian goods:

“I am here today to state clearly: if Russia closes its market to Armenian products, the EU will open the doors of its consumer market to them, with 450 million people.”

The European Parliament and the Council of the EU have already approved a package of temporary trade preferences. The EU will suspend customs duties on a wide range of goods exported from Armenia for two years. The trade preferences will cover around 80% of Armenian exports. The proposed benefits for some groups of goods will be significant and will cover products previously exported to Russia, including:

99% of fresh agricultural produce,

91% of beverages.

In the first seven months of 2026, Armenia’s foreign trade exports totalled around $4.04 billion. Compared with the same period last year, total exports fell by 7.9%.

At the same time, Armenia’s export geography still includes both traditional and new markets.

From January to June this year, Armenian exports to EU countries exceeded $516 million. Compared with the same period last year, exports grew by more than 80%.

From January to July, exports of Armenian-origin goods to other major markets increased by:

100% to India,

66.8% to China,

4.2% to the United States.

Agricultural exports form a separate category. From June to August 2026, Armenia exported:

fruit to 24 countries,

vegetables to 16 countries,

flowers to 28 countries.

World.title: 14 years in power: how experts assess Georgian Dream’s rule
World.content:
14 years of Georgian Dream

On 1 October 2026, 14 years had passed since the Georgian Dream party came to power. Today, assessments of the party’s 14 years in power differ sharply from those voiced just five years ago.

Former government official Beka Natsvlishvili discusses the significance of the events that brought Georgian Dream to power, while representatives of civil society and the diplomatic community point to a critical situation in the country’s democratic development and foreign policy.

Sandro Baramidze, a representative of Transparency International Georgia and former deputy justice minister, believes that although the first years of Georgian Dream’s rule could be viewed positively, the country is now living under a “full-fledged dictatorship”, with democratic institutions no longer functioning properly.

Meanwhile, diplomat and former deputy foreign minister Gigi Gigiadze analyses the changes in Georgia’s relations with the European Union, NATO and Western countries since 2012.

How do they assess Georgian Dream’s 14 years in power, and what has changed in the country since 2012?

Sandro Baramidze

Sandro Baramidze: “Ultimately, the story of the past 14 years began with promises: protecting human rights, building an unprecedented democracy, ensuring Euro-Atlantic integration, promoting economic growth and so on. Bidzina Ivanishvili and Georgian Dream came to power with precisely these promises.

I would say that the first few years were normal. The government carried out certain democratic reforms, including attempts to introduce democratic changes to the judiciary. But gradually, everything first stalled and then changed course, especially after Russia launched its full-scale aggression against Ukraine.

The situation has changed dramatically, and today we are dealing with a full-fledged dictatorship — a dictatorship of one man who runs the country from behind the scenes through his associates. This system has no separation of powers or checks and balances. We have no independent judiciary, either in the ordinary courts or the Constitutional Court, while democratic institutions, civil society, political parties and the media face enormous pressure. Moreover, civil society, once active and strong, is now on the verge of collapse.

Not a single democratic institution functions properly: opposition parties face the threat of dissolution, some political leaders are in prison, while others face new charges that could lead to lengthy prison sentences based on completely absurd arguments. People are arrested every day simply for standing on a pavement or making a statement on Facebook…

In short, we are living under a full-fledged dictatorship. Ultimately, this will inevitably come to an end, although the nightmare they have subjected the country to continues for now.”

Gigi Gigiadze

Gigi Gigiadze: “In 2012, Georgia was one of the European Union and NATO’s closest partners, as well as one of the countries undergoing the fastest transformation. Georgia was a ‘top performer’ among the participants in the Eastern Partnership.

Georgia was more eager than any other country to join the EU and NATO as quickly as possible. It served as a reliable partner for the EU and NATO in the region and took an active part in military exercises and peacekeeping missions organised by both organisations. Moreover, Georgia stood out as the main beacon of hope in Eastern Europe among countries genuinely seeking to join the EU and NATO.

Today, however, the reality looks completely different: Georgia has fallen furthest behind and become the most isolated and distant from the European Union and the West. We are facing a situation in which Georgia has lost all the progress it had accumulated along the way. Georgia is no longer seen as a genuine candidate, a reforming country or a state at the forefront of progress.

Very tough sanctions and extremely negative decisions concerning Georgia are being announced almost every day. We are receiving very low scores on numerous indicators — and this is not new; it started a long time ago. We are witnessing significant regression.

A vacuum has emerged — a situation our country has never faced before. Georgia’s foreign policy had always been crystal clear, and the direction in which we were moving was clearly defined. Everyone knew this, including Iran. Until now, neither Iran’s ambassador nor any other representative of a [state] would have dared to use such rhetoric towards Georgia, make such statements or issue such threats.

Everyone knew exactly what position we held, who our partners were and which camp we belonged to. As Georgia became increasingly isolated and drifted catastrophically away from Europe, the European Union and the West, a natural vacuum emerged, which Iran is now trying to fill with its influence.

Iran understands perfectly well that this is a unique opportunity to strengthen its presence here.

The Iranian ambassador no longer holds back. He believes he can say and do whatever he wants, without feeling constrained by anything or accountable to anyone. This is a natural consequence of the policy pursued by Georgian Dream over the past 14 years.”

Beka Natsvlishvili

Beka Natsvlishvili: “[The victory of Georgian Dream] was not simply a case of the government handing over power as a result of an election. Rather, the United National Movement was forced to give up power while avoiding large-scale violence. I call it a ‘revolution at the ballot box’. In a sense, it was a revolutionary change. A revolution implies systemic change, but unfortunately, the systemic transformation we expected never took place.

The 1 October victory was certainly not solely Bidzina Ivanishvili’s achievement. After all, you cannot simply erase 2012 from Georgia’s history. I returned from abroad in 2006 and actively took part in street protests until 2012. The coalition included people with far more experience in political struggle than I had. The struggle continued regardless, but without Bidzina Ivanishvili’s arrival, it produced no tangible result. His emergence gave the struggle a powerful boost and created an opportunity for a decisive breakthrough. We cannot attribute this success unequivocally to the efforts of one person or any particular group.

1 October is an important date in Georgia’s history. I fully recognise that and am proud to have taken part in those events. When the first parliament was formed, it was a parliament of politicians. At the time, politicians felt much more accountable to society, and they were people with strong individual identities. Breaking their word or abandoning their promises was much harder for them. Later, everything changed.

Georgian Dream decided to build a monolithic party. From a pragmatic point of view, the plan to create a monolithic party made perfect sense. It is very difficult to govern a country when your team includes people with diametrically opposed ideological views. But what is the problem with that? [The problem is that] Georgian Dream never managed to truly unite as a party because it no longer had politicians. The people who had been hardened in the heat of political struggle left. Today, very few politicians remain there; perhaps only a handful are left in Georgian Dream. No one sees the current members of parliament as political figures. The leader of the ruling team is surrounded by close associates who simply make it onto the party lists and enter parliament. They hold political positions, but they are not politicians.”

14 years of Georgian Dream

World.title: Chronicles of Victory: October 6, 2020
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 6. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist", on September 27, 2020, in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline.

The erupted 44-day Second Karabakh War ended with the liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation.

Trend presents the chronicle of the 11th day of the Second Karabakh war:

- President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev gave an interview to Russian "Perviy Kanal" TV channel.

- President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev received a delegation led by the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Türkiye Mevlut Cavusoglu.

- The Ministry of Defense of Azerbaijan reported that as a result of a precise fire strike by the Azerbaijani army, the central ammunition depot located in the Ballija settlement was destroyed. In addition, two BM-21 combat vehicles as part of the Grad field reactive system and D-20 artillery units, belonging to the Armenian armed forces, were destroyed in battles in different directions of the front.

- Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, following the Cabinet of Ministers meeting, stated that the duty of every respected state is to support the struggle of Azerbaijan for the liberation of its occupied territories.

- The Ministry of Defense of Azerbaijan shared footage from Chakhyrly village, Jabrayil district, liberated from Armenian occupation.

- The Defense Ministry published a video of the armored vehicles of the Armenian armed forces captured as trophies.

- As a result of the shelling of the Aghdam district by the Armenian armed forces, an employee of the Ministry of Emergency Situations of Azerbaijan was injured.

- The Parliament of Azerbaijan approved the return of the historical name Sugovushan to the Madagiz village recently liberated from Armenian occupation.

- Azerbaijani Defense Minister Colonel-General Zakir Hasanov said at a special meeting that if Armenia uses Iskander complexes, adequate retaliatory measures will be taken.

- The State Security Service carried out radio interception of the negotiations of terrorists participating in military operations against Azerbaijan.

- During the counter-offensive operation of the Azerbaijani army, two more terrorists - mercenaries who fought on the side of the armed forces of Armenia - were neutralized.

- The Armenian armed forces fired on the territory of Yevlakh, Goranboy and Beylagan districts.

- The Ministry of Defense of Azerbaijan has shared footage of armored vehicles of the armed forces of Armenia, captured by the Azerbaijani army.

- The ammunition depot located in the Ballija settlement was destroyed together with the manpower. Unable to withstand the onslaught of the counter-offensive operation of the Azerbaijani army, the Armenian soldiers left their combat positions and fled.

- The Ministry of Defense of Azerbaijan has published new footage of the captured Armenian post and trophies.

World.title: Mecca Agreement states agree to deploy military forces in Saudi Arabia
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 5. The countries participating in the Mecca Agreement have decided to immediately proceed with the practical implementation of their commitments to joint defense and the prompt deployment of agreed military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.

This was stated in a joint statement issued following an emergency meeting of the alliance committee and published by the Kingdom’s Ministry of Defense.

“The committee decided to immediately proceed with the practical implementation of commitments to joint defense, as well as to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed forces and military capabilities and promptly deploy them in the Kingdom,” the document said.

According to the statement, the relevant measures will be implemented in accordance with the agreements reached and the national legislation of the participating countries. These measures are expected to contribute to enhancing combat readiness, strengthening military integration and bolstering the countries’ collective ability to confront and deter threats.

It should be recalled that Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman, and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif signed the Mecca Defense Agreement. According to the document, which is based on the legitimate right to self-defense enshrined in Article 51 of the UN Charter, an armed attack against any of the three signatory states will be considered an attack against all parties.

World.title: Azerbaijan, Nigeria discussed cooperation on multilateral platforms
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 5. On October 5, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Azerbaijan Jeyhun Bayramov and Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Federal Republic of Nigeria Bianca Odumegwu-Ojukwu discussed the agenda for cooperation on multilateral platforms during a telephone conversation.

This was reported by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Azerbaijan.

The ministers exchanged views on the prospects for developing bilateral relations between Azerbaijan and Nigeria, issues of mutual interest, as well as the agenda for cooperation on multilateral platforms.

In this context, the importance of cooperation within the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), the Non-Aligned Movement, the Inter-Parliamentary Union, D-8 and other platforms was noted, and the importance of strengthening mutual support and coordination was emphasized.

Minister Jeyhun Bayramov noted that Azerbaijan considers the development of relations with African countries as one of the priorities of its foreign policy. In this regard, the importance of expanding cooperation with Nigeria in the political, economic, humanitarian and other spheres was emphasized, including the opportunities provided to Nigerian citizens within the framework of Azerbaijan’s scholarship programs.

The sides also exchanged views on other issues on the regional and international agenda.

World.title: Man carjacked at knifepoint on Sunshine Coast, sparking 160km police chase
World.content:
Two men have been charged over an alleged carjacking on the Sunshine Coast.

Police say a man threatened a 55-year-old man with a knife and demanded his car keys at a shopping centre on David Low Way just before 6:30pm on Monday.

Officers tracked the vehicle with the help of a police helicopter, then used tyre spikes to slow the vehicle at Ebbw Vale.

Police say the vehicle was abandoned in Bundamba, where the driver fled on foot.

A 26-year-old Mount Coolum man was arrested shortly after.

He has been charged with armed robbery and unlawful use of a motor vehicle and is due to face court in Ipswich this morning.

A 29-year-old Yarrabilba man, who police say was sitting in the car when they arrived, has been charged with unlawful use of a motor vehicle.

He was released on bail and is due to face court later this month.

World.title: Landmark gorge reopens to visitors after 'huge job' fixing flood damage
World.content:
A popular tourist attraction and major cultural site in Western Australia's Kimberley has reopened three years after serious damage during the state's worst-ever flood disaster.

In 2023, ex-Tropical Cyclone Ellie dumped record rain along the Fitzroy River catchment, triggering devastating flooding in Fitzroy Crossing, with 1,500 people evacuated.

The flooding wreaked havoc on the area's natural wonders, including Danggu Geikie Gorge National Park.

The visitor centre was washed away as the Fitzroy River rose. (Supplied: DBCA)

One of the town's major tourist attractions and an important cultural hub, it was reduced to rubble and mud when the Fitzroy River broke its banks.

At the time, the Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions (DBCA) said 37 hectares of riverbank washed away, including all tourism infrastructure.

Fitzroy Crossing and surrounding communities were devastated by the floods. (Supplied: Shoal Air)

Lengthy process

DBCA operations manager Elise Nelson said the restoration and rehabilitation had been an arduous process.

"It's different to how it used to be," she said.

"It's been a long process of accepting that and understanding that, and finding a way to move forward with the way the park is now."

Kerry Wallis (left) and Elise Nelson say the long journey has been worthwhile. (ABC Kimberley: Vanessa Mills)

More than 12,000 tonnes of concrete, fencing, cabling and other debris had to be removed, along with the shattered remains of more than 100 trees.

Ms Nelson said despite all this clearance, massive amounts of debris remain.

"We had the park closed to build an access ramp down to the water and use an amphibious excavator to remove the debris that still lies in that water," she said.

A freshwater crocodile swims in the Fitzroy River as it flows through the gorge. (ABC Kimberley: Sam Tomlin)

"The arborist works are ongoing; they still continue every year because the impact of those floods is still seen on the riverbanks despite revegetation. It's a huge job."

A feasibility study is underway to assess when and how boat tours, one of the more popular past attractions, can resume.

The entire park is now open, excluding water access, and will remain open throughout the northern wet season.

DBCA hopes that boat tours could return to the gorge as early as next year. (ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler)

'Hurts a little less'

The flood destroyed significant cultural sites for Bunuba traditional owners, who manage the park with DBCA.

Danggu Bunuba traditional owner Kerry Wallis said it had been a tough three years.

The gorge has long been a drawcard for grey nomads and backpackers. (ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler)

"It was a sad sight to see after the flood; we had such a beautiful park there, and it was a site for everybody to come, sit and enjoy; now it's a little bit different," she said.

"So a bit heartbreaking; but also it's been a long road to try and fix what we can.

"(But) you can't repair what nature has torn away, hectares of country gone with that."

The walls of the gorge show the high-water mark from heavy flooding in previous years. (ABC Kimberley: Sam Tomlin)

There was feedback and collaboration with traditional owners throughout the restoration process.

Ms Wallis said the hurt was still "raw" for many, but each time she went back to Danggu Geikie Gorge, it hurt a little less.

"It's feeling more stable, feeling more and more (like) home," she said.

She urged visitors to be respectful and to remember the park is on Danggu Bunuba country.

"We understand a lot of people come up to the Danggu and love to fish and camp," she said.

"Just make sure you're still following the park rules."

World.title: Smooth sailing for new passenger zones at Melbourne Airport
World.content:
The first passengers to use Melbourne Airport's new drop-off and pick-up zones have reported a seamless transition to the new arrangements.

The airport's departure ramp that was used to drop passengers at the front door of terminals 1, 2 and 3 closed last night after more than 50 years in operation.

The new combined drop-off and pick-up area has been built in the multi-level car park at the airport, with the facility, connecting walkway bridge and supporting road network costing $500 million.

The airport said it aimed to reduce traffic congestion outside the terminals' departure areas and featured almost triple the number of bays compared to the forecourt.

The new Melbourne Airport drop-off zone is in operation. (Supplied: Melbourne Airport)

There have been concerns about the longer walk to the terminal for elderly travellers and people with mobility issues.

But passengers who spoke to the ABC this morning approved of the new arrangement.

This New Zealand traveller says her son had no trouble finding his way to the new drop-off area. (ABC News)

"Our son managed to find his way really well," said one woman who had just been dropped off for a flight home to New Zealand.

"So far it's easy, pretty convenient. The last one was a bit hectic, a bit busy," said another traveller.

This woman says the new drop-off area was less hectic than the previous zone. (ABC News)

"It's pretty great, lots of room," said another woman who agreed the new zone appeared "less hectic" than the previous facility.

Another man said the traffic flowed more easily and he did not mind the longer walk to reach the terminal.

"Get our steps in," his travelling companion added.

This couple said they didn't mind the longer walk to the terminal. (ABC News)

A driver said he felt safer using the new zone, while another said he found it easier to drop off his passengers.

Drivers taking passengers to the airport now have to leave the Tullamarine Freeway earlier, using the exit to Naarm Way.

There was a crash on the freeway this morning, causing delays getting to the airport but it was not known if it was related to the new airport arrangements.

The passenger zone is connected to the terminals through a bridge. (ABC News: Stephanie Ferrier)

The new zone is designed for passengers taking Qantas, Virgin Australia and international flights.

Melbourne Airport said the change would enable work to begin on a $4.5 billion expansion to the international terminal.

Melbourne Airport spokesperson Andrew Lund said the new zone appeared to be working well on the first morning of operation.

"This is a big change and it's going to take everybody, including us, a little of time to get used to," he said.

He said assistance service was being offered for those with mobility needs.

"The trade-off for giving cars and people more space is there is a bit of a longer walk," he said.

"We've got support in the form of buggies and wheelchairs available for people to help them with that and they've been used quite regularly so far this morning."

Travellers began using the new drop-off and pick-up zones this morning. (Supplied: Melbourne Airport)

The airport said it had rostered on dozens of extra staff today and the coming weeks to help passengers navigate the new layout.

World.title: Court hears man ran over partner with Range Rover, causing brain injury
World.content:
A man who ran over his partner with his car near Darwin earlier this year, causing her to suffer a traumatic brain injury, has pleaded guilty in the Northern Territory Supreme Court to dangerous driving.

Christopher Morley also pleaded guilty to breaching a domestic violence restraining order after he ran over his then-girlfriend at a caravan park on the outskirts of Darwin in January.

The court heard the couple were living together at the Oasis Caravan Park in Virginia and had been drinking on the night in question when they became involved in a verbal argument.

The woman was taken to Royal Darwin Hospital before being transferred to Victoria. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Morley was about to leave the caravan park in his Range Rover when the woman stood in front of the car and put her hands on the bonnet before he slowly accelerated, causing her to fall under the front passenger-side wheel.

"The offender continued to drive for approximately 10 metres before coming to a stop," Crown prosecutor Deborah Roussos said.

" The victim was run over by the vehicle, resulting in significant injuries and serious harm. "

The court heard Morley was on the phone to his adult daughter at the time, who heard her father scream "Oh my God, she's just jumped in front of the car and I have just hit her".

Ms Roussos said emergency services arrived to find the woman unconscious and bleeding from the head.

The victim was taken to Royal Darwin Hospital with life-threatening injuries, including multiple skull and facial fractures, brain bleeds and wounds to her knees and elbows.

Christopher Morley denied intentionally causing the woman serious harm. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

She was later transferred to the Alfred Hospital's trauma unit in Victoria where she was diagnosed with a moderate to severe traumatic brain injury.

In the months after the accident, the court heard the woman struggled with her speech and short-term memory and was unable to walk.

The 58-year-old spent four months in rehabilitation to improve her speech and mobility.

Morley's lawyer, Brooke Houen, urged Justice Stephen Southwood to impose a suspended sentence, emphasising that her client did not intentionally cause the victim serious harm.

"He accepts there are horrific consequences for his momentary lapse of judgement," she said.

" But he really wants me to make clear that he did not intend to hurt her in such a serious way. "

Brooke Houen said the defence accepted her client's actions had "horrific consequences". (ABC News: Olivana Lathouris)

Ms Roussos agreed the offending was a "very brief episode", but said it remained "fairly serious" given the extent of the woman's injuries.

"There was certainly a high level of negligence if nothing else, and it certainly is very dangerous driving with someone standing in direct line with the car," she said.

Justice Southwood adjourned the case until later this month to allow time for Morley to be assessed for a supervision order and he will remain on bail until his case returns to court next week.

World.title: Record sheep prices can't save saleyard despite $1 lease offer
World.content:
After almost 60 years counting sheep, you might think 83-year-old Tom Todd would be tired of it.

" If the sheep are big and woolly, you can count them in fives … if you can just let them run nice and even. "

Merino industry stalwart Ross Wells and Tom Todd catch up at the sale. (ABC News: Emily Doak)

Now retired, Mr Todd worked at saleyards across the sheep country of the Riverina and has seen the number of sheep decline due to fluctuations in the wool industry and a move to online sales.

A casualty of this is the Jerilderie saleyard, which will be decommissioned after the Murrumbidgee Council failed to find anyone to take over management.

The 20-year lease was offered for just $1 per year, on the condition the new lessee would commit to upgrade the facility to modern safety and animal welfare standards.

Tom Todd penned and counted sheep for more than 40 years before retiring this year. (ABC News: Emily Doak)

The council agreed to keep the yards open for one final commemorative sale on October 2 where 10,000 sheep were penned.

Livestock agent Trevor Besset said selling the last ever pen of sheep at Jerilderie was an emotional moment.

"We've gone off with a bang and everybody should be proud of themselves," he said.

"The buyers keep coming back knowing the quality of the sheep that they're getting out of the district."

Final sale-o at Jerilderie

Mr Todd was amongst the hundreds of people at the final sale.

"It's the friendship," he said.

" The people that come here … they're from different, vast areas and they remember you from the year before. "

The final sheep sale at Jerilderie saw 10,000 sheep penned. (ABC News: Emily Doak)

Mr Todd has fond memories of long days working in the Jerilderie yards and the celebrations that followed.

"We managed to finish by dark and get to bed by midnight, as a rule, but I have known blokes to still be in their clothes from the day before at 6 in the morning," he said.

"They were good days. The job was still done the next day and there was always a smile on their face."

Georgia Brydon has been working as a trainee agent for about two years. (ABC News: Emily Doak)

At the other end of the career spectrum, trainee livestock agent Georgia Brydon is finding her feet counting sheep in the saleyards.

""I just fell in love with the saleyards and the sheep work," she said.

" I find it very satisfying, the organisation, penning, delivering them and running through all the different type of sheep to see how much they go for. "

A large crowd attended the final sheep sale. (ABC News: Emily Doak)

Generations of saleyard history

The Stonnill family sold 2,000 sheep last week, walking them 20 kilometres from their property near Urana to the saleyards.

"We took a couple of days to get them here," Harry Stonnill said.

"It's a bit of fun and quite social, people stop on the road and I think it's good for the sheep too."

Harry Stonnill was pleased to be able to bring son Ted to the saleyards for the final time. (ABC News: Emily Doak)

Mr Stonnill said the Jerilderie sales have been part of his life since childhood.

"It's always been a pretty good social occasion, so thinking that my son isn't going to get to do that it's a bit sad really," he said.

Tess Kernaghan said the sheep sale at Jerilderie was an annual event to catch up with friends. (ABC News: Emily Doak)

Tess Kernaghan returned to Jerilderie for the sheep sale to mark the milestone.

"I don't think you can beat the physical aspect of coming here, seeing the stock that you want to buy and meeting the people that are growing them," she said.

Record price

The sale set a new Riverina Store Sheep Sale record of $524 per head for merino ewes from Kate and Craig Smith of Innesvale at Oaklands.

Strong livestock prices at other store sheep sales this year have been underpinned by a shrinking national sheep flock, currently 67.1 million head, down 21 per cent from 85.7 million two decades ago.

In its heyday more than 40,000 sheep would be yarded at Jerilderie. (ABC News: Emily Doak)

Jerilderie is not the only town to see its council-run saleyard closed in recent years.

The last sheep sale was held at Cootamundra on the south west slopes in 2024 and saleyards closed in Narrabri and Moree in 2022.

On the North Coast, the Clarence Valley Council has been considering the future management of the Grafton saleyards, establishing a working group to manage the struggling asset.

World.title: Mary Fowler withdraws from Matildas squad for Germany, Haiti games
World.content:
Matildas star Mary Fowler has been withdrawn from the Australian squad for two upcoming internationals, due to personal circumstances.

A release from Football Australia on Tuesday morning said the decision had been taken following discussions between Fowler, Manchester City and Matildas staff.

Fowler has been in solid form, coming on as a sub to spark a comeback win for Manchester City over WSL rivals Arsenal on Monday morning, Australian time.

Fowler's City still perfect in WSL Mary Fowler's landmark 100th game for Manchester City is a bright spot for the beleaguered club, with a big win over Arsenal keeping them with a perfect record on top of the WSL.

There was no talk of injury after the game.

Fowler's partner, Nathan Cleary, is recovering in Sydney after leg surgery.

The Penrith Panthers NRL star went into the preliminary final against Newcastle with a broken foot, before suffering a compound fracture and a dislocated ankle in a hip-drop tackle, requiring emergency surgery.

Fowler has been replaced in the Australian squad by Charlton Athletic midfielder Leah Davidson. Davidson has made four appearances for the Matildas since her international debut in 2024.

The Matildas are playing two international friendlies in Europe as they continue preparations towards next year's FIFA Women's World Cup.

Australia split a two-match series with Mexico in June, with one win each.

Now the Matildas will face Germany in Karlsruhe on Saturday morning, Australian time before taking on Haiti in France on October 13.

World.title: Live: Wantaway Saints star boycotts best and fairest as Cats eye AFL trade
World.content:
Can the Hawks still get Ben King after giving up all our picks for Merrett? - Steve

(Getty Images)

The Hawks cleared the decks a little to get Zach Merrett in, but that may well be a very deliberate play.

Hawthorn is hoping Gold Coast will choose not to match the contract offered to free agent Ben King. If the Suns take that path, they will receive pick seven and the Hawks will give up nothing at all for King.

The alternative is the Suns do choose to match and look to create a trade with the Hawks. The problem there now is that the Hawks don't really have a whole lot to trade anymore. The Suns are eyeing up young key forward Aidan Schubert, but it is more likely that if that happens, it happens in a separate deal so Gold Coast can still net pick seven as compensation.

It reminds me of the move Hawthorn made a couple of years ago when they were chasing Tom Barrass. That year, they pulled off a surprise pick swap with Carlton, effectively removing the picks the Eagles were hoping to get back and forcing the trade deal onto their terms.

TLDR; The Hawks have managed to get Zach Merrett and force the Ben King deal onto their terms in one fell swoop.

World.title: Trump's former press secretary Karoline Leavitt joins Fox News
World.content:
Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt has landed her next gig at Fox News.

One of the most prominent faces of President Donald Trump's second administration, Ms Leavitt will serve as an on-air contributor in November, the network said.

"Karoline's firsthand experience in the White House and on the presidential campaign trail gives her a distinct understanding of today's political landscape," said the network's CEO, Suzanne Scott.

Ms Leavitt said she would bring a "unique perspective" from her time as press secretary, "along with the same energy and candour that defined my tenure".

The 29-year-old announced she was leaving the White House in August. She was the youngest person to hold the role of press secretary.

The Trump family and Ms Leavitt this year. (Supplied)

From the White House to Fox News

When she left, Mr Trump described her as one of his "most trusted aides".

At the time, she said she wanted to spend more time with her two children.

Her second child, Viviana, was born in May, and she has a two-year-old son.

Ms Leavitt is not the first of Mr Trump's press secretaries to join Fox. Kayleigh McEnany joined in 2021 and remains at the network.

The president has hired several Fox News personalities in key jobs in his administration, chief among them Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Mr Trump being interviewed by Pete Hegseth at the White House in 2017. (Reuters: Kevin Lamarque)

Trump's relationship with Fox News

Mr Trump has an increasingly thorny relationship with the network, whose key commentators have long given him favourable coverage.

He has expressed frustration with Fox coverage choices as recently as Sunday, when he bemoaned what he said was the network's lack of coverage of his rallies.

"Sad to see that Fox & Friends (Sunday) is not covering our packed house and incredibly enthusiastic (beyond!) Rally that took place in Ohio last night, or the ones in Alabama, Texas, or Oklahoma over the past two days," he posted on his Truth Social platform.

"They were all sold out, with thousands of people trying to get in, and are absolutely phenomenal, better than ever!

"Remember, Fox tried this act once before, and almost went out of business (and always right before an election!). That can happen again!" he wrote.

He also criticised the recent firing of longtime Fox financial journalist Maria Bartiromo.

The comments came as Mr Trump is embroiled in a stand-off with news outlets whose coverage displeases him, capped by his recent efforts to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from White House grounds.

Mr Trump has recently criticised Fox News. (Reuters: Kevin Lamarque)

A judge has issued a temporary restraining order against the ban, and a hearing is scheduled for Thursday.

Before becoming White House press secretary, Ms Leavitt served as press secretary for Mr Trump's 2024 presidential campaign.

At age 25, she also made an unsuccessful bid for Congress in 2022 from her home state of New Hampshire.

AP

World.title: AFL trade period LIVE: Day two of trade period, mega-deal could be in the works for Butters, Marshall wants out
World.content:
Further to the last post about Rowan Marshall, the St Kilda ruck finished 10th in the Saints’ best and fairest.

As this masthead reported on Sunday, the Saints want Geelong’s first-round draft pick (pick No.14) and a player in exchange for Marshall. They initially asked about small defender Lawson Humphries but have since shelved that inquiry.

From a Geelong perspective, that seems a high price for a ruck who turns 31 next month, though the Saints will argue their demand is fair as he is contracted until the end of next year.

The Cats also have picks 34, 55 and 73 from this year’s draft, and a full suits of selections from 2027 and 2028. Bear in mind, they also need picks to get a deal done for Essendon defender Jordan Ridley, whom the Bombers will ask for decent compensation.

World.content:
Liberal frontbencher Jonno Duniam says AI investment is the “the opportunity of a lifetime for our country”, ahead of today’s parliamentary hearings.

“This committee will be a very, very swift one because time is of the essence, and I believe Australia needs to get this right, or else we will miss the boat, and we will be poorer for it for generations to come,” Duniam, who is the deputy chair of the joint select committee on AI, told News24.

Duniam said Australia had to strike the right balance to protect Australian copyright holders, and safeguards against rogue agents.

“We’ve got to make sure that the economic benefits and the national security benefits that will come with partnering with US-based hyperscalers and becoming the second home here in Australia will flow to Australia,” he said.

World.title: Medvedev disqualified for hitting fan with ball as De Minaur reaches China final
World.content:
SportTennisATP Tour Medvedev disqualified for hitting fan with ball, De Minaur reaches China final Trevor Marshallsea Updated October 6, 2026 — 8:29am ,first published 10:27pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Alex de Minaur will face Novak Djokovic in the final of the China Open after the Serbian star’s semi-final opponent, Daniil Medvedev, was disqualified ‌for hitting a ball into the crowd, causing a spectator to suffer an eye injury. The Australian No.1 had progressed from his semi-final after Poland’s Hubert Hurkacz retired injured when trailing in the second set. Loading Djokovic was leading 7-5, 5-3 in Beijing and serving for the match when the incident happened. After a forehand volley winner from Djokovic, the ball bounced off the advertising boards towards Medvedev, who smacked a backhand that sailed into the stands.



It hit a spectator in ​the front row behind him. He clutched his left eye ​and ​appeared ​to be in ‌pain as he walked out, assisted by stadium ​staff. “Terribly sorry to ‌the spectator, first ⁠of all,” Medvedev told reporters.” I’m trying to get in touch with him, if he ​wants it. Hopefully, I can apologise in person and see how he feels.” Daniil Medvedev after being disqualified in his China Open match against Novak Djokovic. AP Photo/Achmad Ibrahim The Russian world No.5 said he did not cause the incident intentionally. “The ball was bouncing back, so I tried to, like, just hit it anywhere, so it doesn’t go out from the court. When I saw the result, I mean, I felt horrible because, again, I don’t think I was ever close to such a situation.”



Medvedev, 30, has a history of on-court behaviour issues. He was fined after he smashed his racquet seven times during a 6-0, 6-0 loss to Matteo Berrettini at this year’s Monte Carlo Masters. “I was shocked, to be honest... I hope that ​person is not ‌badly injured,” said Djokovic, who was disqualified from ​the US Open in 2020 under similar circumstances. The man who has hit in the face by a ball hit by Daniil Medvedev receives assistance in Beijing. AP Photo/Andy Wong “On the other hand, I also feel sorry for Daniil because I know ​exactly ​how it feels to ​be disqualified in a big match ... ‌I’m sure that Daniil didn’t want to do this intentionally.” De Minaur will be seeking to become the first person to beat Djokovic in 34 matches at the China Open. He has a 1-3 head-to-head record with the Serb.



The winner will leave Beijing ninth in the race to qualify for November’s eight-man ATP Finals with the gap to Medvedev in eighth reduced as the Russian will lose the 200 points he had gained in Beijing. There are two ATP Masters 1000 events to come, in Shanghai and Paris, but ninth may still be enough with Jannik Sinner’s availability uncertain. Alex De Minaur during his match against Poland’s Hubert Hurkacz. Getty Images On Saturday, the world No.1, who last played at Wimbledon, pulled out of Shanghai, which begins on Wednesday with a knee problem. De Minaur was up 6-4, 3-2 and 40-0 when Hurkacz retired with an apparent adductor injury after showing mobility problems.



The world No.9 had broken a tentative Hurkacz in his opening two service games before holding to lead 4-0, then withstood a comeback to take the first set 6-4. Another break in the third game of the second set helped de Minaur build a 3-1 lead. Hurkacz fought desperately to hold serve in the following game – surviving four break points and a marathon deuce game - but was unable to battle much longer. World.title: British author and disgraced politician Jeffrey Archer dies aged 86
World.content:
Breaking CultureCelebrityVale British author and disgraced politician Jeffrey Archer dies aged 86 Kayla Olaya October 6, 2026 — 8:26am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Best-selling British novelist and former Tory politician Jeffrey Archer, who was jailed for perjury in a high-profile libel case, has died at 86, his publisher said on Monday. Archer sold over 300 million copies worldwide during his five-decade writing career and was known for pacy thrillers such as his 1976 debut Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less and the Kane and Abel series. His final novel, Adam and Eve, was set for release on Tuesday. Jeffrey Archer has died aged 86. Kate Elton, HarperCollins’ UK Chief Executive and Archer’s editor, said he died “suddenly and peacefully” at his home. “We’re all devastated to have lost a writer who has brought joy to generations of readers – and a true friend,” Elton said in a statement. A prominent Conservative politician, Archer briefly served as an MP before becoming a senior party official under then prime minister Margaret Thatcher in the mid-1980s.



But Archer faced a very public downfall when he was convicted of perjury and perverting the course of justice in 2001. The charges stemmed from his successful 1987 libel case against the British newspaper the Daily Star, which accused him of hiring a prostitute. Archer had been awarded £500,000 ($948,000). Jeffrey Archer (L) greeting his wife Mary after being released from prison in 2003. REUTERS He was sentenced to four years’ imprisonment and was released in 2003, after which he returned to the House of Lords until retirement in 2024. Just last week Archer visited his old school library, in the village of Wellington in the English county of Somerset, the BBC reported.



“It’s wonderful to come back. What I got a real thrill about when I was walking towards the library is seeing the young boys and girls and thinking, ‘that’s the next generation’,” Archer said, according to the British broadcaster. He said he attended the school because of a scholarship. “I was on a scholarship because we had no money. I came from Weston-super-Mare, and we had no money. I would never have got in without a scholarship.” Born in London in 1940, Archer’s family soon moved to Somerset where, the BBC reports, his parents bought a house from John Cleese’s mother. Elected to the House of Commons at 29 in 1969, Archer was forced to resign five years later after bad investments drove him to bankruptcy. This led him to write his debut novel.



He is survived by his wife Dame Mary Archer, their sons, James and William, and several grandchildren. With Reuters More to come

World.title: Exodus begins as fitness celebrities sever ties with charged health guru Sam Wood
World.content:
NationalCBD Exodus begins as fitness celebrities sever ties with charged health guru Sam Wood Fiona Byrne October 6, 2026 — 8:03am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Celebrities, fitness trainers and businesses have begun cutting ties with former Bachelor star Sam Wood as he remains behind bars on domestic violence charges. Wood’s lawyer has indicated he will defend the charges. Sam Wood’s lawyer has said Wood has vowed to fight the charges. High-profile trainer Tiffiny Hall, whose workout videos appear prominently on the 28 by Sam Wood social media pages, released a statement late on Monday saying she had “no ongoing role or involvement with the program”. “I have zero tolerance for domestic and family violence, and for violence of any kind,” said Hall, who is an advocate for self-defence and women’s safety. “It is unacceptable and entirely at odds with the standards, core values and culture I wish to cultivate.



“I am shocked and disturbed by the charges against Sam Wood reported in the media. As the matter is before the court, I will not comment on it. “Before this news, my time with 28 by Sam Wood had already come to an end and I had moved on to focus on other projects. I have no ongoing role or involvement with the program. Melbourne fitness identity Tiffiny Hall. “My thoughts are with any victim-survivors of domestic and family violence, and with anyone distressed or triggered by these reports. I will continue to empower women to be safe, strong and supported in any way I can.” Influencer, body positive entrepreneur and fellow reality TV contestant Jules Robinson also announced that she had ended her partnership with Wood’s fitness empire.



“Women are my absolute priority. Their safety, wellbeing and empowerment are at the heart of what I stand for,” Robinson, a former Married At First Sight participant who had been working with the 28 brand, posted on social media. “I’m very conscious of who I choose to align myself with, both personally and professionally. My values never falter, regardless of the person or partnership. Former Married At First Sight participant Jules Robinson. Jessica Hromas “While I won’t comment on a matter before the courts, I stand firmly against domestic and family violence in all forms. “In light of the circumstances, I have made the decision to end my partnership with 28 by Sam Wood. This is a decision I have made in line with my values and what I believe is right.



Related Article Updated

Courts An empire on the edge of a cliff: Inside Sam Wood’s rise to fame and fortune “My commitment to supporting, empowering and standing with women will always come first. My thoughts are with everyone affected during what is an incredibly difficult time.” Ready-made meal business Foxes Den continued the exodus, confirming it was stepping away from its links with 28. “We are shocked and deeply saddened to hear of the charges involving Sam Wood,” the Foxes Den statement read. “Effective immediately, Foxes Den has ended its partnership with 28 by Sam Wood.



“We’re aware of the serious charges that have been reported, and while this matter is before the courts, we’ve made the decision to step away from this partnership. “We stand firmly against domestic and family violence in all its forms.” Sam Wood met his wife Snezana on The Bachelor Australia. © Channel 10 One of the first to break ties was Tania Monk, known online as @fitafter40_faf, who was a trainer on the 28 platform. Monk said she was “shocked and deeply saddened” by the news about Wood.



Related Article Updated

Domestic violence Reality TV star Sam Wood denied bail over alleged domestic violence “For many years, I have worked incredibly hard to build a reputation based on trust, integrity and advocating for women. That work means EVERYTHING to me,” she posted on Instagram. “Whether you train with me, follow me here, have been part of my gyms, or trusted me to support you through the 28 menopause program, you are part of a community I am incredibly proud to have built. “You have trusted me with your health, your stories, your struggles and your successes. I don’t take that trust lightly. “My name, my reputation and what I stand for are my own. And I have a responsibility to protect them.



“For that reason, I will not continue professionally under the 28 by Sam Wood brand or attach my name to a program that remains associated with Sam. “This is not a statement about guilt or innocence. World.title: ‘The system shouldn’t be a maze’: Sweeping mental health review pledged ahead of election
World.content:
A major review of the state’s mental health system and the billion-dollar levy used to fund it, along with an overhaul of youth services and the creation of a specialist standalone facility, are part of a sweeping election pledge aimed at improving Victoria’s struggling sector. The Coalition will on Tuesday announce a “mental health reset” if elected in November, promising separate reviews into the Mental Health and Wellbeing Levy, the sector’s independent watchdog and the state’s lagging delivery of its royal commission and commitments. A mental health bed crisis is causing a backlog in emergency departments. Marija Ercegovac Within 100 days of being elected, a new strategy to boost the mental health workforce would be created and supported with a targeted $50 million fund to fill skills and staffing gaps. They will also commit to developing a world-leading Youth Mental Health Centre of Excellence overseen by Orygen, as well as commit $5 million to masterplan a new standalone youth mental health hospital in Parkville. A months-long investigation by The Age has exposed a series of systemic problems plaguing Victoria’s mental health system, more than five years after the state government accepted every recommendation handed down by the Royal Commission into Victoria’s Mental Health System in 2021.





State opposition mental health spokeswoman Emma Kealy is promising sweeping reforms to reset Victoria’s mental health system, if elected. Eddie Jim The watchdog set up to monitor the system and the state’s reforms, the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission (MHWC), would also be assessed and given stronger powers, remit and greater independence. The move comes after The Age revealed a trove of internal documents detailing the Labor government had hobbled the MHWC to such an extent it can no longer effectively monitor the mental health sector or properly track implementation of the royal commission recommendations. But the centrepiece of the Coalition’s plan is a proposed overhaul of the state’s youth mental health system, including the creation of a Youth Mental Health Centre of Excellence intended to bring together the best research, clinical expertise and innovation to improve the care young people receive across Victoria.



Planning for a standalone 50-bed Parkville youth mental health hospital to serve Melbourne’s northwest and sections of regional Victoria would also get the green light, with design and detailed costing to be completed by June 2030. “For a young person struggling with their mental health, the system shouldn’t be a maze. They shouldn’t have to become sicker before they qualify for help, and their parents shouldn’t be left desperately ringing service after service trying to find someone who can help,” Kealy told The Age. “The Youth Mental Health Centre of Excellence will help build a system around young people, from prevention and early intervention through to specialist treatment, acute care, housing and recovery.” Orygen executive director Professor Pat McGorry said in Melbourne’s north-east, an area with more than two million people, there are just 16 youth mental health beds. McGorry said collectively, the promises could make a huge impact, with the creation of a centre of excellence allowing specialists to galvanise and reform the state’s approach to youth care.



“Victoria is in the grip of a youth mental health crisis and has so far failed to respond to this effectively. The commitments announced today represent a major step forward in tackling this crisis,” he said. “Mandating Orygen to become the Victorian Centre of Excellence in Youth Mental Health will enable a collaborative learning health system to flourish across the state within all state health services and will work to ensure that all young Victorians can access high-quality evidence-based care when, where, and for as long as they need it.” Professor Patrick McGorry has welcomed a Coalition pledge to create a Youth Mental Health Centre of Excellence to be overseen by Orygen. Aaron Francis The Coalition has also committed to reforming governance at Parkville Youth Mental Health and Wellbeing Service after its CEO Dr Leanne Geppert resigned in August – one day after The Age revealed she was leading the state’s flagship youth mental health service on a fly-in, fly-out basis from Brisbane. Alongside sweeping reviews of the current system, the opposition has promised to publish a new blueprint on how to reform the mental health sector that will outline funding and timelines for when promises will be delivered.

World.title: Medvedev disqualified for hitting fan with ball, De Minaur reaches China final
World.content:
SportTennisATP Tour Medvedev disqualified for hitting fan with ball, De Minaur reaches China final Trevor Marshallsea Updated October 6, 2026 — 8:29am ,first published 10:27pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Alex de Minaur will face Novak Djokovic in the final of the China Open after the Serbian star’s semi-final opponent, Daniil Medvedev, was disqualified ‌for hitting a ball into the crowd, causing a spectator to suffer an eye injury. The Australian No.1 had progressed from his semi-final after Poland’s Hubert Hurkacz retired injured when trailing in the second set. Loading Djokovic was leading 7-5, 5-3 in Beijing and serving for the match when the incident happened. After a forehand volley winner from Djokovic, the ball bounced off the advertising boards towards Medvedev, who smacked a backhand that sailed into the stands.



It hit a spectator in ​the front row behind him. He clutched his left eye ​and ​appeared ​to be in ‌pain as he walked out, assisted by stadium ​staff. “Terribly sorry to ‌the spectator, first ⁠of all,” Medvedev told reporters.” I’m trying to get in touch with him, if he ​wants it. Hopefully, I can apologise in person and see how he feels.” Daniil Medvedev after being disqualified in his China Open match against Novak Djokovic. AP Photo/Achmad Ibrahim The Russian world No.5 said he did not cause the incident intentionally. “The ball was bouncing back, so I tried to, like, just hit it anywhere, so it doesn’t go out from the court. When I saw the result, I mean, I felt horrible because, again, I don’t think I was ever close to such a situation.”



Medvedev, 30, has a history of on-court behaviour issues. He was fined after he smashed his racquet seven times during a 6-0, 6-0 loss to Matteo Berrettini at this year’s Monte Carlo Masters. “I was shocked, to be honest... I hope that ​person is not ‌badly injured,” said Djokovic, who was disqualified from ​the US Open in 2020 under similar circumstances. The man who has hit in the face by a ball hit by Daniil Medvedev receives assistance in Beijing. AP Photo/Andy Wong “On the other hand, I also feel sorry for Daniil because I know ​exactly ​how it feels to ​be disqualified in a big match ... ‌I’m sure that Daniil didn’t want to do this intentionally.” De Minaur will be seeking to become the first person to beat Djokovic in 34 matches at the China Open. He has a 1-3 head-to-head record with the Serb.



The winner will leave Beijing ninth in the race to qualify for November’s eight-man ATP Finals with the gap to Medvedev in eighth reduced as the Russian will lose the 200 points he had gained in Beijing. There are two ATP Masters 1000 events to come, in Shanghai and Paris, but ninth may still be enough with Jannik Sinner’s availability uncertain. Alex De Minaur during his match against Poland’s Hubert Hurkacz. Getty Images On Saturday, the world No.1, who last played at Wimbledon, pulled out of Shanghai, which begins on Wednesday with a knee problem. De Minaur was up 6-4, 3-2 and 40-0 when Hurkacz retired with an apparent adductor injury after showing mobility problems.



The world No.9 had broken a tentative Hurkacz in his opening two service games before holding to lead 4-0, then withstood a comeback to take the first set 6-4. Another break in the third game of the second set helped de Minaur build a 3-1 lead. Hurkacz fought desperately to hold serve in the following game – surviving four break points and a marathon deuce game - but was unable to battle much longer. World.title: British author and disgraced politician Jeffrey Archer dies aged 86
World.content:
Breaking CultureCelebrityVale British author and disgraced politician Jeffrey Archer dies aged 86 Kayla Olaya October 6, 2026 — 8:26am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Best-selling British novelist and former Tory politician Jeffrey Archer, who was jailed for perjury in a high-profile libel case, has died at 86, his publisher said on Monday. Archer sold over 300 million copies worldwide during his five-decade writing career and was known for pacy thrillers such as his 1976 debut Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less and the Kane and Abel series. His final novel, Adam and Eve, was set for release on Tuesday. Jeffrey Archer has died aged 86. Kate Elton, HarperCollins’ UK Chief Executive and Archer’s editor, said he died “suddenly and peacefully” at his home. “We’re all devastated to have lost a writer who has brought joy to generations of readers – and a true friend,” Elton said in a statement. A prominent Conservative politician, Archer briefly served as an MP before becoming a senior party official under then prime minister Margaret Thatcher in the mid-1980s.



But Archer faced a very public downfall when he was convicted of perjury and perverting the course of justice in 2001. The charges stemmed from his successful 1987 libel case against the British newspaper the Daily Star, which accused him of hiring a prostitute. Archer had been awarded £500,000 ($948,000). Jeffrey Archer (L) greeting his wife Mary after being released from prison in 2003. REUTERS He was sentenced to four years’ imprisonment and was released in 2003, after which he returned to the House of Lords until retirement in 2024. Just last week Archer visited his old school library, in the village of Wellington in the English county of Somerset, the BBC reported.



“It’s wonderful to come back. What I got a real thrill about when I was walking towards the library is seeing the young boys and girls and thinking, ‘that’s the next generation’,” Archer said, according to the British broadcaster. He said he attended the school because of a scholarship. “I was on a scholarship because we had no money. I came from Weston-super-Mare, and we had no money. I would never have got in without a scholarship.” Born in London in 1940, Archer’s family soon moved to Somerset where, the BBC reports, his parents bought a house from John Cleese’s mother. Elected to the House of Commons at 29 in 1969, Archer was forced to resign five years later after bad investments drove him to bankruptcy. This led him to write his debut novel.



He is survived by his wife Dame Mary Archer, their sons, James and William, and several grandchildren. With Reuters More to come

What good are economic forecasts in an uncertain world?
World.content:
Audio player for " Is a loan on my home the best way help my kids? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/business/1749543%2Fwhat-good-are-economic-forecasts-in-an-uncertain-world

Is a loan on my home the best way help my kids? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 13m

Infometrics chief forecaster Gareth Kiernan can remember putting his forecasts together back in 2019, and thinking how boring it was. "Nothing had really changed and things had evolved in line with our expectations."

That had been the way through much of the second half of that decade, he said.

But since then, everything has been different.

Now, forecasts that are a bit boring would be a welcome reprieve.

First there was Covid, where predictions of economic doom turned out to be unfounded - at least at first.

Audio player for " The uncertainty of economic forecasting " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/business/1749543%2Fwhat-good-are-economic-forecasts-in-an-uncertain-world

The uncertainty of economic forecasting Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Then there was the inflation surge, which took the Reserve Bank by surprise.

Russia's moves against Ukraine sent an economic shock around the world, US President Donald Trump's trade tariffs added volatility, and then conflict in the Middle East sent oil prices soaring again. Sharemarkets have continued to hit highs despite warnings of an impending bust.

That's tough going for economic forecasters, who as ANZ's Sharon Zollner once said, have at times had track records that seemed designed to make weather forecasters look good.

What makes forecasting difficult?

Kiernan said forecasting was always more difficult when outcomes could be heavily influenced by the actions of a few people.

"At the moment, President Trump is an individual with a large amount of influence, whose decisions are highly unpredictable and don't seem to follow any logic or consistent ideology."

Infometrics chief forecaster Gareth Kiernan. RNZ / Rebekah Parsons-King

He said it was also hard to forecast for things with no precedent, such as the Covid-19 pandemic, or when variables or outcomes were moving outside historical boundaries. At the moment, that is the case for people trying to make forecasts about what might happen with sharemarkets.

"As a forecaster, these are often the sorts of situations where you need to make a call about when and how quickly a variable might return to normal or, more bravely, why this time is different and we're not going to get a correction.

"Sometimes these variables can be reasonably incidental to a broader forecast, but often the assumptions you make as a forecaster will have significant flow-on effects to other parts of the forecast - a correction in the US stock market could have significant negative effects on business and consumer spending, weighing heavily on broader economic growth as well, stretching government finances further …"

He said when forecasters were making assumptions about things on a continuum, it was easy to be slightly wrong. But when it was a binary outcome, such as whether conflict would continue in the Middle East or not, or whether petrol prices would stay very high and as a result keep household spending down, it started to be a more "all or nothing" forecast.

ASB acting chief economist Kim Mundy said, with every update she tried to make the point that everything could change quickly, because a lot is hanging on what happens in the Middle East, which is very difficult to predict.

Does it matter?

Zollner said it could be a problem when forecasts were being relied on to create policy, such as by the Reserve Bank.

"I don't think we're brave enough to actually ask the question, given our forecasts are so bad, should we even be trying to use those forecasts to set monetary policy or should we just basically have rules based on the here and now with a fairly high threshold to diverge from those?"

She said it would be interesting to research whether that would lead to better outcomes over time.

"I think the best that monetary policy can do is stay nimble and humble, open-minded to all the reasons they could be wrong and to changing their minds."

She said that had been the tone of recent Reserve Bank communications.

"I think they've been quite wise in how they've characterised the uncertainty and the fact that to some extent the market is going to be expected to make up its own minds as the data unfolds."

Zollner said the Reserve Bank was taking a different approach to that of the US Federal Reserve, which had moved to offer markets less guidance.

"There is certainly a range of views out there about what the best reaction to uncertainty is… They have to [take a view]. They can't just abstain and say, oh, I don't know, we'll come back in a year and see how things are looking. They have to do their best to balance the risk of getting it wrong in either direction. They're very open about that, but that's the best they can do and that is what they are trying to do. That's a reasonable approach."

Kelly Eckhold. Supplied / LinkedIn

Westpac chief economist Kelly Eckhold said central banks sometimes used scenario analysis to explain how things could change if inputs changed.

Mundy said it also highlighted one of the reasons why the Reserve Bank was emphasising how data dependent it was, as well as using things like business visits in its work.

"It's also part of why we think the RBNZ will continue to hike over the coming two meetings to get the OCR back towards neutral levels. It's easier to respond to unforeseen developments, such as inflation proving stickier than expected, from neutral settings, than from a position where monetary policy is still accommodative.

"In general, navigating a negative supply shock where uncertainty is elevated is a tricky spot for any central bank to find itself in."

How do we get back to more certainty?

Eckhold said, to return to a more predictable environment, there would have to be a return to a Washington Consensus.

"Instead of pushing individual agendas, there's a greater willingness to work together multilaterally to solve issues, as opposed to going off and starting your own war or your own trade way, all those sorts of things that have been going on in the last 10 years.

"It really picked up most significantly when Russia annexed part of Ukraine...then it's been overlaid with tensions with China, which have ebbed and flowed depending on administrations, then even more aggression with the Ukraine and Russia and now the Middle East as well."

World.content:

Weekly interview with opposition leader, Chris Hipkins Morning Report Download MP3 11m

RNZ's latest political poll - the first during the election campaign - is out, hours before the two major party leaders face off in TVNZ's debate.

National's campaign chair Simeon Brown is acknowledging little more than that the election will be a tight one off the back of its crushing poll result.

World.title: Baby in critical condition after woman charged with attempted murder in alleged West Auckland stabbing
World.content:
A baby critically injured in a triple stabbing in West Auckland has undergone surgery, police have confirmed.

A 33-year-old woman is facing an attempted murder charge in relation to the knife attack at a home on Kirby St in Glendene late on Sunday night.

Detective Senior Sergeant Adam Lough said the person in a moderate condition was recovering at home, while the third person was in a serious, but stable, condition in hospital.

Court documents seen by RNZ said the woman would appear in Waitākere District Court on Tuesday.

Lough confirmed the woman had been charged and thanked neighbours for their bravery on Sunday night.

The Kirby St house on Monday. RNZ/Calvin Samuel

"Neighbours came to these people's aid prior to emergency services arriving on the scene.

"We are very grateful for their assistance and bravery with what can only be described as a very confronting and upsetting scene."

A police investigation was ongoing, Lough said, with police piecing together the events leading up to the incident.

"We appreciate the public's interest in what has occurred here... however, the welfare of two people is at the forefront of this, and their privacy is paramount as they recover from this traumatic event."

All parties were known to each other, Lough said and police weren't looking for anyone else.

World.title: Buildings evacuated as gas main ruptured in Auckland's Newmarket
World.content:
Fire and Emergency are responding to a ruptured gas main on Khyber Pass Road in Auckland's Newmarket.

A spokesperson said they had sent two fire trucks were sent to scene evacuated people in nearby buildings.

The ruptured gas main is outside, on the street.

The spokesperson said a hazmat unit and police are also on the scene, and there will be traffic delays in the area as the leak is fixed.

World.title: Business confidence jumps despite Middle East conflict uncertainty
World.content:
Business confidence improves despite Middle East conflict uncertainty

Net 40 percent expect economic improvement vs +14 pct in June survey

Businesses report softer current demand, but expect bounce back in 2027

Further RBNZ rate rises expected

Inflation pressures weaker, steady profit expectations, investment and hiring improve

Business confidence has improved markedly despite the uncertainty of the US war with Iran and soft trading conditions as firms loom ahead to recovery, according to the latest NZ Institute of Economic Research's (NZIER) Quarterly Survey of Business Opinion (QSBO).

The closely followed survey, conducted during September showed a net 40 percent of firms expect general economic conditions to improve in coming months compared to a net 14 percent in the June quarter.

It was the highest level of optimism in more than a year.

"While the impact of developments in the Middle East on sentiment appears muted for now, ongoing uncertainties over geopolitical conditions and global oil supply remain a headwind for New Zealand's economic recovery over the coming year," NZIER said in a commentary.

Firms' own trading activity was a shade weaker in the quarter, with a net 1 percent reporting worse business.

However, businesses were more optimistic about demand in the next quarter, with 15 percent expecting better trading from 11 percent in the previous survey.

Broad based confidence

Principal economist Christina Leung said the improvement in sentiment was broad based across all sectors.

"The retail sector is feeling particularly upbeat ... despite a fall in new orders and sales."

NZIER senior economist Christina Leung. SUPPLIED / NZIER

Leung said a factor in firms being upbeat despite current conditions might be firms becoming desensitised to fuel price rises, and a feeling that "things can only get better".

The building sector was also more upbeat, with positive reading still from manufacturers and service industries.

Overall firms were more inclined to invest and to hire, although finding skilled labour was re-emerging as an issue.

Inflation pressures softer

Leung said the survey suggested a weakening of inflation pressures.

Firms reporting higher costs fell to 47 percent from 54 percent, while those expecting to increase prices eased to 43 percent from 54 percent.

"Overall, these results suggest a reduced risk of inflation remaining elevated over the coming year," Leung said.

She said said the survey suggested flat growth in the economy over the quarter.

World.title: Election 2026: National promises to cut foreign aid to boost Pharmac's budget, cancer screenings
World.content:
The National Party wants to redirect foreign aid money into funding for new medicines, if it leads the next government.

Leader Christopher Luxon and health spokesperson Simeon Brown announced the policy - that touches on the turf of both its coalition partners - at a cancer treatment room in a private hospital in Epsom, Auckland on Tuesday.

Brown said National had "put patients back at the heart of the health system", delivering the "largest ever boost for new medicines" and expanding free screening nationwide.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406325306112

"Now we want to go further, getting more medicines to Kiwis and catching cancer early, when it is most treatable."

Luxon said National believed that "we should put our country and our people first".

"Make no apology for that choice. New Zealanders facing cancer and other serious illnesses should be prioritised ahead of overseas aid expenditure."

A re-elected National Government would:

Deliver a further $604 million uplift in Pharmac's medicines budget;

Turn responsible fiscal management into more medicines by reducing foreign aid outside the Pacific and making MFAT more efficient;

Set a national target for clinical trials in New Zealand;

Unlock CAR-T cell therapy

Brown said National wanted to invest a further $604m to help Pharmac fund more new medicines and widen access to those already funded.

"We will largely pay for it by reducing foreign aid and associated administration costs by 10 percent, while fully protecting aid to the Pacific."

The total investment cost came to $823.8m including $41.5m in capital spending.

That would be offset by a $431.2m reduction in foreign aid spending, making for a $351.1m total dent in operating budgets.

Brown said New Zealanders were "generous people" but National believed more of their "hard-earned" money should be spent at home, rather than being sent offshore.

Clinical trials and CAR-T would also give New Zealanders access to "cutting-edge treatments," he said, often earlier than they would be available otherwise.

"For someone facing cancer or a rare disorder, that can mean real hope when other options have run out."

Asked if he had spoken to Winston Peters about a potential reduction in foreign aid, Luxon demurred.

"No, it's a National Party policy, but it's very clear to us we want to make this big commitment on medicines. Drugs ... has been a big part of our programme, and where we've put a lot of investment in the last three years. We want to continue that work here."

On whether the policy would get past New Zealand First in coalition negotiations, he said they would "cross that bridge when we get there".

"I mean, as you know, between now and November 7th, I'm making the case very strongly: I want everybody to party vote National. I want National government, I want National ministers, I want National policies, I want as many National ministers around that Cabinet table as possible."

A re-elected National Government would also:

Lower the free bowel screening age to 50 by 2029;

Complete the free breast screening extension to age 74 by 2029;

Launch new screening pilots for prostate and lung cancer;

Deliver free cervical screening for all women aged 25 to 69 from March 2027;

Establish the Healthy Kiwis Programme, offering active prescriptions;

National had lowered the bowel screening age twice already, from 60 to 58 and then to 56.

Brown said "this election is going to be very tight, and the choice could not be clearer".

World.title: Remembering the lost Chinese market gardens that once fed Auckland
World.content:
Located beside Auckland Domain, the Carlaw Park Student Village in Parnell is a cluster of seven residential buildings housing about 700 University of Auckland students.

Each day, students stream between the village and the campus nearby with little indication of what once occupied the land beneath the concrete and glass.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406226404112

More than a century ago, this part of central Auckland was home to market gardens cultivated by Chinese migrants whose labour helped feed the city and became part of Auckland's largely overlooked urban history.

This history has been brought back into focus during this year's Auckland Heritage Festival, which runs from 26 September to 11 October.

Under the theme "Taste of Tāmaki," the festival explores the history and heritage of food and beverages across the city, including the story of Chinese market gardening in central Auckland and the role migrant growers played in feeding a rapidly expanding city.

Ruth Lam visits Carlaw Park Student Village in Parnell during a tour around the former site of a Chinese market garden. RNZ / Yiting Lin

Ruth Lam, an Auckland historian and co-author of Sons of the Soil: Chinese Market Gardeners in New Zealand, said newspaper reports suggested Chinese growers were establishing market gardens in Auckland by the 1870s.

Some of the earliest Chinese market gardeners, she said, were former gold miners who had travelled north from the South Island as the goldfields declined.

Others came directly from China in search of work and income.

Many were single men, while others were married men who had left their wives and children in China.

Lam said Auckland's fertile soil, growing population and access to customers were among the main reasons Chinese growers chose to settle and work in the city.

Chinese market gardens line Khyber Pass Road in Auckland. Queen Street merchant James Ah Kew established vegetable gardens in the area in 1875. (Image has been cropped for publication.) Supplied / Auckland Libraries Heritage Collections, 7-A04654

Central Auckland looked very different in the late 19th century from the urban centre it was today, she said.

Much of the area consisted of scattered streets and roads surrounded by farmland and undeveloped land.

"The first gardens were in areas where there were patches of land," Lam said.

"[Sites] at Khyber Pass, Newmarket, Parnell, down by Mechanics Bay, where it was all industrial area, and the Domain was just bare land."

Chinese gardeners stand in a market garden on Great North Road, Western Springs, in the early 1900s. (Image has been cropped for publication.) Supplied / Auckland Libraries Heritage Collections, 80-BIN185, Photographer / E C Binns
